# Boards used in competition

This page describes board dimensions across competition stages and explains their implications for the existing renderer and game core.

A board's side length affects the amount of information a player remembers, the physical area occupied by the cards and the range of face designs visible in that game. These are related consequences of one numeric size. They are separate from the actual arrangement of those faces, which is discussed in competition deals.

## Dimensions by stage

Competition uses a subset of the sizes already supported by the solo game. Quarterfinals are played on 4x4, semifinals on 6x6 and finals on 8x8. There is no new board geometry involved: each is an existing square grid handled by the current deck and board components.

| Stage | Side length | Cards | Face pairs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Quarterfinal | 4 | 16 | 8 |
| Semifinal | 6 | 36 | 18 |
| Final | 8 | 64 | 32 |

The number of cards is the square of the side length, and each face occurs twice. Moving from the smallest board in this table to the largest multiplies the card count by four. This is a meaningful increase in the amount of visible space and remembered information even though the input model remains familiar.

The stage vocabulary itself belongs to competition rounds. The board currently loaded in the solo application has no stage. A person choosing a size from the ordinary select is choosing a board dimension; there is no current competition context attached to that action.

## Existing support in the core

`GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts` is `[4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16]`. The three dimensions used here are members of that existing list. `isValidSize` checks membership in this list, and `parseBoardCode` uses that check when validating a code.

`generateBoard` creates `size ** 2` positions and initializes their face values with `Math.floor(index / 2)` before shuffling. Consequently the boards above contain face ranges 0–7, 0–17 and 0–31 respectively. A larger board expands the face set rather than merely repeating the small board's faces more often.

`createGame` spreads the generated board into `GameState`. `isWon` compares the number of matched positions with the length of the deck. Neither function branches on an event stage. The game core can therefore represent every board in the table without any competition-specific completion calculation.

`src/game/completion.test.ts` exercises completion at every supported side length. It builds the face pairs from the generated deck and activates both positions of each pair. The core's completion behavior already covers these sizes; the stage-to-size connection is a separate competition rule.

## What the larger face set actually changes

The visual identity comes from `src/game/board/face-design.ts`. The shape is selected by face number modulo eight. Marker direction is selected from the next group of eight, and the outline variant begins at face 64. The game has a total of 128 face designs.

All face numbers used by the boards in this page are below 64, so they use the solid variant. The smallest board contains the eight shapes with the top marker. The middle board includes additional marker directions, and the largest reaches through four marker groups. This gives reviewers a more precise explanation of increasing visual complexity than saying only that there are more cards.

For instance, the circle shape can appear with different marker directions on a larger board. Recognizing a familiar outline of a shape is therefore less informative than recognizing the full face. The player-facing introduction in `Game.tsx` mentions shape and marker for this reason. The deck still compares face numbers; it does not award a partial match for two similar shapes.

Face catalogue, pair identity and card artwork cover those distinctions in depth. They are useful when a playtest report says that two cards looked alike and an engineer needs to determine whether the report concerns face design, remembered position or a misunderstood pair.

## Board dimensions in the layout

`src/game/board/Board.tsx` sets the CSS custom property `--grid-size` from `game.size`. The grid uses that value in its column definition. It does not choose a separate component for a larger stage, and its card keys are position indices.

In `board.css`, `--card-min` is 44px, `--card-max` is 88px and `--card-gap` is 6px. At the minimum card width, the grid content widths for side lengths 4, 6 and 8 are 194px, 294px and 394px. These figures exclude the scroll container's padding and border. They are arithmetic from the current CSS, not additional size targets.

The viewport has `overflow: auto`, `max-width: 100%` and a maximum height of `min(70dvh, 768px)`. Its grid width is clamped between the minimum and maximum card-based widths. This means the presence of scrolling depends on the available space as well as the selected side length. A desktop screenshot cannot establish what the same board feels like on a held phone.

This matters in a shared setting because the device changes orientation and viewing position as it is passed around. A board that fits comfortably on a laptop may involve local scrolling on a narrower device. The existing layout accounts for overflow; the competition stage mapping does not supply a replacement layout. See large board rendering, layout grid and zoom behaviour.

## Positions remain positions

The core uses zero-based row-order indices. The card's accessible name uses a one-based row and column, computed in `src/game/board/card-state.ts`. At size 6, index 17 is row 3, column 6. At size 8, the same numeric index is row 3, column 2. A position number has meaning in the context of its board size.

This is an easy source of misleading manual notes. A researcher can write down “card 17” while watching one board and later open a different size. Without the board context, the note no longer identifies the same visible location. Board codes carry the side length; a loose position number does not.

Keyboard movement also uses the size directly. `navigationTarget` calculates row boundaries and vertical destinations from the current side length, stopping at edges. The number of columns changes the distance represented by an up or down move, while the underlying arrow-key interaction remains the same. Board keyboard navigation covers the existing behavior.

## Review notes and unresolved presentation choices

The important existing distinction is between a size being technically supported and a stage selecting that size. The ordinary `Controls` component renders all seven values from `GRID_SIZES` and delegates changes to `newGame`. It contains no awareness of the stage mapping on this page. A prototype that simply surrounds those controls with competition text has not made that mapping part of its controller.

How that context is presented during a group session remains a separate design subject. The board dimensions for the stages use the existing size support in the source.

One useful comparison in a visual review is the same board early and late in play, at the same viewport width. That isolates the change in exposed artwork from the change in grid dimensions. A second comparison across the three dimensions then makes the actual growth visible. The two comparisons answer different questions and avoid attributing every difficulty on a larger board to its card count alone.
# Competition deals

This page explains deal identity in competition and the existing board-code machinery that can reproduce an arrangement.

The current engine already has a precise way to identify a starting puzzle. A board code describes its generation version, side length and seed. That identity is useful when comparing what people played, investigating an apparent discrepancy or distinguishing a fresh attempt from restored progress.

## Deal identity within an event

A match has a deal identity as well as the identities of its participants. Both players of a match play one board code, and every match in a tournament has a different board code. The identity in that sentence is the complete board code, rather than only the final numeric part or a screenshot of the visible board.

For example, a match associated with `np1-4-73` refers to the arrangement generated by that full string. A later match using `np1-4-74` has a different code. `np1-6-73` is also a different code from the first example: its side length differs even though its seed number is the same. These examples illustrate code identity without introducing a new competition-specific code format.

The distinction between board identity and progress is just as important. A hidden starting board, a board with several pairs exposed and a completed board can all have the same `boardCode`. They are different game states on the same deal. A screen showing more exposed faces does not, by itself, show that a different board was loaded.

## The format already implemented

`src/game/deck.ts` defines the version as `np1`. A code has the form `np1-N-seed`, where `N` is a supported side length and the seed is between 1 and 2147483646 inclusive. The parser accepts decimal notation without leading zeros. It returns the parsed size and seed or `null`.

`boardCode(size, seed)` constructs a string and validates it through `parseBoardCode`, throwing for invalid input. `generateBoard(code)` parses the code, constructs a deck with each face twice and shuffles it. The returned board object and deck array are frozen. There is no participant input in this process.

The exact grammar is in board code format; the fixed generation algorithm is in deck generation. Competition uses this existing deal identity. It does not acquire a new generation algorithm merely because a group is taking part.

The browser entry path has a small distinction from the pure parser. `loadBoard` in `src/game/session/use-game.ts` trims surrounding whitespace before parsing. The parser itself does not perform that trim. This can explain why pasting a code into the UI succeeds while directly passing the same whitespace-bearing string to a core function fails.

## Why a code repeats an arrangement

The deterministic generator begins with the supplied seed. Each state update multiplies by 16807 and takes the remainder modulo 2147483647. The deck starts with consecutive pairs of face numbers, then the shuffle walks backward through its positions and swaps with a selected earlier position or itself.

The bounded draw uses rejection rather than simply applying a remainder to every possible generator output. `SEED_MAX` is the draw range; the accepted interval is the largest multiple of the current bound within that range. A value outside that interval advances the generator again. Those details are part of the existing generation version.

The published example `np1-4-1` produces `[6, 7, 0, 5, 2, 2, 0, 5, 3, 7, 1, 6, 4, 4, 1, 3]`. In that deck, positions 0 and 11 contain face 6. That gives a reviewer a literal check independent of what a screenshot seems to show.

`src/game/deck.test.ts` checks published vectors and each supported size. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements an independent reading using BigInt arithmetic. The independent calculation is particularly helpful when an issue concerns an arrangement: calling the production generator twice demonstrates repeatability, but does not alone show agreement with the specification.

## Freshness is narrower in the current session

The ordinary fresh-deal path is `freshBoardCode` in `src/game/session/fresh-board.ts`. It obtains a value from `crypto.getRandomValues`, rejects draws outside its accepted range and converts the result to a valid seed. When supplied a previous seed, it rejects that seed as well.

`newGame` passes the current game's seed to that function. It prevents the immediate replacement from reusing the previous seed, but it supplies no collection of earlier codes. A sequence can therefore revisit an older seed after an intervening game. The helper has no event memory and no match context.

That is the relevant implementation gap for the rule on this page. A large seed range makes a collision unusual in casual play, but probability is not a record of which codes an event has already used. A mockup that repeatedly invokes the existing New Game action has not demonstrated the event-wide property merely because the first few generated strings differ.

The project has no prescribed allocation strategy. Tracking used full codes and considering candidate codes is one possible design direction; preselecting a set is another. Neither approach is implemented in the game.

## Starting state and saved progress

`createGame(code)` produces a game with no matched positions, a closed selection, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false`. The board description and deck come from `generateBoard(code)`. Calling it again with the same code constructs a fresh game over the same arrangement.

`decodeSnapshot`, by contrast, reconstructs the deal and restores validated progress. Its returned state can include matched positions, a revealed card or a pending mismatch. A snapshot carrying the correct code is therefore not automatically evidence that an attempt began from the initial hidden state. Snapshot format and snapshot selection notes explain those existing fields.

The same distinction appears in the UI. Restart reconstructs the current code through `createGame`. New Game obtains a fresh candidate first. Load board parses an entered code and starts its initial state. Load snapshot restores progress. These controls share some replacement machinery but do not describe the same operation.

## What reproducibility can establish

A code can establish the arrangement produced by the documented generator. It does not establish who was holding the device, whether someone had watched earlier play or how long the group spent discussing the screen before an attempt. Those are social observations, outside the content of the code.

During an investigation, a full board code is more precise than “the small board” or a seed copied without its size. A snapshot can add the state at the moment of interest. A replay can add timed actions. None of these existing artifacts carries a competition participant model. Their usefulness comes from the game information they actually encode.

Sharing FAQ explains the ordinary tools, and competition research explains why reproducibility alone does not settle every concern raised around a shared screen.
# Comparing tied competition results

This page describes competition result comparison and explains the active-time information available from the current game.

A result comparison uses information from completed play. The game core can tell whether a board is complete and can expose its moves and elapsed time. It does not compare two participants or contain a bracket seed, so the competition decision here sits outside the current single-game transitions.

## Comparison order

Moves are the first useful distinction between two completed attempts, but they can be equal. When both players of a match finish in the same number of moves, the lower active time wins, and if that is also equal the higher seed wins. Seed 1 is the highest seed. The comparison is ordered: an earlier distinction settles the result before a later one is considered.

These example results illustrate the first two levels. The elapsed values are milliseconds in game data.

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ada | 12 | 70200 | Ahead on moves |
| Bo | 13 | 58100 | Faster, but more moves |

| Participant | Moves | Active elapsed milliseconds | Result in this example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cora | 15 | 65200 | Ahead on active time |
| Dev | 15 | 65900 | Same moves, greater active time |

The examples deliberately separate efficiency from speed. An implementation that adds moves and seconds together, or sorts by time first, would produce a different comparison. There is no weighted combined score in the existing core or in the decision above.

## When every recorded value looks equal

Two equal move counts and equal active times lead to the seed branch described above.

A fixture with two completely equal game results exercises the seed branch, whereas examples with unequal times never reach it. Competition pairing supplies the bracket context.

The seed settles the equality case without an extra round of play, shared outcome or random choice. The existing code knows nothing about an opponent or an entrant's seed.

## Active time in the current game

`GameState.elapsedMs` is advanced by `advanceGame` in `src/game/game.ts`. That function does nothing before play has started or after `isWon` becomes true. The first valid reveal sets `started: true`; ignored activations do not create another start event.

In the browser, `src/game/session/use-session-clock.ts` observes `performance.now()`. Its `running()` check combines visibility, pause state, the started flag and completion. `elapsedStep` in `browser-clock.ts` calculates the interval since the previous observation and contributes it only when active. This is elapsed active play, not a stopwatch started when the HTML file was opened.

The clock hook synchronizes before applying a card activation. As a result, the final valid activation is evaluated after accounting for the elapsed interval leading up to it. The source comment on snapshot export also points out that rendered state can trail the clock, which is why export synchronizes before encoding.

The 40ms scheduling constant is an update cadence, not the unit of the stored elapsed value. `performance.now()` can return fractional milliseconds, and the core preserves positive finite deltas. `browser-clock.test.ts` exercises fractional values and compares many observations with one observation over the same overall span.

## Display precision is a separate concern

`formatElapsed` in `src/game/elapsed-time.ts` discards sub-second detail for presentation. It is therefore possible for two visibly identical clock strings to correspond to different `elapsedMs` values. A screenshot of the ordinary status area cannot establish exact equality of active time.

The example with Cora and Dev demonstrates this issue: their stored times differ by 700ms even though a coarser presentation can hide that difference. Reading the rendered text back into a result comparison would throw away information the game already holds.

Snapshot serialization changes precision too, although less dramatically. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` to a whole millisecond. It rounds a pending mismatch's remaining interval upward so that interval remains representable. The game in memory may have fractional time that the snapshot no longer contains.

Current in-memory values, exported values and visible text have different precision, so an implementation review needs to identify which representation a prototype actually compares. Treating these as interchangeable would make exact equality depend on an undocumented conversion.

## Pauses and interruptions

The current browser session excludes hidden-page time and time spent waiting for Resume after an unfinished snapshot import. It does not offer an ordinary manual pause control. Sitting with the visible started board while talking still contributes active elapsed time, even when no cards are activated during that conversation.

A miss also contributes time. The two exposed nonmatching faces remain visible for 800 active milliseconds, during which activation is blocked. That wait is part of the same active timeline as elapsed play. Hiding the page pauses both the elapsed clock and the remaining mismatch interval.

These facts explain some apparent discrepancies in human timing. An observer measuring from the moment the device is handed over will include time before the first reveal. A wall stopwatch will include time while the page is hidden. A person looking only at clicks may overlook the visible thinking intervals between them. Those observations can all differ from `elapsedMs` without demonstrating a clock defect.

Elapsed time rules, clock design and mismatch interval describe the existing mechanisms.

## Completion and boundary values

`isWon` checks whether matched positions cover the deck. Before that condition holds, a board can have many matched pairs and a plausible-looking move count while still being unfinished. A current status reading is not equivalent to a completed result merely because the player has stopped interacting.

The core caps moves at 999999 and elapsed time at 359999999ms. Matching and completion continue at those caps. These limits can increase the number of equal numeric values in artificial boundary fixtures. They do not create an uncapped hidden counter from which a comparison could recover a distinction.

`src/game/move-cap.test.ts` covers completion at the move boundary. The browser and core clock tests cover elapsed behavior separately. Those tests are evidence about single-game values; there is no competition result comparator test in the current source.

## Useful evidence for a disagreement

A disputed outcome can involve several separate questions: whether both attempts completed, which values were captured, how those values were compared and whether the participants understood the result. A screenshot may help with the last question, but it is weak evidence for sub-second equality. A snapshot gives structured game values but applies the integer export precision described above.

A replay can reconstruct card actions on a logical active timeline. In the current core it begins with a code, advances time before each action and advances again to its ending timestamp. It provides no record of the human circumstances around those actions. Replay format explains the available evidence without turning it into a competition log.

For a prototype review, the move-first example, the time-second example and an exact-equality example exercise distinct branches. Together they are more informative than many examples where one participant is better on every measure. They also make comparison errors visible before a polished result screen hides them.

# Module layout policy

This page explains how Neon Pairs places behavior in the source tree and how to extend that structure without obscuring the game rules.

The current tree is small enough to read directly. It has no application framework around the game, no route hierarchy and no general service container. `src/main.tsx` mounts `Game`; the application then divides into rule functions, a session adapter and components for the board, controls and status. Source layout is the file inventory. This page explains the choices behind it.

## Follow behavior before file type

The board directory contains `Board.tsx`, `Card.tsx`, `Face.tsx`, navigation helpers, card descriptions, face design, styles and focused tests. Its contents answer a coherent set of questions: how a position is presented, how focus moves and how a face becomes visible. A separate top-level directory for every hook, type or stylesheet would make those questions harder to answer.

The session directory has a different responsibility. It connects rules to React state, browser observations and saved preferences. A feature lives in src/game/FEATURE/, and its rules live in src/game/FEATURE/rules.ts, which imports neither React nor any browser global. That placement gives a reader a predictable starting point for a feature's decisions, with the integration code close enough to inspect alongside them.

This convention applies to feature work; existing behaviors also use other filenames. The current core is in `game.ts`, `deck.ts`, `selection.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts` and `replay.ts` directly under `src/game`. The board already uses focused names such as `keyboard.ts` and `card-state.ts`.

## The dependency direction

The central rules know about game data. `game.ts` imports the deck generator and the selection union. It does not import `Game.tsx`, `Board.tsx` or the session hook. `snapshot.ts` rebuilds and validates a game using those same definitions. `replay.ts` applies logical advances and activations to a game without rendering it.

The session layer points inward. `session.ts` calls `activateCard`, `advanceGame`, `createGame` and `isWon`, then adds session feedback, import pause state and best-score decisions. `use-game.ts` provides callable actions to components. The UI receives values and actions; it does not become the only place where a legal turn can be computed.

There are intentional lateral imports. `storage.ts` uses `GRID_SIZES` and `MOVES_MAX` to validate preferences against actual game limits. `card-state.ts` uses `faceDesign` to describe a visible face. These relationships connect meanings that genuinely belong together. They do not form a general helpers layer with unrelated operations.

A useful way to inspect an unfamiliar change is to start at its public behavior and follow direct imports toward the core. A card click leads through the controller to `activateSession` and `activateCard`. A loaded snapshot leads through `decodeSnapshot`, `readMatched` and `readSelection`. The direction remains visible because there are no barrel files hiding which definition is used.

## State is divided by meaning

`GameState` extends the board description with matched positions, the current selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and a start flag. It does not store a focus position or a form draft. The board description includes its code, size, seed and deck. `generateBoard` freezes the description and deck at runtime, while the TypeScript interfaces expose readonly fields.

`Session` wraps that game with `paused`, `generation`, `feedback`, `loadNotice`, `announcement`, `celebration` and `preferences`. A generation identifies a replacement deal. It is not a move count and does not belong in a snapshot. Feedback belongs here because turn results and imports need session-level presentation, while replay needs only the final game state.

The board hook owns its remembered focused index. `Reproduction` owns the textarea draft. `BoardCodeForm` uses an uncontrolled input initialized from the current code, with its generation key causing a fresh input on replacement. These values have useful local lifetimes. Moving them into `GameState` would make serialization and rule transitions depend on presentation details.

## Splitting a file

Technology specification T06 sets an aim of 100 lines and a ceiling of 200 authored TypeScript lines per file. The source audit checks the ceiling across `src`, `scripts`, `tests` and `art`. The aim is a reading aid, not a reason to scatter every function into a separate module.

The current snapshot split is instructive. `snapshot.ts` owns the outer format, byte bound, numeric fields, serialization and consistency checks. `snapshot-selection.ts` owns the nested selection and matched-position interpretation. Both operate on the same domain, but their validation tasks are distinct enough to read independently. `saved-format.ts` holds the small operations actually shared by snapshot, replay and preferences.

The clock split follows a different seam. `browser-clock.ts` performs arithmetic on supplied observations. `use-session-clock.ts` owns observation, scheduling, visibility and cleanup. Splitting those by arbitrary line count would lose the reason for the boundary. Clock design follows the interaction in detail.

A file can stay short while still carrying several unrelated concerns. Conversely, a dense type and a straightforward exhaustive branch may reasonably live together. The existing architecture asks for splitting by behavior, so a review considers what a reader would need to understand together before considering the final line count.

## Imports expose the owner

The source uses static ESM imports with `.ts` and `.tsx` suffixes. Types are imported with `import type` or an inline `type` marker. `use-game.ts` imports the snapshot decoder directly from `../snapshot.ts`; it does not import an application-wide registry. `Controls.tsx` imports `GRID_SIZES` from `../deck.ts`, where supported sizes are defined.

That directness matters when a symbol changes. `SelectionKind` is the owner of the selection discriminants; both rules and validators use it. `MISMATCH_MS` is defined beside turn resolution and imported where an interval bound is needed. A second constant with the same current number would hide a semantic disagreement until a later change.

The source convention tests also inspect exported values. They look for an importer for every recognized export and a single owner for each recognized exported constant name. This is a lightweight check, not a complete module system. Its practical effect is to discourage speculative public helpers and ambiguous exported constants. Source audit notes describes the exact text patterns and their limitations.

## Components and their adjacent styles

Component imports make stylesheet ownership explicit. `Game.tsx` imports `game.css`; `Board.tsx` imports `board.css`; `Card.tsx` imports `card.css`; the controls share `control.css` and add their own layout sheets. These are global CSS files, not generated CSS modules. Adjacency helps locate a selector, but it does not automatically scope one.

A board change can therefore involve both a local sheet and root styling. `board.css` defines `.board-viewport`, whose geometry is consumed by focus scrolling. `game.css` defines the global focus outline and the page width. Reading only the nearest stylesheet is sometimes insufficient. CSS organization traces these dependencies without turning visual requirements into module rules.

## Test support and application support

`game.fixture.ts` supplies a documented example code, a literal deck, its pairs and specification vectors. Application modules do not import it. Browser support in `tests/game-fixture.ts` loads a fixed board through the reproduction controls. `tests/deal-oracle.ts` implements the documented shuffle with BigInt arithmetic so the browser suite can reason about deals independently.

The separate `art` entries reuse application components but remain separate builds. `art/face-sheet.tsx` renders the real card component for each face. `art/session/session-harness.tsx` mounts the game beside an unmount button so teardown can be measured. Neither entry is imported by `src/main.tsx`.

That distinction explains why a helper can be useful without belonging in the shipped game. A fixture has permission to know the complete fixed deck. A hidden card in the application receives `null` instead of its face until revealed. Moving diagnostic knowledge into runtime code would bypass that deliberate presentation boundary.

## Examples of placement decisions

A correction to arrow-key edge behavior belongs first in `board/keyboard.ts`, which computes a target index from an index, size, key and modifiers. Its React caller translates a target into DOM focus. A change to the scroll behavior belongs in the hook or `nearest-scroll.ts`, because it concerns the browser's focus and scrolling behavior. Neither change calls for a new game-state field.

A correction to imported mismatch validity belongs in `snapshot-selection.ts`; a change to the loading pause belongs in `session.ts` or `use-game.ts`. They may share a user journey, but they answer different questions: whether the submitted data describes a valid game and how the browser enters that valid game.

A turn-count defect belongs in `activateCard`. The displayed statistic and exported snapshot already consume its result. Fixing the number in `GameStatus` would leave replay, completion and storage observing the old value. These examples are consequences of the existing structure, not extra parallel implementations.

For review, Code review guide starts from the behavior changed and follows these seams. For the larger rationale, Architecture remains the specification of the core, browser session and component boundaries.
# Persistence overview

This page explains the small amount of browser data Neon Pairs saves and the boundary between remembered preferences and an active game.

The game has one application storage key, `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. Its value remembers the selected board size and the lowest completed move count for each size with a record. It does not contain a saved game. Reloading the page reads those preferences and creates a fresh deal at the remembered size. This is the most useful distinction to establish before investigating a report that something disappeared.

## The durable part of a visit

`src/game/session/storage.ts` defines the persistence data and its reader and writer. The in-memory `Preferences` interface has two properties: `size`, a number, and `bestMoves`, a read-only mapping from size strings to move counts. The writer adds `schemaVersion: 1` when serializing it. A representative stored value is:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":6,"bestMoves":{"4":9,"6":20}}
```

Here the next page load starts a new 6x6 game. The best displayed while playing that size is 20. Choosing 4x4 exposes the independent best of 9. There is no record for 8x8, so the status displays `none` for that size. The selected size does not have to be the only size represented in the score map.

The list of supported side lengths comes from `GRID_SIZES` in `src/game/deck.ts`: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16. `DEFAULT_SIZE` uses the first entry, currently 4. A missing or rejected preference value therefore produces a playable 4x4 start with an empty score map. Storage is useful for continuity between visits, but the game does not depend on it to construct a board or resolve a turn.

See Preferences store for the exact validation and React effect. Best score records covers the gameplay meaning of the numbers rather than the browser mechanism that holds them.

## What remains in this page's memory

The active session includes the game, pause state, session generation, feedback, load notice, announcement counter, celebration flag and preferences. Only the preference portion reaches `writePreferences`. The session's game contains the board description, deck, matched positions, selection, moves, active elapsed time and started flag. None of that game progress is automatically written to browser storage.

This has several visible consequences:

- Reloading during a mismatch produces a fresh board rather than restoring the two exposed cards.
- Reloading after a win retains an eligible best, but it does not restore the completed board or its banner.
- Restart repeats the current deal only within the active session. Reload is a separate operation and starts a fresh deal.
- A loaded snapshot can change the remembered size even though its matched cards and elapsed time will disappear on reload.
- A draft in the reproduction controls is not a browser save. Typing text there does not itself create a durable preference change.

These are ordinary consequences of the data boundary, rather than separate recovery modes. A screenshot showing a nonzero move count says nothing about whether that count was stored. A storage dump showing a best says nothing about the last board code. For progress transfer, the explicit snapshot controls are the relevant tool; see Snapshot format and Reproduction panel.

## When preferences change

`useGame` obtains a browser store once through `useState(browserStore)`. Its session initializer calls `readPreferences(store)` and then `initialSession(freshBoardCode(preferences.size), preferences)`. The size affects board creation, while the score map is retained alongside the new game. `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)` connects that object to the writer after rendering.

Replacing a game goes through `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts`. It makes a new preference object with `size: game.size`, preserving the existing score map. This path is shared by changing size, New Game, Restart, a valid board-code load and a valid snapshot load. Consequently, replacing a game can cause a preference write even when the selected size has not numerically changed. The effect follows object identity; it does not compare serialized strings.

Invalid board-code and snapshot loads take an earlier exit. They update feedback through `notice`, leaving preferences alone. A rejected draft therefore does not alter the last accepted size. The browser test `valid board loads save their size while invalid loads keep that preference` exercises this distinction with a valid 6x6 board followed by invalid text and a reload.

During ordinary turns, the session continues carrying the same preferences object. On completion through card activation, `activateSession` calls `rememberBest`. A first result for a size or a strictly better result makes a new score map and preference object. Equal and worse counts return the original preference object. Clock ticks and intermediate reveals change game state without scheduling preference writes merely because time or moves changed.

## Why the stored value stays small

The preferences answer two recurring questions: which size did this browser use, and what is its best completed move count for this size? They can answer both without retaining every attempt. There is no attempt log, record timestamp, saved deck, player identity, sound option or theme preference in the current schema. There is also no automatic snapshot written on every move or on page exit.

This keeps browser effects out of game rules. `rememberBest` is a pure transformation; the session decides when it applies, and the hook performs the browser write later. Storage denial cannot stop a match, because matching does not ask storage for permission or wait for a successful write. A page can remain fully playable with the store represented by `null`.

The small payload also limits synchronous work. `localStorage` uses a synchronous API, but this implementation serializes a compact aggregate instead of the whole active board repeatedly. It does not store artwork, assets or the distribution HTML there. Offline delivery comes from the built file, not from browser preference storage. Offline delivery describes that separate concern.

## Locality and lifetime

The storage belongs to the browser context and origin that opened the game. A second browser profile has its own data. A different HTTP port can put an otherwise identical build in another origin. Moving between direct disk delivery and a local HTTP address is therefore not a reliable way to carry preferences over. The technology specification uses a local HTTP origin for saved-preference checks because disk URL storage behavior varies.

The app does not synchronize preference changes between open tabs. Each tab reads its initial value and then writes its own in-memory aggregate. One tab can overwrite another tab's changes; the specification explicitly leaves several simultaneous game windows outside the supported journeys.

Browser policy, explicit site-data deletion and private-session cleanup can also end a stored value's lifetime. The app has no server copy from which to recover it. Private browsing notes and Storage quota notes separate these environmental issues from the application's own replacement behavior.

## Reading this group of pages

The existing preference representation is older than the feature-level storage conventions described in Persistence envelope. The existing writer continues to emit the preference aggregate. Likewise, Retention policy concerns saved lists; the current best-score map is an aggregate, not an attempt list.

For failures, begin with the operation that failed. Accessing `window.localStorage`, reading a key, parsing its string and writing a replacement are distinct stages. Storage failure policy covers unavailable storage and the feature behavior built around it. Corrupt data policy covers values that can be read but cannot be accepted. Both cases lead to usable in-memory state, but their evidence and timing differ.

Storage testing guide maps the unit and browser evidence to the boundary being investigated. It also explains how a served origin, isolated context and operation-specific store double make a persistence report reproducible.
# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See Format versioning guide and Data exchange policy when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

Preferences store documents the complete aggregate reader. Persistence overview explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks

`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.

The object checks are structural, not class checks. `isJsonObject` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` accepts an object if it is non-null and not an array. That helper alone says nothing about which fields are present. The reader supplies the field-specific checks after narrowing the parsed value.

There is a useful asymmetry here. Snapshot validation has an exact-key helper available in the shared format module, but the preference reader does not call it. Extra top-level preference properties are ignored if the fields the reader uses are valid. A successful read returns a freshly constructed `Preferences` value containing only `size` and the validated score map. The current preference format accepts extra top-level properties.

The feature envelope's boundary should not be inferred from that lenience. Its stated outer shape is its own contract. A convenience helper existing nearby does not decide which parser uses it or what a particular version accepts.

## Version labels answer different questions

The project has a product specification version, a preference schema version and explicit interchange format versions. They are not one counter. The current specification identifies itself as 2.2 while the preference discriminator remains 1. A feature envelope uses the numeric version described in its own boundary. A board code's prefix describes its generation algorithm rather than the layout of browser preference JSON.

Keeping those meanings distinct avoids a common support mistake: assuming a newer app release must reject every older saved object. The preferences are accepted according to `PREFERENCES_VERSION` and field validation. The product release number is not read from storage, compared to storage or written into the preference object.

There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.

## A value moves through several representations

It helps to follow one ordinary preference update from the UI rather than treating storage as a single operation. Selecting a different grid size creates a new game. `replaceGame` copies the session preferences and changes `size` to the new board's side length. React renders using that state. The save effect then calls `writePreferences`, which constructs the versioned object, serializes it and passes the string to the supplied store.

The domain state is therefore not the same thing as the serialized object. `Preferences` has no `schemaVersion` field. The writer adds it at the boundary. The reader removes that boundary concern by returning a `Preferences` value with known fields. This is why callers can use `preferences.size` without repeatedly checking a schema version in components.

An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.

## Empty data and invalid data

An empty preference score map is valid. It means no supported size has a saved best in that aggregate. The selected size is still meaningful. By contrast, an absent score-map field, an array in its place, or a map with an impossible score invalidates the preference value. Missing storage and invalid storage reach the same fallback state through different branches.

For a feature collection, an empty array describes a collection with no records. Corrupt data policy deals with rejection and replacement; it is the place to examine how a failed read interacts with later saving.

Empty data should also be distinguished from unavailable storage. A reader can return an empty state after a denied read, but that return value alone does not prove that the browser is ready to accept a future write. In the preferences API, failure information is intentionally not returned to the caller. The feature failure presentation described in Storage failure policy consequently cannot be obtained just by inspecting an empty map.

## Inspecting a captured value

A useful investigation begins with the exact key and original string. A JavaScript object shown after parsing is already one transformation removed from the browser value. Parse failures depend on the text, while field failures depend on the parsed structure. Retaining the original string in an isolated reproduction makes these stages separable.

For preferences, compare the inner `schemaVersion` with `PREFERENCES_VERSION`, then the selected size with `GRID_SIZES`, then each score key and value with the reader's checks. A key spelled `04` is rejected even though converting it to a number yields 4. A score of 7 for a 4x4 board is rejected because eight pairs require at least eight moves. A value can be syntactically valid JSON while failing either of those semantic checks.

For a feature collection, inspect the outer representation before speculating about domain records. A test result for preference JSON is not evidence about feature-record acceptance. Stored values can share a storage mechanism while using different validators.

# Retention policy

This page explains retention for saved feature lists and contrasts it with the compact best-score aggregate in the current game.

Retention describes how much accepted data remains after a save. It is separate from parsing a malformed value, clearing site data in browser settings or losing a private browsing session. The game currently remembers one best move count per supported size rather than preserving individual completed attempts. A browser dump of those bests cannot reconstruct the order or number of games played.

## Saved lists

A list can grow as a feature saves additional records, even when every individual record is small. Its retention boundary applies during saving, rather than acting as an expiration clock while the player is idle. A stored list keeps its newest 10 records and drops older ones when a new record is saved. This bounds the retained collection while leaving the active interaction independent of an ever-growing history.

This rule concerns a saved list. It does not turn the existing `bestMoves` object into a history or add a timestamp to it. Record types, sort fields and tie-breaking conventions are separate from the amount retained. The preference store implements the best-score aggregate rather than a feature list.

The list representation is discussed in Persistence envelope. Parsing and validation failures are covered in Corrupt data policy, because retention of accepted records and recovery from rejected input are different operations.

## The current aggregate retains outcomes, not attempts

`Preferences.bestMoves` is a `Readonly<Record<string, number>>`. The key is the canonical decimal side length, such as `4` or `12`, and the value is the best completed move count for that size. The selected board size lives separately in `Preferences.size`. Selecting another size does not discard the previous size's best.

The supported set has seven entries. Once read validation has succeeded, the score map can therefore contain at most seven different supported size keys. It can also contain fewer, including none. This bound follows from `GRID_SIZES` and canonical key validation, not from trimming an attempt history. Multiple completed games at the same size compete for the same map entry.

For example, suppose a browser has a 4x4 best of 10. Finishing later in 9 moves replaces that one number. Finishing in 11 moves leaves 9 in place. Finishing in 9 moves again also leaves it in place. Those outcomes do not append three records; there is still only one 4x4 entry. Best score records explains the completion rule in gameplay terms.

The selected size can change while all best entries remain identical. A visit that chooses 16x16 and then reloads may store `size: 16` alongside a score map containing only a 4x4 result. That is a valid aggregate. The remembered preference describes the next board size, while the map describes earlier eligible completions.

## Why no clock drives current retention

The preference format contains no creation date, last-played time or expiry value. `readPreferences` does not inspect the current time. It cannot tell whether a valid best was written a minute ago or on a much earlier visit. There is no scheduled cleanup effect, idle purge or age-based deletion in `use-saved-preferences.ts`.

This makes the data easy to explain: a valid best remains available across normal reloads until another relevant event changes the storage or the value is rejected. A better result can replace it. Browser policy or a person's site-data action can remove it. Another tab can overwrite the aggregate. None of those is an application age policy.

The distinction matters when comparing evidence from two visits. A gap between visits does not by itself identify the cause of a missing best. If the origin changed, the second visit may have read another storage area. If the value was edited into an invalid shape, the reader may have used its fallback. If the browser cleared data, the key may simply be absent. Storage quota notes discusses environment-driven loss without treating it as list pruning.

## Save time is an application event

The preference writer runs from a React effect whose dependencies are the preferences object and store. This is not a page-exit flush. On initial mounting, the effect writes the current preference state. Later, a new preference object causes another effect run. There is no dependency on active elapsed milliseconds or every move in the game.

`replaceGame` always constructs a preference object with the new game's size. New Game and Restart consequently pass through a save-capable path even when the size value stays the same. Valid board-code and snapshot loads do so as well. Invalid loads update feedback without replacing preferences.

`rememberBest` returns the original object for equal or worse results. The session can still render a completed game, but the preference identity need not change. This keeps the storage effect aligned with meaningful preference updates in that path. It is not a universal deduplication layer: replacement actions can still write the same serialized preference contents again.

For list work, the save event named by the retention rule should be understood in the feature's own operation. The existing preference effect has no generic event log or timer that scans all browser keys. There is no central list manager in this source tree.

## Retained locally does not mean backed up

The app has no account or service that copies the aggregate elsewhere. A best kept in one profile remains local to that browser's storage context. Opening the same HTML in another browser does not fetch it. Exporting a snapshot copies game progress, not a backup of the browser's accumulated bests or selected-size history.

The UI has no general preference export, browser-data restore or clear-records control. A developer can inspect or change storage manually, but those are debugging actions rather than product controls.

## Retention and capacity are related, but different

A bounded collection makes its record count predictable. It does not guarantee every write succeeds: browser access can be blocked before capacity matters, and another application on the same origin may consume storage. A small value can fail to write even though its own size is well below a browser's nominal limit.

Conversely, a successful write does not prove indefinite lifetime. The browser can later clear data, a private context can end, or the person can remove site storage. Those environmental conditions are outside the saved-list retention operation. Private browsing notes describes how a value can survive a reload yet disappear when the browsing session ends.

The current score aggregate illustrates the same separation at a smaller scale. It has a naturally small set of keys and bounded integer values, yet `setItem` remains inside a `try` block. Capacity savings reduce the amount being written; they do not change the need to continue play if the browser refuses it.

## Checking retention with feature records

The existing test suite establishes preference behavior rather than a list API. `storage.test.ts` checks independent minimums for two sizes and object identity for equal and worse results. Browser journeys check that completed bests survive reloads and game resets. None of those tests asserts a sequence of saved feature records.

For a feature-list review, concrete before-and-after examples can expose the retention boundary without adding fields to the product format. Records can be identified by the already defined domain representation in that feature's tests. The useful observation is which accepted records are present after a save, compared with the preceding accepted collection. Examples can use the feature's existing record fields.

It is also useful to keep failed writes separate from successful retention checks. A denied store can leave the feature's in-memory state ahead of the browser value. Inspecting the old browser string then proves only that the write failed, not that the retention calculation chose the wrong records. Storage testing guide describes the store doubles that make this separation observable.

## What bests retain

The best map cannot answer how many attempts occurred, which deal produced a best, how long that attempt took, or whether two equal results happened on different days. None of those fields is retained. A new feature that needs a collection has a different persistence concern from calculating a size-specific minimum.

Keeping that distinction explicit avoids a misleading implementation shortcut: interpreting every best-map update as if it were an append to a historical list. The code's result is an aggregate with replacement semantics. The saved-list rule belongs to collections, while the current aggregate remains documented and tested according to its own source behavior.
# Storage failure policy

This page describes how unavailable browser storage affects play and how saved-record features present that limitation.

The current game isolates storage failures from the active game. It catches errors while obtaining the browser store, reading the preference key and writing its replacement. The session can hold its selected size and best results in memory even when no durable write succeeds. There is no current preference-storage warning in the rendered game.

## Features with saved records

For a feature that presents saved records, the unavailable-storage state belongs near the data it affects. The active interaction can still use its current in-memory state even though later visits cannot rely on finding that state again. When browser storage is blocked, a feature keeps working in memory and shows "Progress won't be saved on this device." where its saved records would appear. This ties the explanation to the missing persistence rather than turning it into a failure of the whole game.

The preference adapter does not yet expose a blocked-status result. `readPreferences` returns a `Preferences` value in all cases, and `writePreferences` returns `void`. Neither return type carries an availability flag or failure reason. `Game.tsx` renders no preference-storage warning; saved-record features have separate failure feedback.

The existing status display remains driven by session state. A best achieved during a visit can appear there after a failed write because it is already in `session.preferences`. A visible best is evidence of the in-memory result; persistence across a later reload needs separate evidence. Persistence overview describes the data boundary.

## Three browser operations can fail independently

The first operation is acquiring the storage object. `browserStore` in `src/game/session/use-saved-preferences.ts` returns `window.localStorage` inside a `try` block. If the property getter throws, the function catches the exception and returns `null`. A denied property getter is tested in `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` by defining a getter that throws a `SecurityError` before the game initializes.

The second operation is reading the key. A browser can expose an object whose `getItem` later throws. `readPreferences` protects that call and returns `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` on failure. Its optional call also accommodates a `null` store. A successful read can return no value, a malformed string or valid preferences; those are separate outcomes from a thrown read.

The third operation is writing a serialized replacement. `writePreferences` encloses both serialization and `setItem` in its `try` block. A thrown error is swallowed so it cannot interrupt play. A browser may accept reads and refuse writes, so successful startup does not establish successful saving. Quota exhaustion is one possible write failure; browser policy is another.

These stages explain why a single boolean based on the existence of the storage property would be a weak diagnostic. The game doesn't use such a probe. It attempts the real operation at the boundary and catches failure there.

## What the current fallback preserves

Storage failure does not bypass the game's own rules. Card eligibility, move counting, matching, elapsed time and completion still use their normal state transitions. The fallback affects the initial preference value and the durability of subsequent changes. It does not substitute a different deck algorithm or change how many moves a result takes.

After a denied startup read, the game starts at the default size with no saved bests. Choosing another supported size updates the active session. Completing a game can produce a best for that size in memory. New Game and Restart preserve those in-memory preferences because `replaceGame` copies the session preference object rather than rereading the browser store.

If storage remains unavailable, a page reload starts another session from the fallback. The earlier in-memory best is gone with the old page. This is the expected consequence of unsuccessful saving, even though play in the earlier page was complete and valid. A report that a score survived Restart but disappeared on reload is consistent with a write failure.

An imported unfinished snapshot remains usable under the same conditions. The snapshot text is decoded into game state, then the session handles pause and resume. That path does not require a successful preference write. The accepted board size may be retained only in the current session if the browser refuses the later save.

## No implicit retry service

The hook is a small effect:

```ts
useEffect(() => {
  writePreferences(store, preferences);
}, [preferences, store]);
```

There is no queue, timer-driven retry, backoff or unload handler. Another dependency change can cause another attempt, but the code does not poll for a browser setting to change. A returned `null` store is captured in state for the lifetime of that mounted game; enabling storage later does not replace that state value automatically.

If the captured store object exists and its methods change behavior, a later effect can succeed using the same object. For example, a test double can reject its first write and accept a later one. That is different from reacquiring a previously inaccessible property. Both cases can be modeled without making the game rules aware of browser error names.

The writer's lack of a success result also means the existing UI cannot distinguish a rejected write from a successful one. This is a deliberate limit of the current adapter, not a hidden confirmation mechanism. Any investigation that needs that distinction can observe the supplied store in a test.

## Read failure and corrupt data have different evidence

A denied read and an invalid JSON value both lead to fallback preferences. Only the former establishes that an operation could not be completed. A parse failure establishes that the browser returned text which the application could not use. Confusing the two can lead to a misleading message about browser settings when the actual issue is an edited value.

Similarly, a quota error does not mean the existing value is invalid. The old string may remain perfectly readable while the new result exists only in memory. A person may see a better current best and then see the older best after reload. That sequence is a useful way to reproduce a failed update without damaging a valid baseline.

Corrupt data policy follows the rejection branches in detail. Storage quota notes explains why the small size of this app's own payload cannot establish that a shared origin has available space.

## Errors do not authorize deleting other data

The source only calls `getItem` and `setItem` for `PREFERENCES_KEY`. It has no storage-wide clear call, key enumeration or cleanup routine. `PreferenceStore` exposes only those two methods. The storage unit test explicitly seeds an unrelated key and checks that a preference write leaves its value intact.

This matters in shared local environments, where another page can occupy the same origin. A rejected preference write does not cause Neon Pairs to free space by deleting that page's values. The current fallback is simply to continue without a successful save. The app also does not switch to cookies, a server endpoint or another browser database after failure.

When reproducing capacity problems, a disposable origin or isolated browser context keeps artificial fill data away from a person's real preferences. That is a testing technique rather than an extra product recovery path. The test can remove the keys it created afterward; the shipped game contains no such test cleanup behavior.

## Evidence in the test suite

`storage.test.ts` uses a denied store whose read and write methods both throw. It checks that reading yields the default size and that writing does not throw. It also covers `readPreferences(null)`. This verifies the API boundary directly, without needing to configure an actual browser's privacy settings.

The browser environment test covers a different boundary: acquisition of `window.localStorage`. It installs the throwing getter before loading the game, loads a fixed board and matches a known pair. The harness gathers uncaught page errors and checks that none occurred. That demonstrates continued play after an acquisition failure, not persistence in that denied context.

These tests don't establish every browser policy or a physical disk limit. They also don't assert the saved-record feature notice described earlier. Reading the test title alone can obscure those limits; the actual injection point and assertions show what each test proves. Storage testing guide extends that evidence into an investigation workflow.

# Import safety policy
This page explains how Neon Pairs validates untrusted exchange text before a browser session or replay result can use it.

The important boundary is between a draft and accepted game data. A text field can contain arbitrary edits, and a replay file can contain arbitrary bytes decoded as text. Neither is treated as a `GameState` just because JSON parsing succeeds. Shape checks, numeric checks and game-specific consistency checks happen before the browser commits a replacement.

## Field diagnostics and the current implementation

A field outside a format's declared shape is a validation failure, including inside a selection or replay action. The diagnostic policy makes that particular mistake identifiable to a person correcting copied data. An import with a field its format doesn't define shows "Unknown field: NAME." for the first such field and leaves the current state unchanged. This applies to the field diagnostic; it does not make an incomplete object or an unsupported version acceptable. The format's own required fields and state constraints still determine acceptance.

The implementation already rejects extra keys, but does not yet produce that field-specific notice. `hasExactKeys` returns a boolean, `decodeSnapshot` returns `null`, and the browser displays `Invalid snapshot.` for all snapshot failures. `readReplay` provides problem categories rather than the offending key name. The current adapters reject extensions without identifying the offending field as the diagnostic policy requires.

The existing code does not define a traversal order, object-path syntax or combined-error format for a field-specific diagnostic. Its boolean exact-key helper cannot report a first key. Those details cannot be inferred from a `null` result. For current behavior, examine the published notice and replay problem category rather than expecting a key name.

## Validation before replacement

`useGame.loadSnapshot(text)` calls `decodeSnapshot(text)` first. A failed result calls the notice helper and returns `false`. Only a successful result reaches `clock.reset()` and `replaceGame(current.current, game, true)`. There is no earlier step that installs the imported code or clears the existing matched positions.

`useGame.loadBoard(code)` follows the same broad shape with a board-code parser. It trims the control's draft, checks the result, and only then resets the clock and constructs a replacement game. A valid board-code string is sufficient for a fresh deal; a snapshot needs the additional position checks because it claims progress.

Failure changes visible feedback and the announcement counter. It does not replace the game, reset the running clock, save a different size or discard the edited draft. “Keeps the game” therefore does not mean that every field of the containing `Session` has reference equality: notices are session fields too. Nor does it freeze the active game while someone corrects text. A running game can continue to gain elapsed time after an unsuccessful load.

This distinction is visible in `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts`: the test enters bad board and snapshot drafts, verifies the notices and retained text, then advances the clock and verifies that the prior game is still running. A test that expected elapsed time to remain fixed indefinitely after rejection would assert behavior the product does not have.

## The shared JSON boundary

The small helpers in `src/game/saved-format.ts` separate JSON mechanics from game validation:

| Helper | Meaning at this boundary |
| --- | --- |
| `isWithinBytes(text, maxBytes)` | Measures UTF-8 encoded length, inclusively |
| `parseJson(text)` | Returns parsed unknown data, or `undefined` after a parse exception |
| `isJsonObject(value)` | Accepts non-null objects except arrays |
| `hasExactKeys(value, keys)` | Checks own-key count and presence of every expected own key |
| `isNonnegativeSafeInteger(value)` | Accepts numeric safe integers greater than or equal to zero |

`JSON.parse` can produce `null`, a list, a string, a boolean or a number. Those are valid JSON texts and invalid snapshot or replay roots. The object guard is what distinguishes them from a malformed text error. This is especially visible in replay results: `{` produces `malformedJson`, whereas `null` produces `format`.

`parseJson` does not execute input as code. A string containing script-like characters is still a string and fails where an object or number is required. The decoder does not merge the parsed object into the live session wholesale. It constructs the accepted state from a generated board and the fields it has validated.

Exact keys are checked as a set, not as an ordering constraint. Missing fields fail as well as extra fields. Nested objects are checked at their own format boundaries. A `closed` selection with an `index` is invalid even if that index would be an eligible position in a different selection variant. A replay action with an annotation field is invalid even if `atMs` and `index` are otherwise good.

The helpers operate on the parsed object, not the original token stream. JSON duplicate property names are consequently handled by `JSON.parse` before exact-key checking; the decoder does not retain a record of earlier overwritten occurrences. Likewise, numeric notation such as `1.0` becomes the number `1`. The integer predicate checks the value it receives rather than enforcing a preferred spelling of a JSON number.

## Resource bounds are checked at the text boundary

Snapshot decoding measures its input before parsing and rejects text above `SNAPSHOT_MAX_BYTES`, which is `65_536`. Replay reading checks `REPLAY_MAX_BYTES`, which is `1_048_576`, before parsing. The replay parser then rejects more than `REPLAY_MAX_ACTIONS`, which is `10_000`. Trailing JSON whitespace is legal within the byte budget and still consumes that budget.

These checks bound the accepted format, but they should not be described as a streaming parser. `TextEncoder` allocates an encoded representation for measurement. The CLI also calls `readFile` before `readReplay` checks text size. A very large input can therefore already have been read into memory when it is rejected. The code provides explicit acceptance limits rather than a promise that arbitrary input has no allocation cost.

The browser textarea's `maxLength` is a separate character limit. Multibyte text can satisfy that limit and exceed the decoder's byte limit. The existing byte helper test uses an accented character to establish that bytes, rather than JavaScript string length, control acceptance. Snapshot format discusses how this interacts with readable export text.

## Snapshot checks depend on the regenerated deal

After validating the version and board code, `decodeSnapshot` generates the board used to interpret positions. `readMatched` checks unique in-range positions and requires both copies of every represented face. An even-length list alone is not enough: on `np1-4-1`, `[2, 6]` is a pair while `[0, 1]` is not.

`readSelection` checks availability against that matched list. A mismatch needs different positions with different faces and an integer remaining interval from `1` through `800`. It cannot describe a same-face pair awaiting closure, because normal play resolves matching cards immediately. When every position is matched, availability also prevents any nonclosed selection.

The full decoder checks counter bounds, a minimum move count and consistency with `started`. These checks establish the stated constraints without reconstructing every earlier action. Snapshot format gives the complete validation sequence; Snapshot selection notes explains the board-dependent helpers.

## Replay checks and isolated evaluation

`readReplay` checks root shape, version, board code, action count and `endMs` before walking actions. Each action then needs its exact object shape, safe nonnegative numbers, a nondecreasing timestamp no later than `endMs`, and a position inside the deck. Its index into the action array is included in action-specific failures.

Evaluation can already have computed earlier actions when a later action fails. That is safe because the evolving state is local to `readReplay`; no browser session has been committed. The function returns a problem rather than that partial state. This is different from a streaming UI that visibly applies each imported action as it reads.

An in-range activation during a mismatch is valid replay data even though the game ignores it. So are an activation of an already matched card and a repeated activation of the current first card. Validation checks whether the action is well formed; `activateCard` decides whether it changes play. Treating every ignored activation as a corrupt replay would conflate these two jobs.

Action timestamps may be much larger than the elapsed clock cap. The replay evaluator advances the logical timeline using safe integers, while `advanceGame` caps the resulting elapsed counter. That distinction prevents a legitimate long timeline from being rejected merely because the visible clock has saturated. Replay format explains exact timeout edges and equal-time order.

## Failure reports that preserve the evidence

For current snapshot failures the decoder deliberately supplies no reason. The most effective local investigation isolates a single change against a known accepted object: replace just the selection, just the code, or just one counter. The tests in `snapshot.test.ts` use this pattern so that an unrelated invalid baseline cannot hide a missing check.

Replay reports have more detail. `readReplay` distinguishes file size, JSON syntax, root format, board code, actions array, end time, individual action shape, time order and index bounds. The CLI translates these into stderr text and uses a one-based action number for readers. Internal action positions remain zero-based. Mixing these conventions can lead an engineer to inspect the wrong action.

Retaining original text matters when a failure depends on bytes or syntax. Parsing and reserializing a padded document can remove the very length excess that caused its rejection. A screenshot of a notice cannot establish whether an extra property was nested or at the root. For the current accepted shapes, use Board code format, Snapshot format and Replay format; for the browser steps around them, use Sharing FAQ.
# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
