The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure.

The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen.

Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns.

## Why the card board is not a table

Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model.

The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle.

There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts.

## What the caption contributes

An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures.

The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy.

A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret.

## Column relationships and reading order

The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure.

A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface.

Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details.

## Narrow layouts and long values

The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow.

There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence.

Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface.

The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context.
# Announcements policy

This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering.

The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards.

## Publication point

`Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature.

The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source.

Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader.

## Session data behind the paragraph

The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `<span key={session.announcement}>{session.feedback}</span>`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text.

The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it.

A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`.

## Turn results

`activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal.

After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications.

| Result | Text produced by the session |
| --- | --- |
| First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` |
| Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` |
| Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` |
| Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` |

Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count.

A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game.

## Consecutive identical results

Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them.

The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity.

The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card.

There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game.

## Changes that stay quiet

`tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause.

Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result.

New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load.

Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains.

## Load outcomes share the publication path

The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again.

For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch.

Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel.

Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication.

## Completion and persistent reading

GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time.

The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game.

A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did.

## Automated evidence

`session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser.

`tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure.

The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role.

The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance.

## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result

A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text.

For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page.
# Focus policy

This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen.

Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things.

## Existing page and future screens

`Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen.

A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists.

The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus.

## Initial load is quiet

The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method.

The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board.

A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing.

## Deal actions retain their location

New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call.

The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms.

A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place.

Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. Error display guide follows those cases in detail.

## Remembered board focus

Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`.

Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched.

Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. Board keyboard navigation provides the calculations and edge behavior.

## Resume transfers before removal

Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target.

In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices.

The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment.

The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location.

## Visible focus and scroll clearance

`game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area.

The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail.

`useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible.

The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately.

## Focus is not completion feedback

Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched.

Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched.

These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries.

## Review evidence

The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring.

A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. Interface review checklist gathers these journeys with layout and input checks.

For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior.
# Time policy

This page describes how Neon Pairs accounts for active play time and keeps browser timing separate from logical game transitions.

There are three related values to distinguish: a browser observation, the delta between observations and the elapsed milliseconds stored in a game. The browser adapter observes; the clock arithmetic determines a delta; the rules apply that delta. The displayed statistic is derived from stored elapsed time rather than from a second independent stopwatch.

## Where observations enter

`use-session-clock.ts` owns browser observation and scheduling. Its neighbor `browser-clock.ts` accepts observations as arguments and computes a numerical step. Game code reads time only through the session clock. Only files in src/game/session/ may call performance.now, and no game code may use Date. Rule functions therefore receive elapsed amounts directly and can be exercised without a wall clock.

This boundary does not mean every file in the session directory performs an observation. `session.ts` transforms data and delegates logical advancement to `advanceGame`. `browser-clock.ts` creates an observation record from a supplied number. Their placement keeps time-related behavior together while the browser hook contains the actual calls.

The tests have their own environment control. Browser fixtures can install a Playwright clock and test scripts can set the observation that the application sees. Those are verification mechanisms outside the game source, not additional application clocks.

## Conditions for active time

The hook's `running()` predicate reads the latest session ref. It returns true only when the document is considered visible, the session is not paused, the game has started and the game is not won. The rules independently refuse to advance a game that has not started or has already been won.

A first accepted card activation sets `started` to true. The synchronization before that activation treats the preceding wait as inactive. The next active observation can therefore measure from the activation boundary rather than from page load. Repeated activation of the same revealed card is ignored by the rules but synchronization still accounts for time that passed before the attempted action.

An unfinished imported snapshot is paused by `replaceGame`. Its saved elapsed time and mismatch remainder remain game data, while the session prevents further active advancement until Resume. Resume resets the observation baseline and clears pause-related notices. It does not restart the imported game or give a pending mismatch a new full interval.

Completed games stop logical advancement. A completed imported game is already won, so it does not acquire an active timer. Completion through a final match is synchronized before that match, which makes the final stored elapsed time reflect play up to the finishing activation.

## Delta arithmetic

`ActiveClock` stores `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` creates that record. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes `delta = now - clock.observedAt`; it returns the delta only when active, finite and positive. Otherwise it returns zero. In both cases it returns a new clock whose baseline is `now`.

Advancing the baseline during an inactive observation is essential. Suppose the last active observation was 100ms, the page becomes hidden at 150ms and becomes visible at 5150ms. The hidden-to-visible event synchronizes while the stored visibility flag is still false. That step contributes zero and moves the baseline to 5150ms, so the following active observation excludes the hidden interval.

The arithmetic keeps fractional milliseconds. There is no per-observation integer rounding or tick counter. Several submillisecond positive deltas can add up just as one longer delta would. The tests compare totals with a floating-point tolerance where necessary.

A backward observation or a nonfinite delta produces no advancement. This is defensive handling of supplied values, not a claim that such a sequence is a normal browser clock behavior. The clock still records the supplied observation, so later arithmetic is based on that new baseline. Clock design discusses this small function and the hook separately.

## Scheduling is an opportunity to observe

`CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS` is 40. The hook uses a timeout that reschedules itself. For a mismatch it asks for the smaller of 40 and `remainingMs`; otherwise it uses 40. A scheduled delay is not added directly to the game. When the callback runs, the hook obtains a new observation and computes the actual delta.

This difference handles delayed callbacks. If the browser runs a 40ms timeout after 80ms, the measured active interval is 80ms. The rules are not told that exactly one nominal tick occurred. Conversely, receiving more callbacks does not make time pass faster, because each callback advances from the previous observation.

When the running predicate is false, scheduling stops. The visibility listener remains available to re-evaluate the state on return. Changes to generation, start state, pause state and victory also affect the hook's effect lifecycle. React rerenders alone do not supply elapsed milliseconds.

## Synchronize at action boundaries

The controller calls `clock.synchronize()` before `activateSession`. That ordering can close an overdue mismatch before the new activation is evaluated. A busy browser can delay the scheduled callback, but it does not make a logically expired interval block the next click indefinitely.

The controller also synchronizes before exporting a snapshot. Rendered state can trail the current clock by part of a scheduled interval. Serializing that rendered state directly would make exports depend on when the last render occurred. The controller instead encodes `current.current.game` after synchronization.

Fresh deals, restart, valid board loads and valid snapshot loads reset the observation baseline before replacing the game. Resume resets it before unpausing. Invalid load attempts publish a notice but do not replace the game or reset its baseline. The eventual valid synchronization still accounts for the active interval during that interaction.

## Mismatch time and elapsed time

`advanceGame` ignores a nonfinite, zero or negative amount. For a started unfinished game it adds a positive amount to `elapsedMs`, capped at `ELAPSED_MAX_MS = 359_999_999`. If the selection is a mismatch, it also subtracts the amount from `remainingMs`.

A positive remainder keeps the mismatch with its new remainder. A zero or negative remainder closes the selection. The function does not carry a queue of delayed closing events, and it does not truncate elapsed advancement to the mismatch remainder. A 900ms advance against an 800ms mismatch closes it and adds 900ms of active elapsed time.

The mismatch remainder and elapsed total serve different purposes. The total can reach its cap while a new mismatch still has time to resolve. `advanceGame` continues processing the selection even after the total is capped. Similarly, the move cap does not stop matching, time or victory. These limits protect stored/displayed numbers rather than ending play.

The 800ms mismatch interval is defined beside turn resolution as `MISMATCH_MS`. Browser scheduling reads the current remainder; snapshot validation imports the same bound. Mismatch interval covers the player-visible rule, while this page explains how the interval survives browser lifecycle events.

## Serialization has a rounding boundary

Active play retains fractions. `encodeSnapshot` floors `elapsedMs` and rounds a mismatch's `remainingMs` upward. A positive remainder smaller than one millisecond therefore exports as 1, preserving a valid pending interval. Rounding the remainder downward could produce a mismatch object with a zero value that the decoder rejects.

The decoder accepts only nonnegative safe integer elapsed values within the cap and a mismatch remainder from 1 through 800. This means the serialized representation is intentionally coarser than the in-memory state. The rounding happens at export, not after every callback.

The display uses `formatElapsed`, which floors to whole seconds and derives minutes and a two-digit seconds component. That formatter is presentation; it does not determine when cards close or when a game finishes. Elapsed time rules covers the visible statistic and limit.

## Deal generations and stale work

Every `replaceGame` call increments `generation`. A scheduled callback captures the generation from its effect. The hook checks that captured generation before observation, and `tickSession` checks it again before applying a delta. An earlier deal's callback cannot spend time in the replacement deal through the normal path.

The effect also has an `active` flag. Cleanup marks it false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The flag handles callbacks associated with a retired effect; the generation handles replacement ownership. These are related protections with different scopes.

Restarting the same board still changes the generation. Reusing the same code does not mean reusing the old progress or pending browser work. `Game.tsx` also keys `Board` by generation, which resets local board focus state on replacement. This shares a lifecycle marker without putting focus inside the time model.

## Test evidence

Arithmetic, session transitions and browser integration have separate checks. The clock suite covers fractions, inactivity and observation frequency; the session suite covers pause and generations; browser journeys cover between-tick export, overdue clicks, hidden intervals and teardown. Clock design follows those cases in detail, and Test policy explains the runners.

# Elapsed time rules

This page explains active elapsed time, browser clock accounting, and display formatting in Neon Pairs.

`src/game/elapsed-time.ts` contains the formatter. Accumulation belongs to `advanceGame` in `game.ts`, and the browser decides which durations to supply through `session/use-session-clock.ts` and `session/browser-clock.ts`. Reading those three layers separately explains why rendering frequency does not define the measured duration.

## What counts as active

Elapsed time begins with the first valid reveal. Before that, `advanceGame` returns the existing state because `started` is false. Reading the controls or waiting at a fresh hidden board does not accrue game time.

Once started, time counts while the page is visible and the game is unfinished, unless an unfinished imported snapshot is awaiting Resume. It includes time spent looking at one revealed card, considering a choice between turns, and viewing a mismatch. It does not measure only the time when a pointer or keyboard is moving.

The browser running predicate combines four conditions:

```text
page visible
and session not paused
and game started
and game not won
```

The core knows only started and completion. Visibility and imported pause are browser-session concerns. Direct calls to `advanceGame` assume the caller has supplied an active duration.

There is no ordinary manual pause control during a played game. Resume is associated with loaded unfinished progress. Page visibility is based on `document.hidden`; the hook does not use window focus, pointer idleness, or the reproduction panel's open state as additional clock gates.

## Core accumulation

`advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` ignores a duration that is nonfinite or nonpositive. It also ignores it before start or after victory. For a valid active step:

```ts
const elapsedMs = Math.min(ELAPSED_MAX_MS, state.elapsedMs + milliseconds);
```

`ELAPSED_MAX_MS` is 359,999,999. The current implementation retains fractional milliseconds in memory, since monotonic browser observations can include fractions. It does not round each observation down before adding it.

The same call subtracts its delta from a pending mismatch. A large step can close the mismatch while adding the entire active duration to elapsed time. The 800-millisecond mismatch duration is not an upper bound on how much elapsed time that call can add.

Elapsed saturation does not end play. It also does not stop a mismatch countdown, because that countdown uses the original supplied delta. See Mismatch interval.

## Observing the browser clock

`browser-clock.ts` stores one observation in an `ActiveClock`: `observedAt`. `createClock(now)` initializes it. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` computes the difference from that observation, returning a positive finite difference only when active is true.

Every result includes a new clock observed at `now`, even when no duration was counted. Advancing the observation during inactivity is essential: the next active observation can then exclude the period spent waiting, hidden, or paused.

The browser hook reads `performance.now()` and uses recursive timeouts with a usual 40-millisecond interval. It measures the actual difference between readings. It does not add a fixed 40 merely because a callback ran.

For example, active readings at 0, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 3.7, and 10.9 accumulate the same duration, within floating-point precision, as a single active observation from 0 to 10.9. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks this property, along with fractional durations and inactive intervals.

That example concerns logical observation, not a guarantee of a 40-millisecond browser paint. A busy task can delay a callback. When it runs, the measured difference catches up the game to the observed active time.

## Start, actions, and completion boundaries

Before processing a card activation, `useGame.activate` synchronizes the clock. At the first reveal, the game is still unstarted during this synchronization, so earlier waiting is discarded and the observation point moves to the reveal's time. The activation then sets started to true.

Later activations synchronize while the game is active. This captures duration between rendered ticks and ensures an overdue mismatch can close before a new card is considered. At the final activation, synchronization captures time up to that action before the game becomes won.

After victory, the running predicate is false and `advanceGame` also refuses additional duration. The completion time is retained without waiting for the completion banner's visual effect to finish.

Export also synchronizes before encoding a snapshot. Thus exported progress can be ahead of the last ordinary rendered tick, while still corresponding to the current active clock. It does not rely on a status string that was formatted earlier.

## Visibility boundaries

The visibility listener synchronizes before changing its stored visibility flag. On the transition to hidden, it counts the active interval up to that observation. On the transition back to visible, it observes the intervening duration as inactive, then resumes scheduling.

Suppose the game starts, runs visibly for 300 milliseconds, then a miss runs visibly for another 200. Hiding for five seconds adds nothing. On return, another 600 active milliseconds finish the mismatch. The total elapsed duration is 1,100 milliseconds: 300 before the miss plus the miss's full 800 active milliseconds.

Counting wall-clock time between first reveal and completion would include the hidden five seconds and disagree with the game's definition. A reproduction of a clock issue needs the visibility changes as well as the overall wait.

The hook clears its scheduled timeout while inactive. The implementation also handles a synchronization request made during inactivity by updating the observation without counting that period.

## Imported pause and resets

An unfinished import retains its elapsed value and waits paused. Resume resets browser observation before clearing that pause, excluding the time spent inspecting the position. If started is false, the clock still waits for a valid first reveal. Completed imports remain stopped by victory.

Successful replacements also reset observation. New Game and Restart receive zero game time from `createGame`; snapshots retain their imported value. Invalid loads do neither reset nor replacement. New Game and Restart compares these operations.

## Display conversion

`formatElapsed` first floors milliseconds divided by 1,000. It then divides that whole-second count into minutes and a seconds remainder, padding the seconds to two digits:

```ts
const seconds = Math.floor(milliseconds / 1000);
const minutes = Math.floor(seconds / 60);
return `${minutes}:${String(seconds % 60).padStart(2, '0')}`;
```

| Stored milliseconds | Formatted value |
| ---: | --- |
| 0 | `0:00` |
| 999.9 | `0:00` |
| 1,000 | `0:01` |
| 59,999 | `0:59` |
| 60,000 | `1:00` |
| 3,600,000 | `60:00` |
| 359,999,999 | `5999:59` |

There is no separate hour field. Minutes continue past 59. `GameStatus` places the `Time:` label alongside this formatted value, and completion feedback uses the same formatter.

The formatter does not enforce the game's domain or cap its argument. It assumes a valid duration supplied by state. The cap is enforced by advancement and snapshot validation, so a direct unsupported call to the formatter is not an alternative game input path.

## Snapshot precision

`encodeSnapshot` floors elapsed milliseconds to a whole number. It rounds a pending mismatch remainder upward. These opposite rounding directions preserve the external constraints: elapsed is a whole nonnegative duration, and a still-pending mismatch has at least one millisecond remaining.

For an in-memory elapsed value of 11.75 and a mismatch remainder of 799.25, export writes elapsed 11 and remaining 800. Import restores those integer values. The live game keeps its fractions; export does not replace it with the rounded representation.

A round trip can therefore change submillisecond precision in the restored copy. That is expected at the format boundary. It does not justify rounding every browser tick, which would repeatedly discard fractions and make accumulated time depend on observation frequency.

The fractional browser test uses quarter milliseconds so its test values are exactly representable in binary. It checks both elapsed export and a final quarter-millisecond mismatch remainder exporting as 1.

## Replay uses explicit active time

Replay advances to each action's logical timestamp before activation, then to its end time. Waiting before the first valid reveal is ignored, and completion stops later advances. Hidden intervals and import pauses are omitted from this active timeline. Compare active durations when comparing replay and browser results; see Replay format.

## Source evidence

`elapsed-time.test.ts` covers the cap, exported capped progress, and rejection above the cap. `browser-clock.test.ts` checks fractional accumulation and inactive observations. `tests/clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` exports between scheduled ticks. `tests/idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` checks untouched hidden and paused intervals.

These are distinct checks: a formatter example verifies text, a core advance verifies arithmetic, and a browser journey verifies which intervals reach that arithmetic. A correct-looking status string alone cannot prove that a hidden period was excluded or that the final click was synchronized.
# Clock design

This page traces `browser-clock.ts` and `use-session-clock.ts`, including scheduling, visibility changes, action synchronization and cleanup.

The clock has a small arithmetic part and a browser-lifecycle part. The arithmetic keeps an observation baseline; the hook decides when to observe and when an interval counts as active play. `advanceGame` remains responsible for what a positive amount of logical time does to the game. Time policy states the ownership boundary; this page follows the implementation.

## The arithmetic record

`browser-clock.ts` exports `CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS = 40`, `createClock` and `elapsedStep`. Its private `ActiveClock` interface contains only `observedAt: number`. It does not store accumulated active time, a mismatch deadline, a timer identifier or a pause flag.

`createClock(now)` returns `{ observedAt: now }`. `elapsedStep(clock, now, active)` subtracts the previous observation, accepts the delta only if active, finite and positive, and returns `{ clock: createClock(now), milliseconds }`. Accumulated elapsed time remains in `GameState`; the clock only supplies the next contribution.

An inactive step still updates the baseline. That is the mechanism that discards waiting time without asking the game rules to subtract it later. A backward or nonfinite delta contributes zero, but its supplied observation still becomes the baseline. The function has no hidden memory beyond the record passed by its caller.

## Fractional values survive observation

The arithmetic never floors the delta. For observations at 0, 0.3, 0.8, 1.1, 3.7 and 10.9, adding the active steps gives the same total as one active observation at 10.9, allowing ordinary floating-point tolerance. A timer frequency change therefore does not inherently change elapsed accounting.

This matters particularly for a mismatch opened between integer milliseconds. Its remaining interval is a positive number in memory and decreases by actual observed active time. Export is the separate rounding boundary: elapsed rounds downward and a positive pending remainder rounds upward.

`browser-clock.test.ts` checks fractional steps, hidden intervals, waiting before start, backward observations, NaN and independence from observation frequency. These tests do not schedule anything. Their purpose is to isolate the arithmetic contract from browser event behavior.

## Hook inputs and persistent refs

`useSessionClock(session, current, commit)` receives the rendered session, a ref to the latest session and a function that commits a new value. It creates a ref for the arithmetic clock and another for the stored visibility state, initialized from `!document.hidden`.

The expression supplied to `useRef(createClock(performance.now()))` is evaluated as the hook renders, while React retains the first ref value. Later evaluations do not by themselves reset that retained baseline. Explicit reset updates `clock.current`. This distinction helps when tracing observations in a render-heavy test: evaluating an initializer expression and replacing a ref value are different operations.

The hook derives `won = isWon(session.game)` for effect dependencies. Inside asynchronous work, `running()` uses `current.current` to read pause, start and victory state, along with the visibility ref. It does not decide activity from a session captured several renders earlier.

## Synchronization step by step

`synchronize(generation = current.current.generation)` begins with a generation check. A mismatched captured generation returns before observing or updating the baseline. Otherwise it reads a fresh browser observation and calls `elapsedStep` using the current running predicate.

It always installs the returned clock record. If `milliseconds` is nonzero, it commits `tickSession(current.current, generation, milliseconds)`. The session function performs another generation check and a pause check, then delegates to `advanceGame`.

The second check is data-layer protection. The first check also prevents an old callback from disturbing the new game's observation baseline. A session-level refusal alone would stop an incorrect game advance but would not explain ownership of the clock record.

The hook's returned `reset()` replaces the baseline with a new observation. It does not clear the game elapsed total or selection. Controller actions combine reset with the appropriate game replacement or resume transition, which is where progress semantics are defined.

## One rescheduling chain

The effect captures the rendered generation, sets `active = true` and holds an optional timer identifier. Its `schedule()` function first clears the current identifier. It then returns if the effect is inactive, the generation no longer matches or `running()` is false.

If active, it reads the current selection. A mismatch uses `Math.min(CLOCK_INTERVAL_MS, selection.remainingMs)` as the requested delay; other states use 40. The timeout callback checks `active`, synchronizes with the captured generation and schedules again.

This is a recursive timeout chain rather than a fixed interval. The next delay is chosen from current state after the previous callback. A mismatch near expiry can request its smaller remainder, and an inactive session stops producing periodic work. The nominal delay is never treated as the actual amount elapsed.

## A delayed callback

Suppose active play has a baseline of 100ms and a timeout requested for 40ms runs at 180ms. Synchronization contributes 80ms. It does not contribute one unit of 40ms merely because one callback fired. The rules update elapsed time and any pending mismatch using that measured contribution.

If the remaining mismatch was 60ms, the same 80ms advance closes it. The rules still add the whole active 80ms to elapsed time, subject to the cap. They do not reduce total elapsed to 60ms just because the selection closed partway through the interval.

This is why callbacks are observation opportunities rather than authority over time. A busy event loop can delay visible updates, but the next synchronization catches the game up from the last observation. Mismatch interval covers the visible duration independently of this scheduling mechanism.

## Visibility event ordering

`visibilityChanged()` first checks effect activity and generation. It then calls `synchronize(generation)` before assigning `visible.current = !document.hidden`, and finally calls `schedule()`.

On a visible-to-hidden event, synchronization sees the previously visible state and accounts for active time up to the hide observation. The flag then becomes false, and scheduling clears the pending timeout and stops.

On a hidden-to-visible event, synchronization sees the previously hidden state. It contributes zero while updating the baseline to the return observation. The flag then becomes true and scheduling resumes. This order excludes the hidden interval without relying on browser timer throttling behavior.

Reversing that assignment and synchronization would misclassify the interval ending at the event. The relevant state is the activity during the time since the previous observation, not merely the new visibility value after the event. The current order makes that distinction explicit.

## A visibility timeline

| Observation | Stored visibility used for the step | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start accepted at 100ms | Not started before the activation | Zero for waiting before start |
| Hide event at 350ms | Visible | 250ms active play |
| Show event at 5350ms | Hidden | Zero for the hidden interval |
| Next active observation at 5390ms | Visible | 40ms active play |

The table assumes no intervening observations and an unfinished, unpaused game. It describes the same arithmetic as many short periodic steps. Hidden time is excluded because the baseline advances on return, not because the system clock stopped.

Headless Chromium does not naturally supply the hidden-tab behavior these journeys need, so browser tests override `document.hidden` and dispatch `visibilitychange` at the adapter boundary. This drives the actual handler while keeping the rule functions unchanged.

## Action synchronization is deliberate

The controller synchronizes immediately before activation. Consider a mismatch whose logical interval has expired while its scheduled callback remains queued. A click can land first. Synchronization closes the old mismatch through `advanceGame`, then `activateSession` sees the newly closed selection and accepts the click as the next first reveal.

`fractional-clock.e2e.test.ts` tests this in one browser task: it updates the controlled observation and invokes a button click before any timer can run. That makes the action-boundary behavior observable without depending on machine load.

Export has the same need for current data. The last rendered state can trail the clock by less than a scheduled interval or more under load. `exportSnapshot` synchronizes and encodes the latest ref. It does not serialize the session value captured by the prior render.

## Replacement, pause and Resume

New Game, Restart and valid loads reset the baseline before replacement. `replaceGame` increments generation, causing the prior effect to become obsolete. An earlier callback checks both activity and generation before affecting the replacement.

An unfinished snapshot import installs its saved state but pauses the session. No active scheduled loop runs while paused. Resume resets the baseline before clearing `paused`, so waiting at the Resume control is not charged to the imported game. Its saved elapsed total and mismatch remainder remain intact.

An invalid load only changes notices. It neither replaces the game nor resets its baseline. An export during active play also does not pause. The controller's action semantics therefore determine which intervals count; the reproduction panel's visibility is not itself a clock state.

## Effect dependencies and cleanup

The effect depends on `session.generation`, `session.game.started`, `session.paused` and the derived `won`. Those values describe changes that start, stop or replace the scheduling lifetime. Ordinary elapsed updates do not restart the effect on every render.

Cleanup marks `active` false, clears the timeout and removes the visibility listener. The callback's activity check handles a callback associated with a retired effect. The generation check handles a replaced game. Removing the listener prevents a later visibility event from invoking obsolete session work after unmount.

The timer identifier may be undefined before anything is scheduled. The browser clear operation is used both at the start of `schedule` and at cleanup, keeping one ownership path. There is no independent timeout per mismatch stored in the core state.

## Completion and numeric caps

When the final match is accepted, the controller has already synchronized. `isWon` then becomes true, the effect's victory dependency changes and the running predicate becomes false. Further logical advances return the won game unchanged.

At `ELAPSED_MAX_MS`, however, victory need not be true. The game can continue, including resolving pending mismatches, even though the elapsed total no longer increases. The hook does not treat the cap as a reason to stop scheduling. This is consistent with the core's independent handling of elapsed accumulation and selection remainder.

The move cap has no direct role in this hook. It is part of activation logic. Separating those bounds avoids turning a display/storage limit into an accidental lifecycle stop.

## Evidence that isolates the risks

The arithmetic tests establish numerical behavior. Session tests establish generation and pause gating. `clock-edges.e2e.test.ts` exports at amounts that are not multiples of the 40ms interval, demonstrating action synchronization. Fractional tests preserve submillisecond mismatch origin and export a final quarter-millisecond as a valid pending interval.

`idle-clock.e2e.test.ts` waits through a hidden period without inspecting the game repeatedly, then checks the remaining active interval on return. A separate case imports a paused mismatch and waits before Resume. These cases expose bugs that incidental observations during inactivity could conceal.

`timer-lifecycle.e2e.test.ts` instruments timeouts and visibility listeners in the separate session harness, unmounts the actual game and checks both counts return to zero. It also starts another mismatch in the same deal after an earlier one has closed. That case distinguishes stale work inside one generation from stale work across replacement.

When investigating drift, the useful trace contains observations, active conditions and resulting deltas. Counting callbacks or inspecting the displayed seconds is too coarse to distinguish a rounding defect from a baseline defect. The two-file design makes each of those quantities available to focused tests without adding diagnostic state to the shipped game.
# Data exchange policy
This page explains which Neon Pairs data crosses a file or text boundary and how the existing formats relate to future exports.

The game has three exchange formats with deliberately different jobs. A board code identifies a starting deal. A snapshot describes a position on that deal. A replay describes activations on a logical timeline and produces a position when evaluated. Choosing the smallest useful format keeps a report understandable: a wrong shuffle needs a code, a wrong revealed state needs a snapshot, and a timeout ordering problem usually needs a replay.

The detailed contract is Reproducibility. This page describes the boundary between those formats, browser session data and developer tooling. It is not an additional wire-format definition.

## Existing formats and new exports

The current snapshot and replay formats are JSON objects with numeric `version: 1`. The board code is a string whose prefix is `np1`. Their definitions predate the general policy for new JSON exports. Every new exported JSON object has a "format" of "neon-pairs/KIND", naming what it holds, and a whole-number "version", with its keys in alphabetical order at every level. Formats that already exist stay as they are. In particular, adding a discriminator to a version 1 snapshot would make it fail the existing exact-key check, and changing the board-code string into JSON would remove its usefulness in the Board code field.

There is an important distinction between naming a new exchange format and modifying a known one. `snapshot.ts` is still the authority for the fields of an exported snapshot. `replay.ts` is still the authority for a replay input. The general policy does not silently widen either accepted object. See Format versioning for the compatibility decisions around those boundaries.

Current snapshot output is readable JSON produced by `JSON.stringify` with a two-space indentation argument. It writes fields in the construction order used by `encodeSnapshot`: `version`, `boardCode`, `matched`, `selection`, `moves`, `elapsedMs`, `started`. This order is not alphabetical. An importer accepts any object-key order when the required keys and values are present. The distinction matters when comparing documents: a change in whitespace or object-key order need not change the represented state.

## Choose the artifact by the question

| Question | Useful artifact | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Did two runtimes generate the same deal? | Board code | Which cards the player activated |
| Can another browser show this position? | Snapshot | The complete earlier action sequence |
| Does a click at the mismatch boundary get accepted? | Replay | The browser's real scheduling behavior |
| Does a loaded position show the right controls? | Snapshot plus browser steps | How that position was originally reached |
| Did a local best survive reload? | A storage-focused reproduction | An exported snapshot carries no best record |

A board code is short enough to copy into a report without a separate file. Its meaning is stable because the prefix fixes generation. A snapshot contains enough progress to avoid playing back a long game. A replay is the most explicit description of action order, but the browser does not currently record or load replay files through its reproduction panel. Developer tooling evaluates them through the core and CLI.

A screenshot may accompany any of these, but it does not replace their machine-readable information. A picture of two cards cannot tell an engineer the exact pending milliseconds. A board code plus an action sequence can distinguish a bad card layout from a bad state transition. The appropriate artifact depends on whether the disputed behavior is generation, state, time or presentation.

## What the exchange formats carry

A board code carries generation version, supported side length and seed. `generateBoard` derives the immutable deck. The result contains face identifiers in position order; the code does not carry artwork, card names or a language setting. Loading it creates a fresh hidden state with no moves and no elapsed time. The algorithm and literal example are documented in Board code format.

A snapshot carries `boardCode`, matched position indices, a tagged selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the `started` flag, alongside its format version. It does not duplicate the deck. Pair count and completion are derived after loading. Omitting those derived values avoids accepting a record in which the supplied pair total disagrees with the matched positions. Snapshot format gives the complete field and validation reference.

A replay carries `boardCode`, an ordered array of `{atMs, index}` actions and `endMs`, alongside its version. It starts from the hidden deal rather than from an imported snapshot. The action timeline advances game time before each activation. The final time is advanced even when no action occurs there. This is how a replay can describe a mismatch closing after the final click. Replay format covers the timeline and diagnostic result.

None of these objects contains a browser storage key, a saved size preference, a per-size best record, a focus location or an animation flag. Those values have different lifetimes and authorities. A loaded board's size becomes the chosen size through session replacement; that is a browser consequence of loading, not a separate field in the artifact. A completed import is displayed without recording an import as a new played result.

## Browser text is an explicit boundary

The reproduction panel is a native `details` element with the summary “Reproduce a game”. It contains the Board code input and Snapshot JSON textarea. Editing either field only edits a draft. `Load board` or `Load snapshot` performs the actual load. This separation lets a player inspect and correct copied text without replacing a running game on each keystroke.

`Export snapshot` fills the textarea with a point-in-time representation. The player can select and copy that text manually. There is no dependency on the Clipboard API, no upload step and no account exchange. Export does not put the live session into the imported pause state. If the source game keeps running while the text is copied, the later source position may differ from the exported one.

The Board code control permits 32 characters and trims surrounding whitespace in `useGame.loadBoard`. The parser used inside JSON does not perform that trim. The Snapshot JSON control permits 65536 characters, while decoding separately enforces 65536 UTF-8 bytes. These are different measurements. A text field limit is an input affordance; the decoder remains the format boundary for programmatically supplied text too.

Successful load resets the board's remembered tab stop to its first position through a new session generation. Load and export buttons retain focus, with Resume handling its own disappearing-button focus transition. Focus is not serialized, so sharing a position cannot restore where the sender last tabbed. See Reproduction panel and Focus policy for interface details.

## Core functions and effectful adapters

The pure format functions operate on strings and game data. `parseBoardCode` returns size and seed or `null`; `decodeSnapshot` returns a reconstructed state or `null`; `readReplay` returns a final state or a classified problem. They do not operate browser controls, write storage or read files.

The browser adapter in `session/use-game.ts` decides when accepted data replaces a session. The CLI adapter in `scripts/replay-cli.ts` reads UTF-8 text and converts accepted replay results through `encodeSnapshot`. Pasting that output into the browser adds normal snapshot import behavior, including a pause for unfinished progress. The replay evaluator itself has no pause field.

## Trust and interpretation

All copied or loaded data is untrusted. “Valid snapshot” means that the object satisfies the documented state constraints, not that its claimed result has a verified play history. A hand-edited object can be accepted if its fields remain consistent. That is useful for debugging and does not provide evidence of a person's performance.

Replays give a more explicit history, but they still contain author-supplied actions and times. The evaluator applies normal rules, including ignored activations, and does not attest who supplied the file. There is no authentication or signed result in the current exchange model. Local best moves are local game records, not a remote ranking service.

A board code also reveals enough information for a developer to regenerate the whole deck. That is its purpose. The browser still keeps hidden face identity out of hidden-card DOM content. Those facts are compatible: the shareable deterministic deal is a debugging tool, while the ordinary board presents the information available during play. Import safety describes validation and replacement behavior in more detail.

## Following a reported disagreement

For a generation mismatch, begin in `src/game/deck.ts` and compare the literal vector. For a rejected position, follow `snapshot.ts` into `snapshot-selection.ts` and `saved-format.ts`. For an unexpected action result, follow `replay.ts` into `advanceGame` and `activateCard` in `game.ts`.

A useful report preserves the original artifact and says which boundary was exercised. “The CLI rejected this replay” and “the browser rejected the CLI's output” refer to different decoders. Keeping that distinction often removes an entire round of reproduction work.
# Format versioning guide
This page explains which versions Neon Pairs exposes and how to assess compatibility when its exchange behavior changes.

The current product specification is version 2.2. Board generation, snapshots and replays still use their original format versions. A product release and an exchange format answer different questions: the release says which application behavior was delivered; the format says how an artifact is interpreted. The package's `1.0.0` version is another independent value and does not select a decoder.

## The version map today

| Surface | Version marker | Source authority |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting deal | `np1` prefix inside the board code | `BOARD_VERSION` in `deck.ts` |
| Progress position | Numeric root `version: 1` | `SNAPSHOT_VERSION` in `snapshot.ts` |
| Action timeline | Numeric root `version: 1` | `REPLAY_VERSION` in `replay.ts` |
| Product behavior | Specification status 2.2 | Existing game specification |

The JSON version does not absorb the board generation version. A snapshot is version 1 and contains a separately parsed board code. A replay has the same layering. Its action semantics and its starting arrangement both matter, but they are represented by different fields.

This is why replacing a JSON `version` with a product release string fails. The current readers compare the parsed value directly with their numeric constant. The string `"1"` is also different from number `1`. There is no negotiation, version range or “closest supported version” branch.

## Compatibility follows the reader

An existing snapshot reader accepts exactly seven root fields and three exact selection shapes. An existing replay reader accepts exactly four root fields and two action fields. Adding an optional annotation may look harmless to its writer, but an unchanged reader rejects it. In these formats, an additive field is not automatically a compatible change.

Property order and whitespace are different. Both readers parse JSON before checking key sets, so a reordered object with the same values is accepted. Formatting can still cross the byte limit. An export style change can therefore be semantically neutral for small files and affect acceptance near a size boundary.

Accepted array order depends on the field. A snapshot's matched list is validated by membership and whole-face counts; export sorts it numerically. A replay's action list is chronological data with stable ordering at equal times. Sorting a replay action list to make output look tidy can change its result even if no timestamp changes.

The general policies for future exchange objects and field diagnostics are in Data exchange policy and Import safety. They are separate from the accepted version 1 wire definitions. Reading a policy page does not make the current decoder accept fields absent from its exact-key lists.

## A board prefix fixes more than a seed

The reproducibility specification explicitly ties `np1` to the generation algorithm and says that a generation change requires another version. That includes initial paired-face ordering, Park-Miller constants, rejection sampling and backward shuffle order. A different unbiased shuffle is still a different meaning for the same seed.

An implementation refactor that preserves every generated deck leaves that meaning intact. A change that silently produces different cards for an existing code breaks the artifact even if the code still parses. This is the most direct compatibility promise in the exchange model because a short board code appears inside both JSON formats too.

The current `parseBoardCode` supports one prefix. No older-prefix dispatch table, migration helper or multi-version generation registry exists. Future support cannot be assumed from the fact that the prefix contains a digit. Board code format documents the actual parser and vectors.

## Semantic changes can matter without a new key

A replay's meaning includes advancing time before activation, preserving equal-time array order and resolving a mismatch at its exact closing boundary. Reversing one of those operations would change a version 1 result without changing its object shape. Comparing field lists alone would miss the compatibility effect.

Snapshot meaning includes the lower move bound, the range of pending mismatch time, and the distinction between unstarted and started-zero-move states. Loosening a check can accept objects an older reader rejects. Tightening one can reject previously accepted files. Either observation is more precise than calling the change “validation cleanup”.

Presentation changes have a different scope. Redrawing a face while preserving its numeric matching identity does not alter the generated deck. Changing a visible load notice does not alter accepted JSON. Those changes may need interface or acceptance evidence, but they do not automatically change the exchange format's interpretation.

## What this code does with unsupported data

Snapshot decode returns `null` for an unsupported version; replay read returns the `format` problem. The browser reports its existing generic snapshot failure, while the CLI explains that the file is not a version 1 replay with the exact root fields. Neither tries a best-effort fallback to another version.

There is also no automatic snapshot upgrade on page load. Active progress is not read from local storage. The user explicitly supplies a snapshot through the reproduction controls, and the current decoder accepts or rejects it. Preferences and per-size bests belong to a separate storage contract described in Persistence overview.

The CLI's successful output is version 1 snapshot JSON even though its input is a replay. It does not preserve the replay's actions, and it does not stamp the output with the package release. This conversion can be used as evidence that a replay's interpreted final position is stable across an implementation change.

## Reviewing a proposed change

The useful comparison starts with concrete artifacts. A generation change can be checked against the published seed states and deck. A snapshot change can be checked against an initial position, a one-card position, a pending mismatch and a completed state. A replay change can be checked with equal timestamps, an exact timeout action, ignored activations and an endpoint beyond the elapsed cap.

Those are existing semantic boundaries. They reveal different failure modes: parser acceptance, reconstructed state, action order and output serialization. A test that only checks that JSON parses cannot establish compatibility at the latter three levels.

For an old artifact, ask whether the new reader accepts it and whether it represents the same position or actions. For a new artifact, ask whether the old reader accepts it at all. Exact-key formats often give different answers in those two directions. Recording the direction avoids a vague claim that a change is simply “backward compatible”.

The source currently supplies only single-version readers, not a general migration framework. Any future version handling will need concrete design work at the affected format. The existing boundaries remain the starting evidence: Snapshot format, Replay format and Reproducibility.
# Persistence envelope

This page describes the feature storage envelope and distinguishes it from the preference format already implemented in Neon Pairs.

The source currently serializes a preference aggregate, not a collection of feature records. Its key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and its discriminator is `schemaVersion: 1`. The existing reader and writer continue to use that preference format; values already stored in browsers require a code migration to change shape.

## The feature value boundary

A feature's stored collection has an outer representation and a collection of domain records inside it. The envelope carries the format identity at that outer boundary, before any individual record can be interpreted. Every value a feature adds to browser storage is a JSON object with exactly two keys: "v", the number 3, and "items", the array of records. The records carry the feature's data, while the outer object identifies the representation used to hold that collection.

This makes a feature value inspectable without relying on the name of a variable in the UI. A reader can distinguish an outer format mismatch from a problem in a particular record. The envelope is separate from the record schema, storage key, ordering field and identity scheme. The current preferences implementation stores a selected size and a best-score map rather than feature records.

The envelope also does not change board-code, snapshot or replay formats. Those are interchange representations with their own version identifiers and validation. A snapshot copied by the player is not a preference save, and a replay read by the developer command is not a browser collection. See Format versioning guide and Data exchange policy when following a value across those boundaries.

## The existing aggregate, precisely

The current storage writer does this:

```ts
JSON.stringify({ schemaVersion: PREFERENCES_VERSION, ...preferences })
```

`PREFERENCES_VERSION` is 1. With the ordinary session value, this produces `schemaVersion`, `size` and `bestMoves`. For example:

```json
{"schemaVersion":1,"size":8,"bestMoves":{"4":8,"8":40}}
```

This object remembers a selected 8x8 size, a 4x4 best of 8 moves and an 8x8 best of 40. The score map is keyed by board size rather than represented as a sequence of attempts. It has no recency information. Its version number is not inferred from the suffix on the storage key: the reader checks the numeric discriminator inside the value as well.

There is no feature-envelope serializer or decoder in `src/game/session/storage.ts`. `readPreferences` expects the existing aggregate, and feeding it a feature-shaped collection returns the default preference state. Conversely, no current browser code loads feature records and turns them into the preference map. The two representations have different jobs and are not interchangeable encodings of the same object.

Preferences store documents the complete aggregate reader. Persistence overview explains why active progress is absent from that value.

## What the preference reader actually checks

`readPreferences` starts with `{ size: DEFAULT_SIZE, bestMoves: {} }` as its fallback. It obtains the stored string, passes it through `parseJson`, requires a non-null non-array object, checks the version and selected size, and then checks the score map. A single rejected map entry returns the fallback for the whole preference value.

The object checks are structural, not class checks. `isJsonObject` in `src/game/saved-format.ts` accepts an object if it is non-null and not an array. That helper alone says nothing about which fields are present. The reader supplies the field-specific checks after narrowing the parsed value.

There is a useful asymmetry here. Snapshot validation has an exact-key helper available in the shared format module, but the preference reader does not call it. Extra top-level preference properties are ignored if the fields the reader uses are valid. A successful read returns a freshly constructed `Preferences` value containing only `size` and the validated score map. The current preference format accepts extra top-level properties.

The feature envelope's boundary should not be inferred from that lenience. Its stated outer shape is its own contract. A convenience helper existing nearby does not decide which parser uses it or what a particular version accepts.

## Version labels answer different questions

The project has a product specification version, a preference schema version and explicit interchange format versions. They are not one counter. The current specification identifies itself as 2.2 while the preference discriminator remains 1. A feature envelope uses the numeric version described in its own boundary. A board code's prefix describes its generation algorithm rather than the layout of browser preference JSON.

Keeping those meanings distinct avoids a common support mistake: assuming a newer app release must reject every older saved object. The preferences are accepted according to `PREFERENCES_VERSION` and field validation. The product release number is not read from storage, compared to storage or written into the preference object.

There is no migration chain in the preference store. An unsupported discriminator produces the same fallback as a malformed value. No code attempts to guess an older shape, rename its fields or convert a saved sequence into a best map. A migration requires a code change with observable effects.

## A value moves through several representations

It helps to follow one ordinary preference update from the UI rather than treating storage as a single operation. Selecting a different grid size creates a new game. `replaceGame` copies the session preferences and changes `size` to the new board's side length. React renders using that state. The save effect then calls `writePreferences`, which constructs the versioned object, serializes it and passes the string to the supplied store.

The domain state is therefore not the same thing as the serialized object. `Preferences` has no `schemaVersion` field. The writer adds it at the boundary. The reader removes that boundary concern by returning a `Preferences` value with known fields. This is why callers can use `preferences.size` without repeatedly checking a schema version in components.
