An envelope serves a similar boundary role for its own record collection, but there is no existing generic persistence framework to extend. The source uses direct imports and a two-method store interface. There is no registry, adapter hierarchy or global storage coordinator.

## Empty data and invalid data

An empty preference score map is valid. It means no supported size has a saved best in that aggregate. The selected size is still meaningful. By contrast, an absent score-map field, an array in its place, or a map with an impossible score invalidates the preference value. Missing storage and invalid storage reach the same fallback state through different branches.

For a feature collection, an empty array describes a collection with no records. Corrupt data policy deals with rejection and replacement; it is the place to examine how a failed read interacts with later saving.

Empty data should also be distinguished from unavailable storage. A reader can return an empty state after a denied read, but that return value alone does not prove that the browser is ready to accept a future write. In the preferences API, failure information is intentionally not returned to the caller. The feature failure presentation described in Storage failure policy consequently cannot be obtained just by inspecting an empty map.

## Inspecting a captured value

A useful investigation begins with the exact key and original string. A JavaScript object shown after parsing is already one transformation removed from the browser value. Parse failures depend on the text, while field failures depend on the parsed structure. Retaining the original string in an isolated reproduction makes these stages separable.

For preferences, compare the inner `schemaVersion` with `PREFERENCES_VERSION`, then the selected size with `GRID_SIZES`, then each score key and value with the reader's checks. A key spelled `04` is rejected even though converting it to a number yields 4. A score of 7 for a 4x4 board is rejected because eight pairs require at least eight moves. A value can be syntactically valid JSON while failing either of those semantic checks.

For a feature collection, inspect the outer representation before speculating about domain records. A test result for preference JSON is not evidence about feature-record acceptance. Stored values can share a storage mechanism while using different validators.

# ADR 003: Distribute one HTML file

This record explains the single HTML distribution and the distinction between delivery and source organization.

## Context

A player should be able to save the game, open it later and still have the complete board, artwork and controls. A directory full of scripts, images and fonts creates several opportunities for a copied game to become incomplete. Moving just the HTML can lose a stylesheet; a remote font or sprite can stop loading away from the network. The original distribution discussion therefore focused on what a player actually receives.

The chosen artifact is `dist/index.html`. It contains the script, styles and artwork needed for play and can open directly from disk. The source remains a set of focused TypeScript, TSX and CSS files. Single-file delivery was never an argument for putting the whole implementation into one authored module. Source layout documents the source arrangement.

## Build decision

Vite combines React transformation with `vite-plugin-singlefile`. The main configuration sets the target to `es2023` and disables module preload. A preload helper would have no useful chunks to fetch in the final inline page. The source comment records that reason, and `build-output.e2e.test.ts` inspects the HTML for the unwanted fetch and preload code.

The source `index.html` is an entry document containing a root element and a module reference to `src/main.tsx`. It is not itself the final self-contained game. Copying it before a build would preserve a development entry path rather than deliver the playable artifact. This distinction matters when reporting that an offline test passed.

## What the choice buys

An offline copy is straightforward to archive and pass between machines. Inline SVG faces need no image directory. The system font needs no font request. There is no runtime account or service configuration to carry alongside the file. These choices reinforce the artifact boundary; see ADR 004, ADR 007 and ADR 027.

Browser tests cover the built artifact, including opening from a file URL with network access blocked. This is more informative than observing that a development server happened to have everything cached. The browser test command builds current source before running, so its distribution evidence refers to the current implementation.

## Tradeoffs

A single HTML file gives up separate long-lived asset caches. An update replaces the complete artifact rather than just a changed script. For a small game with generated artwork and no remote resources, that cost was accepted in exchange for reliable copying and local opening. The bundle is still a real bundle, so package size and build output remain relevant; ADR 040 discusses the compact-artifact aim.

Saved preferences are a separate concern. Storage behavior for file URLs varies between browsers. The project uses a local HTTP origin when checking persistence, while direct disk opening checks that the game plays. A usable offline artifact does not promise that every browser treats its file storage like a stable web origin.

The diagnostic face sheet and session harness also have single-file builds, but they are separate outputs under `.art` and `.session`. They are not extra files a player needs, and they are not embedded debugging routes inside the shipped page. ADR 051 explains why that separation is useful.

## The distribution configuration

The same configuration used by the build keeps development watcher exclusions separate from the offline output settings.

```ts
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react';
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { viteSingleFile } from 'vite-plugin-singlefile';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react(), viteSingleFile()],
  // One inline file has no chunks to preload, so leave out the preload helper and its fetch call.
  build: { target: 'es2023', modulePreload: false },
  server: {
    watch: {
      ignored: ['**/.browser-work/**', '**/.playwright-browsers/**', '**/.npm-cache/**'],
    },
  },
});
```
# ADR 057: Split the view by behavior

This record explains the component boundaries and the targeted rendering work that keeps large boards responsive.

## Context

A single game component could contain the select, status, 256 buttons, snapshot editor, timers and storage effects. That would be quick to start and difficult to review once input, import and visibility interact. The project instead separates the view by behavior while keeping the composition easy to follow.

`Game.tsx` is the assembly point. `Controls` owns deal actions, `GameStatus` renders progress and completion, `Board` renders and navigates cards, and `Reproduction` owns the disclosure and drafts. Browser session behavior lives behind `useGame`. These boundaries correspond to real responsibilities rather than a generic component taxonomy.

## Small does not mean responsibility-free

`Card` is a leaf button with the state descriptor, face renderer and event callbacks it needs. `Board` calculates face-up and matched membership and supplies positional props. `useBoardFocus` owns remembered focus and navigation. The session controller decides how an activation changes the game and when browser time is synchronized.

This arrangement prevents a card from reading storage or deciding whether a snapshot load should pause. It also prevents the controller from querying every button to paint its revealed state. Each layer can be understood in terms of the data or browser effect it actually owns. React boundaries explains those connections.

## A concrete rendering concern

The active clock can update often, and a 16x16 board contains many buttons. The board memoizes the face-up set from matched positions and selection, and separately memoizes matched membership. It passes a stable activation callback that reads the latest handler through a ref. `Card` is memoized.

A pure clock tick that preserves selection and matched arrays therefore does not force every unchanged card to render again. The optimization follows an observed repeating update. It is not a reason to make every value global or to hide the data flow behind a subscription framework.

## Styles and tests follow the boundary

Card styles sit with `Card`, board layout with `Board`, status styles with `GameStatus`, and control styles with controls. The diagnostic face sheet renders the actual card outside the main controls to verify that its appearance does not depend on unrelated parent styling. That is useful evidence that the component owns its own presentation.

Focused tests sit near the associated behavior, while browser journeys span the assembled application. The source-size specification aims for 100 lines per TypeScript file and limits authored files to 200 lines. The audit checks that ceiling. These constraints keep authored files reviewable.

## Alternatives

A monolithic component would reduce imports but mix unrelated reasons to change. Splitting every few lines into a new component would create indirection without a stable behavior boundary. A generic reusable-control framework could add configuration for cases this game does not have. The chosen middle ground uses small named pieces with concrete jobs.

Props do repeat some data, but that repetition is visible and type checked. A reviewer can trace how a closed card receives `null` instead of a face ID. Hiding that relationship behind an ambient store would make the information boundary harder to inspect.

## Consequences

More files mean more navigation, so direct imports and meaningful ownership matter. The payoff is that a focus bug, parser fix or status-layout change usually has an identifiable home. ADR 001, ADR 016, CSS organization and Source layout are the companion pages. The aim is understandable behavior with targeted rendering work, not file count as an end in itself.

## Stable card inputs in the board

The board keeps membership calculations and callback identity stable across clock-only renders, while the latest controller callback remains reachable.

```tsx
const { size, deck, matched, selection } = game;
  const { viewport, element, focused, focusRemembered, navigate, cardFocused } =
    useBoardFocus(size);
  useImperativeHandle(ref, () => ({ focusRemembered }), [focusRemembered]);
  // A clock tick keeps both arrays, so the cards' props stay equal and no card renders again.
  const faceUp = useMemo(() => faceUpCards({ matched, selection }), [matched, selection]);
  const matchedCards = useMemo(() => new Set(matched), [matched]);
  // The game passes a new handler on each render. Cards keep one callback that calls the latest.
  const latestActivate = useRef(activate);
  useLayoutEffect(() => {
    latestActivate.current = activate;
  });
  const activateCard = useCallback((index: number) => latestActivate.current(index), []);
  const style: BoardStyle = { '--grid-size': size };
```
# ADR 054: Verify complete player journeys

This record explains why acceptance combines rule evidence with complete input, reproduction and delivery journeys.

## Context

A game can pass isolated assertions and still fail at the boundary between them. A new deal can look correct until an old mismatch callback closes a newly revealed card. A loaded snapshot can look correct until its Resume button disappears with focus still on it. Acceptance needs sequences that cross those boundaries.

The decision is to express acceptance as journeys tied to the existing product requirements. The acceptance specification explicitly says those examples add no rules beyond their defining documents. This record explains why journeys are useful evidence rather than another source of behavior requirements.

## The highest-value sequences

The play journey completes every supported size and checks move accounting, matches, misses and best records. The interruption journey starts or restarts during a mismatch and waits beyond the old interval. The keyboard journey enters the board, learns names, resolves turns, completes, leaves with Tab and starts again.

Reproduction journeys round-trip snapshots, reject malformed drafts and load unfinished progress. They attempt input while paused, Resume and check remaining active time. Delivery opens the freshly built HTML from disk with requests blocked, while persistence uses an HTTP origin. Each sequence joins behaviors that separate unit tests cannot establish by themselves.

## Example: a stale callback

A focused game test can prove that `createGame` returns zero moves and a closed selection. A session test can prove that a mismatched generation is ignored. The browser journey supplies the final connection: perform the mismatch, restart through the actual control, reveal a card and let earlier work become due. The newly revealed card must reflect the current game, not an old callback.

This is not redundant testing of one function at three levels. Each level answers a different question about the same product risk. Session module, ADR 013 and Regression catalogue explain the related mechanics.

## Example: accessibility as a sequence

A button can have a correct name in isolation while the whole game is difficult to traverse. The complete 4x4 keyboard journey checks controls, positional names, revealed faces, turn feedback, final summary and exit. Browser accessibility-tree evidence makes those observations reviewable.

A screen reader was not run during the recorded automated verification. Spoken confirmation belongs to user acceptance, as does the real-device long-press context menu. Keeping those boundaries explicit makes the automated evidence credible rather than overstating what browser automation can observe. Screen reader notes gives the player-facing account.

## Why not only end-to-end tests

Journey tests are expensive places to enumerate malformed JSON or every seed rejection edge. Focused tests isolate those cases faster and report more local failures. Acceptance selects meaningful combinations and user-visible consequences; it does not replace the core test suite.

Likewise, a screenshot at the end of a game cannot establish every transition that led there. Exact clock edges and parser invariants need structured assertions. The strategy uses complementary evidence rather than demanding that one test style prove everything.

## Build provenance and limitations

The browser command type checks and builds current source before journeys begin. Diagnostic entries are built separately, and the wrapper records runtime versions. A passing journey therefore has a concrete artifact and tool context. It still does not establish behavior on every browser, device or unsupported gesture.

Acceptance, ADR 017, ADR 018 and ADR 051 are the companion references. The decision keeps acceptance close to the player's actual task while preserving a clear boundary between requirements and examples that demonstrate them.

## The fresh-build browser command

The command sequence ties journeys to current source. A failed game or diagnostic build prevents the browser test process from running.

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite --host 127.0.0.1",
    "typecheck": "tsc -p tsconfig.app.json && tsc -p tsconfig.node.json && tsc -p tsconfig.e2e.json",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "build": "npm run typecheck && vite build",
    "build:art": "vite build --config vite.art.config.ts && vite build --config vite.session.config.ts",
    "test:e2e": "npm run build && npm run build:art && node --test --test-concurrency=1 \"tests/*.e2e.test.ts\"",
    "replay": "node scripts/replay.ts",
    "format": "prettier --write .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check ."
  }
}
```
# ADR 041: Allow short names as typed

This historical record explains the retired one-to-thirty-two-character name limit and literal storage choice.

Status: Superseded by Name length policy

## Original context

The early name-entry discussion favored a small amount of validation. Names were expected to be short labels, not account identities, and the team wanted to avoid transforming a person's text unexpectedly. The initial rule allowed names with 1 to 32 characters and stored them exactly as typed.

That choice belonged to an earlier interface design discussion. The game has no player-name entry field in its current control tree. Its text fields are a board code and snapshot JSON, with format-specific limits.

## Decision as originally made

The lower limit excluded an empty label. The upper limit was intended to keep an entry reasonably compact on a phone while allowing more than a very short nickname. Saving the original text was meant to preserve capitalization, spacing choices and the visible spelling a person had entered.

The team treated name validation as a presentation concern rather than an identity-verification system. No account lookup or remote uniqueness check was involved. That matched the broader local-game approach: a label helped readers recognize an entry, but did not establish a trusted person behind a result.

## Reasoning

Transforming text can surprise people when the displayed result differs from the field they submitted. Literal storage looked easy to explain and easy to debug: the saved value would match the original draft. A modest length range appeared sufficient for a prototype with only a few entries.

A larger range would have made wrapping and compact layouts harder to assess. A much smaller range risked excluding ordinary names without a clear gameplay reason. The original 32-character ceiling was a pragmatic visual estimate, not a result derived from the deck or scoring model.

## Alternatives considered then

Fixed abbreviations would have kept rows compact but shifted the burden to users to shorten their own labels. Automatically truncating would have silently changed identity cues. Rejecting a long draft was considered clearer than saving a shortened version that might become ambiguous.

The literal-storage choice also avoided deciding which edits were harmless cleanup and which changed the user's intended name. That restraint had an appeal, but it left several text questions outside the simple range check: what counted as a character, how visually identical strings compared, and how invisible spacing affected display.

## Why the record is superseded

The old decision's simplicity was incomplete. A numerical range and literal persistence did not by themselves define a predictable text-entry experience. The later policy handles the current name-length decision.

Name length policy is the replacement authority. The top status link matters because a reader finding this record by its title could otherwise treat the old range as current. The historical value is the reasoning about preserving user intent and avoiding silent truncation, not continued authority over accepted input.

## Connection to existing controls

The current board-code field has a 32-character control limit for a completely different reason: its canonical code syntax is bounded and validated by a parser. The snapshot textarea has its own much larger limit plus a UTF-8 byte check. Those limits should not be generalized from this retired name decision.

Text entry policy, Form layout guide and ADR 042 are useful related pages. They concern the interaction around entering and correcting text, while this record preserves one specific historical validation choice.
# ADR 056: Keep one product behavior path

This record explains why the playable game has no feature-flag system and how test switches remain separate.

## Decision

The current game has one supported product behavior for each documented action. It does not choose between old and new turn rules through runtime feature flags. There is no flag client, remote configuration request or player-facing experimental-mode control in the application.

This follows the bounded local scope. A board code should identify the same deck, a snapshot should have the same meaning, and an activation should follow the stated rules. Hidden switches would multiply those interpretations and make a bug report harder to reconstruct unless every switch traveled with it.

## Why a flag system was unnecessary

Feature flags are useful when a deployed service needs staged rollout or different cohorts. Neon Pairs is distributed as a complete offline artifact. A person retains the file they have, and the project can build another revision. There is no runtime service coordinating a rollout across players.

A flag around a changed generator would be especially dangerous if the public code prefix stayed the same. The format version already provides the relevant boundary for generation changes. A flag around an import parser could likewise make the same JSON load on one copy and fail on another without an explicit format distinction. Format versioning guide explains the existing mechanism.

## Branches that are not feature flags

The application naturally branches on state. A mismatch blocks activation; an imported game may be paused; a completed board shows a banner; reduced-motion preference changes effects. These branches express documented session and browser behavior. They are not alternate product experiments controlled by a rollout service.

Tests also have configuration switches. `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION` asks the browser wrapper to verify exact runtime versions. `PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` can select a browser executable. Those values are read in test infrastructure, not by the shipped game to change matching or formats. The source-conventions test limits environment reads to the runners that need them.

## Diagnostic builds are separate

The artwork sheet and session harness are separate entries with separate Vite configurations. They do not use a production flag to reveal hidden test controls inside the game. This keeps the distributed entry focused on documented controls and reduces the risk of shipping a diagnostic branch accidentally.

A hash that secretly switches the face sheet into a session harness would blur that boundary. The art test explicitly checks that such a hash does not change the page's role. ADR 051 explains the evidence structure.

## Alternatives and costs

Keeping an old implementation behind a toggle can make rollback look convenient, but both branches then need coherent tests and format interpretation. A local development boolean is also easy to forget when building the final artifact. For this small game, normal source history supplies the record of retired approaches without keeping them executable in every copy.

The cost is that the game does not support selectively enabling unfinished features for different players. That capability is outside the current product and would require its own design if ever justified.

ADR 016, ADR 027, Source audit notes and ADR 052 explain the neighboring choices. The useful outcome is a reportable behavior path whose important variations are already named in game state, browser preferences and versioned data.

## Environment reads belong to runners

The source convention compares environment-read locations with the command and test runner needs. These are tooling controls, not product rollout flags.

```ts
test('source reads only the environment its command and test runners need', async () => {
  const reads = (await typescriptFiles()).flatMap((file) =>
    [...file.text.matchAll(ENVIRONMENT)].map((match) => `${file.path}:${match[1] ?? match[2]}`),
  );
  const runners = [
    'scripts/replay-cli.ts:INIT_CWD',
    'scripts/replay.test.ts:npm_execpath',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:EXECUTABLE_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:NAMED_COMBINATION_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:NPM_AGENT_ENV',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:TEMP',
    'tests/browser-test.ts:TMP',
  ];
  assert.deepEqual([...new Set(reads.map((read) => read.replaceAll('\\', '/')))].sort(), runners);
});
```
