item.aggregated_output: # Tables policy This page records the markup policy for ordered result data and explains why the current game statistics use a different structure. There is no result table in the current UI. `GameStatus.tsx` displays four properties of a single game in a definition list. Reproduction controls use forms, and the board is a CSS grid of buttons. None of those structures is evidence that ordered records have already been implemented. ## Policy for result data When the content represents records with comparable columns, its relationships need to survive reading beyond the visual arrangement. CSS alone can align text while leaving those relationships absent from the document structure. Ranked or bracket data is a table element with a caption and th scope="col" header cells. The caption identifies the collection being read, while the column headers connect each record's values to their meaning. This is a content-specific policy. It does not make the game board a data table because it has rows and columns, and it does not require converting every compact summary to tabular markup. The distinction begins with what the content means: interactive card coordinates, a property's value and a record in an ordered result collection are different things. No such result feature is present in `Game.tsx`. The policy applies when result data is introduced. Native controls guide discusses the broader preference for native semantics without adding another result format. ## Why the statistics are a definition list GameStatus renders Moves, Pairs, Time and Best as four `dt`/`dd` groups inside a `dl`. Each term names a property of the same current game. There are no peer result rows and no column whose meaning changes with the row being read. The layout happens to use flex and can wrap. At a wide width, those groups may look like cells in a horizontal strip. At a narrow width, they can flow to multiple lines. Neither visual arrangement changes the definition-list relationship. Replacing the wrapper with a table solely to preserve one desktop arrangement would confuse layout with content structure. The Best value is one saved move count selected by current size. It does not present a list of people or a comparison across many records. `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]` chooses the value before it reaches GameStatus. A single local best is not an implemented ordered-results screen. Status bar documents those expressions and labels. The present statistics model has no result columns. ## Why the card board is not a table Board renders a named region containing an inner `div.board` and native card buttons. CSS Grid places those buttons in row order. Each card has its own coordinate and state in its accessible name, and keyboard movement follows a dedicated spatial model. The table policy does not turn that interactive surface into a data table. A card is activated, can reveal a face and participates in remembered focus. A result cell is read as part of a record. They have different purposes even if both appear in a rectangle. There is also no ARIA grid role on the current board. Its native buttons and movement handler implement the specified interaction without declaring a separate composite widget role. Board keyboard navigation traces that behavior. A review of result markup should not accidentally rename or restructure the card controls because the word “row” appears in both contexts. ## What the caption contributes An ordered collection needs context. A visible title elsewhere on a page can be helpful, but a table caption directly identifies the collection associated with the table. That matters when reading the table independently or navigating between document structures. The policy does not specify caption text. The source has no existing results title. A feature's actual subject supplies the wording. Describing that subject is different from attaching a technical explanation of table markup to product copy. A caption also does not supply missing column meaning. A reader needs to know whether a number represents moves, a position in an ordering or another property. The required header cells carry the column relationships; the caption names the whole collection. Combining all labels into a caption would leave the row values harder to interpret. ## Column relationships and reading order The `scope="col"` attribute makes the header's direction explicit. It communicates that the header applies to values down its column. A bold `td`, a styled `div` or text positioned above a column can look similar while having a different structure. A reviewer can inspect the table DOM and the browser's accessibility representation separately from the screenshot. The screenshot establishes visible arrangement. The DOM establishes element choices and attributes. The accessibility view helps establish that the browser exposes a meaningful table structure. No single one of these views proves all aspects of the interface. Row headers, column order, numeric alignment and sorting controls depend on the result feature. The current game has no result implementation with those details. ## Narrow layouts and long values The current game already separates outer page width from board overflow. Result data would have its own content and width behavior; it cannot simply inherit the card board's scroll logic by sharing a class name. A table's relationship between headers and values remains meaningful even when its viewport is narrow. There is no table stylesheet in the source and no prescribed responsive table transformation here. A reviewer can still observe whether a proposed layout makes values readable and associated with their headers. Changing a collection into a stack of unrelated labels solely at a breakpoint can affect more than appearance, so both DOM and visual behavior are relevant evidence. Name text can also vary in width without changing its accepted value. Typography and wrapping are layout concerns. The name policies remain separate from table structure; accepted names retain their displayed representation. Typography and Form layout guide explain nearby layout decisions in the existing interface. The existing accessibility journey covers game controls and completion, not a result table. Evidence for a future result view would identify its actual markup and readable rows; the current statistics tests cannot establish that structure. Accessibility audit provides the wider review context. # Announcements policy This page describes how event feedback is published, repeated and kept separate from routine game rendering. The game has many visible updates, but only some represent a new result. A clock tick is a changing value; resolving a turn is an event. Treating those as the same kind of update would make a memory game noisy and would bury the information a player needs after selecting two cards. ## Publication point `Game.tsx` places the game result between the board instructions and the Board itself. Its paragraph has `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`, with the current feedback inside a span. The page has exactly one live region, the status paragraph in Game.tsx. New status text, such as whose turn it is, goes through that region. The current game publishes pair results and load outcomes there; it has no turn-owner feature. The paragraph remains mounted while its content changes. It is inside `.game-result`, which has a minimum height of `56px`, flex alignment and margins. The wrapper reserves a readable area near the board without making the scrollable card content itself the announcement source. Polite publication allows the browser and assistive technology to schedule the result around other speech. Atomic content indicates that the paragraph's result is treated as a complete update rather than an isolated changed number. These attributes express the intended exposure; the actual spoken experience still needs user acceptance with a screen reader. ## Session data behind the paragraph The session owns `feedback` and an integer `announcement`. Game renders `{session.feedback}`. Updating the key replaces the child span even when its text is identical to the preceding result. This gives repeated events a DOM change without adding a hidden counter to the spoken text. The counter is event identity, not a statistic presented to the player. It does not track moves, matched pairs or elapsed seconds. A failed load can advance it without adding a move, while the first card reveal changes game state without advancing it. A broad render counter would be wrong for this job. Session renders occur for time and selection changes that should not repeat the last turn result. The explicit event field makes the distinction inspectable in `session.ts` and `use-game.ts`. ## Turn results `activateSession` calls the pure `activateCard`. If the game object is unchanged, it returns the current session. If the result has selection kind `one`, it returns the updated game without changing feedback or announcement identity. That covers the first eligible reveal. After the second eligible reveal, the result is either a mismatch or a match. The session builds the appropriate text and increments `announcement`. Completion is checked at this same boundary, so the winning match gets a combined result rather than two competing event publications. | Result | Text produced by the session | | --- | --- | | First matched pair | `Pair found. 1 pair matched.` | | Later nonfinal pair | `Pair found. M pairs matched.` | | Mismatch | `No match. Cards close after a short pause.` | | Winning pair | `Pair found. All pairs found in N moves and time.` | Here `M` and `N` are replaced with the actual counts, and `time` is the output of `formatElapsed`. The singular branch is based on `game.matched.length === 2`. The final branch takes precedence over the nonfinal pair count. A card's accessible name also changes when it reveals or matches. That is the focused control describing its own state, not a second turn-result producer. The text in the event paragraph summarizes what the two-card attempt achieved. Screen reader notes follows those two sources in a complete game. ## Consecutive identical results Two misses in a row produce the same sentence. Updating only a string state can leave the DOM text unchanged, which gives no new mutation for the second event. The keyed span avoids relying on a different visible sentence to distinguish them. The current sequence is concrete. Initial feedback is empty. Revealing index 0 on `np1-4-1` changes selection to `one` without publishing. Revealing index 1 produces a mismatch and advances the event identity. After the interval closes, choosing those two indices again produces the same text with a later identity. The counter advances once for each resolved attempt in that sequence, not once for each card action or timer update. A third activation during the mismatch is ignored by the game and leaves the event unchanged. The same is true of a repeated activation on the first revealed card. There is no temporary blanking timeout between identical results. The implementation does not clear text, wait a guessed number of milliseconds and restore it. That avoids adding announcement timing to the game clock or introducing a second lifecycle that can outlive a replacement game. ## Changes that stay quiet `tickSession` advances the game and returns a new session with that game, leaving feedback and announcement fields intact. Mismatch closure is part of this advancement. It does not publish a new “cards closed” result. The earlier mismatch sentence already told the player that closure would follow a short pause. Arrow movement is local board focus state. It does not call the session feedback path. Clock renders update Time in GameStatus, while card memoization prevents unchanged cards from rendering again. Neither operation is a new turn result. New Game and Restart call `replaceGame` with `imported: false`. That replacement clears the prior feedback and load notice while keeping the announcement number. A successful board-code load follows the same replacement path. These operations clear old context; the current source does not add a success sentence for a board-code load. Clearing text is still a DOM change and may appear in a mutation trace as an empty result. It is different from republishing a turn sentence. The accessibility journey's expected record includes the new-game clearing event, so a raw count of every mutation is not a substitute for reading what each event contains. ## Load outcomes share the publication path The controller's `notice(feedback)` helper assigns both `feedback` and `loadNotice`, then increments `announcement`. Invalid Board code publishes `Invalid board code.`; invalid Snapshot JSON publishes `Invalid snapshot.`. Repeating the same invalid submission is a new load attempt and advances the identity again. For valid snapshot import, `replaceGame(..., true)` increments the identity and publishes either `Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.` or `Loaded completed snapshot.`. The former corresponds to a paused unfinished game, the latter to completed progress. Valid board-code loading does not use the imported-snapshot branch. Reproduction also renders `loadNotice` in its ordinary paragraph with id `load-notice`. The load buttons reference it through `aria-describedby`. That keeps the outcome visible beside the text tools and associates the description with their actions without creating another event publisher in that panel. Resume clears feedback and loadNotice without increasing the event identity. It also transfers focus to the board before its button disappears. Reproduction panel and Focus policy describe those effects independently of event publication. ## Completion and persistent reading GameStatus shows a completion paragraph whenever `isWon(game)` is true. A newly won game can give it the celebration class; an imported completed game shows it statically. That paragraph is persistent reading content containing the final moves and time. The winning turn's feedback already contains the match and win in one result. The status paragraph does not need to separately announce a matched pair, then publish a second completion sentence. This avoids having two updates compete at the most significant turn in the game. A completed snapshot instead publishes its load outcome, because import is the event that just occurred. The game is visibly complete, but no new card match happened. This distinction preserves a useful account of what the user actually did. ## Automated evidence `session.test.ts` checks that first reveal, mismatch closure and repeated mismatch events affect announcement identity as expected. It also checks import outcomes and completion transitions without involving the browser. `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes DOM mutations in the status paragraph. It resolves a mismatch, moves focus, runs the mismatch interval and repeats the same attempt. The expected result history contains the mismatch sentence once for each resolved turn, with no extra result from movement or closure. The same test submits each snapshot load kind and each invalid-load kind twice, checking the publication history and the visible load notice. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` checks that the result remains beside the board during large-phone play and that the reproduction panel has no competing result role. The accessibility journey reads Chromium's tree for the polite and atomic properties and the result text at each turn. That establishes exposure in the tested runtime. Spoken scheduling and verbalization are assessed in user acceptance. The repository records spoken review as user acceptance. ## Diagnosing a repeated or missing result A missing second identical result suggests checking event identity before changing the sentence. A repeated result on every clock tick suggests checking whether routine advancement touches the publication fields. A load notice visible near the textarea but absent from event output suggests checking whether the controller used `notice` or only changed local text. For a report, the useful sequence is the action, feedback string, announcement number and observed mutations. That evidence can show whether the session failed to publish, React had no relevant change or the browser exposed the expected update but a spoken review behaved differently. The policy gives a single publication boundary; diagnosis follows it from the event to the paragraph rather than adding more announcers around the page. # Focus policy This page records focus behavior in the current game and the policy for a feature that changes the main screen. Focus tells a keyboard user where input will go next. It is related to game selection but is not stored as part of a turn or snapshot. The current interface deliberately keeps deal-action focus, remembered board focus and card reveal state as distinct things. ## Existing page and future screens `Game.tsx` currently renders one main area with an h1, deal controls, statistics, instructions, turn output, the Board and reproduction controls. It has no alternate-screen branch or screen-level h2 focus target. Replacing a deal remounts the board within that page; it does not replace the page with a different screen. A feature that introduces a screen replacement has a different orientation problem from resetting a deck. When a feature replaces what the main area shows, focus moves to that screen's h2, which has tabindex="-1". This gives the new screen a programmatic landing place without adding that heading to ordinary Tab traversal. The current deal and load callbacks can still be understood on their own terms; they are not evidence that such a screen transition already exists. The policy applies to the feature-level replacement described here. Expanding native details, updating statistics, closing a mismatch or displaying the completed-game paragraph does not currently create a new screen. Those operations retain the page structure and follow the existing behavior below. Dialog policy covers a separate interaction with its own opening focus. ## Initial load is quiet The hook `useBoardFocus(size)` initializes `focused` to zero. Board gives index 0 a tab index of zero and the other card buttons a tab index of minus one. This makes the first card available on entry, but no mount effect calls its focus method. The browser's current focus therefore remains where it is at initial load. The page does not jump down to the board before a player has found Grid size or New Game. The board help paragraph describes how to enter and operate it. Its region uses `aria-describedby="board-help"` to associate those instructions with the board. A remembered entry point is often described casually as “focus on the first card.” In this code that wording is incomplete. There is an entry point ready at the first card, while actual focus may be on the document, a deal button or another native control. Keeping those concepts separate prevents accidental mount-time focus stealing. ## Deal actions retain their location New Game and Restart are native buttons that call the session controller. Neither callback moves focus into the board. After either action, a keyboard user remains on the button they used and can repeat the action or Tab toward the board. The size select uses its native interaction and likewise does not issue a board focus call. The replacement increments `session.generation`, used as Board's React key. The newly mounted hook begins with a remembered index of zero. Thus the next board entry goes to the first card, even if the previous deal's memory was near its end. Actual action focus and future board entry are updated through different mechanisms. A valid board-code load also increments generation. BoardCodeForm focuses its Load board ref on successful submission because its input is keyed by generation and will be replaced. That is especially important when the action was Enter in the input. An invalid submission keeps the input node and does not call the button ref, so correction can continue in place. Clicking the load button starts with focus on that button, and an invalid click leaves it there. The distinction is based on the action's origin and successful input replacement, not on a general rule that all errors move focus into a field. Error display guide follows those cases in detail. ## Remembered board focus Board focus memory is a local hook state containing a card index. The `onFocus` callback updates it whenever a card receives focus. Board renders exactly that index with `tabIndex={0}`. All other cards remain programmatically focusable with `tabIndex={-1}`. Arrow movement uses the DOM order of the deck and never changes game selection on its own. Tab and Shift+Tab are left to the browser, so the board is one stop in the page sequence rather than a trap. Returning to it finds the last focused card, even if that card is now matched. Matched positions stay in the navigation geometry. A player does not need to relearn how many arrow presses separate two coordinates after a match. During a mismatch, focus can also move while activation is blocked. The same is true while imported unfinished progress waits for Resume. Board keyboard navigation provides the calculations and edge behavior. ## Resume transfers before removal Resume is the current exception to retaining focus on the action button. It exists only while `session.paused` is true. Clearing that flag removes the button, so leaving focus there would leave a disappearing target. In `Game.tsx`, the local `resume()` function first calls `board.current?.focusRemembered()` and then `controller.resume()`. Board's imperative method focuses the remembered card with `preventScroll: true` and then brings it into view. Only after that does the controller clear the paused state and notices. The ordering is observable. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` installs a focus listener and confirms that Resume is still present when the card receives focus. A visual assertion after the fact would not establish this timing. The focus-entry test also remembers a far card on a large imported board, scrolls away and confirms that Resume returns to that location with nearest alignment. The remembered location after import is initially the first card because the import replaced the board. The player can change it while paused. Resume uses that current memory rather than the snapshot's revealed index or a hard-coded first card. A snapshot stores game progress, not the browser's last navigation location. ## Visible focus and scroll clearance `game.css` defines `:focus-visible` as a `3px` white outline with a `2px` offset. `card.css` gives cards `scroll-margin: 6px`. This combination accommodates the ring when the card is brought to the edge of the scroll area. The focus hook uses `card.matches(':focus-visible')` before scrolling in `cardFocused`. Keyboard movement can scroll immediately; pointer focus avoids moving a card under a held press. Board scrolls a clicked card after the click completes. The timing is part of reliable focus behavior, not only a visual polish detail. `useNearestScroll` stores the board's last reported scroll position, restores it and then invokes `scrollIntoView` with nearest alignment. The source records the Chromium-specific reason: Tab or Shift+Tab can center a newly focused card before the handler runs. Starting from the prior view preserves the player's location as much as possible. The helper leaves the outer page's scrolling to the browser. A review therefore measures both the card inside the board viewport and its visibility inside the window. A ring can be uncut by the board yet still sit partly below the window if the outer document did not move appropriately. ## Focus is not completion feedback Winning does not move focus to the completion paragraph in GameStatus. The final card stays the current control, and the completed summary becomes available in document order. The final turn's feedback is published through the game's event output. The component does not force the player to leave the board simply because all pairs are now matched. Likewise, a mismatch closing does not restore focus to either of its cards. Focus may have moved elsewhere while the pair was visible. The game-state update closes the faces while the user's navigation choice survives. An ordinary clock tick also leaves focus untouched. These examples are useful when evaluating a proposed effect that focuses something whenever `game` changes. Game changes for elapsed time, first reveals, turn results and resets. An effect tied to that broad object would combine very different events and could interrupt typing or navigation. The existing code places its explicit focus operations at narrower action boundaries. ## Review evidence The keyboard browser check covers Tab exit, remembered re-entry and matched-card focus. `tests/status-controls.e2e.test.ts` covers Enter submission from Board code. `tests/focus-entry.e2e.test.ts` covers nearest alignment and the switch from pointer use to keyboard arrows. `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` checks outline clearance on large boards, including an interior card where container padding alone cannot protect the ring. A useful focus report names the source control, action, destination and whether the source remains mounted. For example: “Enter in Board code loads 6x6, replaces the input and leaves Load board focused.” That is more precise than “load focuses correctly,” and it exposes why failure has a different result. Interface review checklist gathers these journeys with layout and input checks. For new screen work, the source review begins by locating the actual replacement boundary. For changes within the existing game page, it begins with the current action-specific behavior above. Screen replacement and the established board lifecycle have separate focus behavior. # Name length policy This page defines how the name-length check is interpreted and separates it from native text-field limits. The current game has no person-name field or name validator. Its existing text limits belong to Board code and Snapshot JSON. They are useful examples of browser entry constraints, but neither is an implementation of the name policy on this page. ## The checked value The length check concerns the accepted name representation, after the processing described in Text entry policy. Counting the raw draft instead can produce a different result from counting the value that the feature will store and display. A name has 2 to 20 Unicode code points after normalization. Anything else blocks the action and shows "Use 2 to 20 characters." This check therefore belongs at the point where a draft would become an accepted name, rather than being inferred from the field's apparent width. The message is the user-facing explanation of this failure. The numerical bounds are inclusive: the endpoints pass, and values outside them fail. The policy does not define an exception for a one-character name, a separate limit for a family name or an alternate bound for another script. A failure blocks the action that is trying to accept the name. It is not a request to silently cut the entered value to fit. Truncating a longer string would accept a different name and would conceal which action failed. The policy specifies feedback and blocking rather than a repair that guesses the user's intended spelling. ## Code points, code units and visible text JavaScript string `.length` counts UTF-16 code units. That is not always the number required here. Many characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane occupy two code units but one Unicode code point. For example, `A😀` has three code units and two code points. A user-perceived symbol can also contain several code points. An emoji sequence joined with a zero-width joiner may look like one symbol while contributing multiple points. A base letter plus a combining mark can be another example, depending on whether canonical composition produces a single point in the accepted form. The policy chooses code points, not rendered glyph count or grapheme cluster count. A font can draw two code points as one ligature, and an input method can produce a composed-looking sequence. Neither observation changes which unit the check uses. Reviewing only a screenshot cannot establish that the correct unit was counted. In JavaScript, iterating a string by code point is different from indexing its individual UTF-16 units. `Array.from(value).length` or a spread-based count illustrates that distinction for well-formed text. This is an explanatory example, not a requirement to allocate an array in a particular implementation. The source has no name helper. ## Boundary examples The examples below assume that the value shown is already in its accepted representation. They illustrate the count, not an additional character allowlist. | Value | Code-point count | Length result | | --- | --- | --- | | Empty string | 0 | Fails | | `A` | 1 | Fails | | `Al` | 2 | Passes | | `A😀` | 2 | Passes | | Twenty ASCII letters | 20 | Passes | | Twenty-one ASCII letters | 21 | Fails | | Twenty supplementary-plane symbols | 20 | Passes | The supplementary-plane example can expose a validator that accidentally uses `.length`: it sees forty code units instead. The opposite mistake is counting a joined visual sequence as one merely because it occupies one displayed cell. A correct boundary check is about the string's code points after representation processing. “Passes” here means that the length condition is satisfied. It does not imply that an action with other applicable checks is guaranteed to succeed. The Duplicate names policy addresses a separate group-level condition without changing the unit used by this check. ## The order is observable A raw draft may have surrounding or repeated spacing that will not be retained in its accepted form. Counting before the representation step can reject a value that would fit after processing, or accept a value whose later transformations were not what the length helper expected. The policy's ordering avoids having the stored name disagree with the checked name. A reviewer can follow one candidate from field submission to accepted model and then display. The decisive value is the same one used for the count. An implementation that checks one temporary string but saves a different raw draft has two representations and cannot establish the stated condition simply by having a correctly named length function. There is no instruction here to run the full action after every individual keystroke. Composition and editing are part of the input experience. The check governs acceptance, while timing of draft feedback is not otherwise specified by the current code or this policy. ## Scope of current evidence There is no name-length test in the repository. Keyboard and reproduction checks establish native field labels, draft preservation and load outcomes. They do not verify the name count merely because they type strings into controls. When this policy is implemented, its evidence can name the processed candidate and observed outcome at the boundary. That is enough to distinguish a counting defect from a display problem or another group-level validation failure. The policy stays narrow: one accepted value, one counting unit, one inclusive interval and the stated blocking message. # Duplicate names policy This page explains the group-level name comparison policy and the distinctions a reviewer needs when checking it. The current source has no name list or group editor. A board code identifies a deal, a card label identifies a position and face state, and a local best is indexed by board size. None of those is a collection of person-entered names. The policy below belongs to a feature that introduces such a collection. ## Comparison boundary The group being edited supplies the comparison scope; the draft alone cannot establish whether it repeats an existing entry. The candidate's accepted representation comes from Text entry policy. Names in one group compare without regard to case, after normalization. A repeat blocks the action and shows "Each name must be different." This lets the same visible spelling with different capitalization be recognized as a repeat without requiring that all displayed names be rewritten in one case. The scope is one group. Neon Pairs has no global name registry across devices, browser origins or unrelated groups. A local comparison can answer whether an entry repeats within the group being acted on without implying that the person owns a unique account name. The check concerns names, rather than board positions or face identities. Two cards intentionally share a face, and a replay can intentionally activate the same position more than once. Those repetitions follow their own game rules. A generic “remove duplicates everywhere” helper would not express this policy's subject or scope. ## Display value and comparison value Case-insensitive comparison does not by itself prescribe changing a name's displayed capitalization. `Mira` and `mira` can compare as the same candidate while the accepted display spelling remains the one chosen by the person who entered it. Showing a lowercased comparison key as the name would conflate two purposes. A useful implementation trace therefore distinguishes the value displayed, the value accepted into the group and whatever representation is used to compare it. The comparison representation is an internal tool. It is not a new user-visible identifier, a format field or a replacement for the accepted name. The policy does not specify locale selection or a particular Unicode case-folding API. That matters for names whose case behavior differs across languages or scripts. Name normalization retains diacritics and does not transliterate names. Examples with ordinary Latin letters illustrate the unambiguous case while case behavior across Unicode varies. The representation step is also not a license to treat all visually similar strings as equal. Latin and Cyrillic lookalikes, differing accents and compatibility characters can resemble one another without being the same processed string. Visual similarity would be a broader identity rule than the policy states. ## Small examples | Existing accepted name | Candidate | What the example demonstrates | | --- | --- | --- | | `Mira` | `Mira` | A direct repeat | | `Mira` | `mira` | Capitalization does not distinguish the names | | `Mira` | `MIRA` | The comparison is not limited to the first letter | | `Ada Lovelace` | The same name after representation processing | The comparison uses accepted name text | | `Mira` in another group | `Mira` in this group | The stated scope is the group being edited | These cases are illustrations of the policy rather than a complete Unicode test corpus. They also do not decide length validity; Name length policy covers that independent check. A candidate can satisfy length and still repeat an existing name. A group with several entries can expose a bug that a two-entry example misses. If only the immediately preceding name is checked, a repeat of the first entry can slip through after a different middle entry. The policy speaks about the group, so the relevant evidence is membership across that group rather than adjacency in the rendered form. ## Blocking has a concrete meaning A repeated candidate does not become an accepted additional name as part of the failed action. The exact feedback above explains why acceptance stopped. Automatically adding a suffix, changing capitalization or deleting one of the existing names would implement a different outcome from the one stated. This policy does not decide which error wins when several checks fail at once. It also does not add live validation on every keystroke, a suggestion picker or a search across previous games. Those are separate interaction choices, and none is present in the source. The current reproduction handlers demonstrate an explicit acceptance boundary: parse first, replace only on success, otherwise publish a notice. A name feature can be reviewed with the same question—where does a candidate become accepted?—without reusing the board parser or claiming that load errors are name errors. Error display guide provides the current feedback mechanics. ## Evidence a reviewer can assess Because no name feature exists, the existing tests do not establish this policy. A screenshot containing distinct visible names would be weak evidence even for a future feature: the comparison bug might only appear on submission, on an edit or after a change in capitalization. Useful examples include an exact repeat, a case-only repeat, a repeat that is not adjacent in the displayed list and a different accepted name. An edit scenario reveals whether the current entry is being confused with another entry. A separate-group example reveals whether an implementation accidentally enforces a broader scope than the policy states. For a defect report, the accepted group values, candidate value, action and observed message make the comparison reproducible. Display order can be recorded as context, but it does not define identity. The policy stays about equality within the group, and its representation and length dependencies remain in their own linked pages. # Competition results and local records This page explains the boundary between competition play and the ordinary saved preferences in Neon Pairs. The solo application stores a preferred board size and best move counts by size. Those values describe ordinary use of the device, rather than named participants. Competition introduces a different context for completed games, so reusing the solo session without examining its side effects can produce a correct-looking board and incorrect saved preferences. ## The competition boundary A shared device may already contain records from someone who is not taking part in the event. Tournament games never change best scores or the saved board size. This separates the event's results from the device's ordinary play preferences without changing the meaning of a completed memory board. For example, suppose the saved size is 10 and the saved best for size 4 is 12 moves. A competition attempt can produce a completed four-column board with 8 moves while those ordinary saved values remain size 10 and best 12. The game result and the preference record describe different things; the competition boundary prevents one from being substituted for the other. The comparison between participants is in competition ties. Competition adds no extra points, multiplier or group total. In the existing core, progress is the number of matched pairs, and a completed game also has its move count and elapsed time. ## What the game saves today `src/game/session/storage.ts` defines `Preferences` with a numeric `size` and a `bestMoves` map keyed by size strings. `PREFERENCES_KEY` is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`. `writePreferences` serializes a schema version together with those values. An example stored value is: ```json { "schemaVersion": 1, "size": 10, "bestMoves": { "4": 12, "6": 24 } } ``` There are no participant names or board codes in that value. A best belongs to a board size across ordinary games, rather than to a particular generated deal. A person who sees the size-4 best is not seeing the result of the current board code unless the circumstances happen to coincide. The reader validates the schema version, supported size and best-score map. Score keys have to represent supported sizes in canonical numeric-string form. Values are nonnegative safe integers within the move cap and at least the number of pairs for that size. An invalid record falls back to default preferences rather than being partly interpreted as an event history. Preferences store and best score records explain the ordinary mechanism. The competition decision does not add fields to this saved value or define another persistence format. ## Two ordinary paths have side effects The first path is game replacement. `replaceGame` in `src/game/session/session.ts` copies preferences and assigns `size: game.size`. The ordinary browser actions for starting a new deal, restarting and successfully loading a board or snapshot use that replacement function. Its purpose is to keep solo play's chosen size in sync with the current game. The second path is completion. `activateSession` calls `activateCard`, recognizes a won game and calls `rememberBest(session.preferences, game.size, game.moves)`. That helper compares the new moves with the previous entry for the size. A better value produces a new map, while an equal or worse value returns the original preference object. Both behaviors are correct in the current solo context. Both matter to a competition extension. Avoiding the completion update alone would still leave size changes on the replacement path. Avoiding size selection alone would still leave a best-score update when ordinary activation completes a game. There is no competition argument or mode check in either function. The source therefore does not currently implement the boundary described on this page. This is a concrete integration gap, not an indication that `rememberBest` has the wrong behavior for its existing caller. ## Where saving actually happens `useGame` reads preferences at initialization and calls `useSavedPreferences(store, session.preferences)`. That hook has an effect that invokes `writePreferences` whenever the preference object or store dependency changes. It also runs when mounted. Consequently, hiding the Best statistic would not prevent saved records from changing. The display does not own the write. Similarly, suppressing one call to `localStorage.setItem` would not explain what happened to the in-memory preferences that a later effect might serialize. The distinction between values and writes is useful here. The competition sentence concerns the best-score and size values. It does not itself introduce a blanket prohibition on all storage API calls. A review that counts only writes can miss an in-memory change; a review that looks only at the current screen can miss a persisted change after reload. `rememberBest` returning the original object for equal or worse ordinary results can reduce preference effect activity. That identity behavior is an implementation detail with a clear purpose, but it is not a substitute for deciding which context owns a completion. Persistence overview and React boundaries cover those existing responsibilities. ## Why completed snapshot import is a partial analogy The current solo application already treats imported completion differently from completion through card activation. `replaceGame(session, game, true)` sets the imported state without calling `rememberBest`. A completed snapshot arrives with its banner static and without a celebration. An unfinished imported game can later be resumed and completed through ordinary activation, which can record a best. That existing distinction is helpful evidence that rendering a won board and recording a local best are separate operations. It is not a complete solution for competition: snapshot replacement still updates the preference size, and later completion of unfinished imported progress follows the ordinary best-score path. `src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks those differences. It verifies that normal completion records a best, completed import does not, and finishing restored incomplete progress can record one. Reading the full set of assertions prevents an engineer from generalizing the completed-import exception to every game associated with a snapshot. ## A concrete review example Begin conceptually with the saved value shown above and a competition board at size 4. There are two distinct moments to inspect: the moment the board replaces the previous game, and the moment its final pair is activated. In the unmodified solo session, the former can change size to 4 and the latter can improve its stored best to 8. The boundary for competition preserves the original values through both moments. This example exposes both source paths with a small amount of data. It is more informative than starting from empty preferences, because an empty map makes an accidental new best look like an ordinary first result. A further comparison with ordinary solo play matters when reviewing an implementation. The existing solo behavior still provides the baseline: `tests/persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` exercises better, equal and worse completed results across reloads, as well as successful and unsuccessful load effects on saved size. Those tests describe the current game; they do not exercise a competition screen. The useful evidence is the before-and-after preference content alongside the completed game, with the active context made clear. # Competition pairing This page describes entry-order seeding and the opening bracket for shared-device competition. Pairing connects a group of people to an event structure. It is separate from choosing a board, recording a finished attempt or interpreting a tied result. The game has no participant collection; competition extends the existing solo controller. ## From the entry list to the opening matches Entry order gives the group a sequence that can be inspected without any information about previous performance. Seeds follow entry order, so the first player entered is seed 1. A bracket of four meets as 1 against 4, then 2 against 3. A bracket of eight meets as 1 against 8, 4 against 5, 3 against 6, then 2 against 7. This fixes the opening arrangement while leaving the existing memory-game engine concerned with cards rather than people. The ordering of the eight-person case deserves attention. Writing opposite ends of the entry list together produces the right collection of opponents, but a straightforward loop over the first half of the list would display them in a different order. The sequence in the paragraph above is therefore relevant to the shape of the bracket, not just to membership of each opening match. Here is a worked example with eight entrants. | Entry position | Entrant | Seed | | --- | --- | --- | | First | Ada | 1 | | Second | Bo | 2 | | Third | Cora | 3 | | Fourth | Dev | 4 | | Fifth | Emi | 5 | | Sixth | Finn | 6 | | Seventh | Gia | 7 | | Eighth | Hal | 8 | Reading down the opening matches gives Ada with Hal, Dev with Emi, Cora with Finn, then Bo with Gia. This example is useful during a design review because every participant is visibly accounted for, and a swapped middle match is easy to spot. It also avoids relying on the geometry of a bracket drawing to explain who is involved. ## What a seed means here In this scope, the seed identifies a place derived from entry. It is not an estimate of memory skill. The current game has no account history, participant rating or service from which to obtain such an estimate. A developer looking for an existing ranking calculation in `src/game` will not find one. This distinction makes the entry list meaningful to the group. If people entered themselves while passing the device around the table, that physical sequence explains the resulting seed values. Alphabetical sorting would tell a different story; sorting by an ordinary local best would tell a different one again. Neither transformation follows from the entry-order definition above. There is a separate ambiguity between the seed in a bracket and the seed in a board code. `src/game/deck.ts` uses `seed` for the numeric input to deck generation. That number describes an arrangement of cards, not a person. For instance, the last number in `np1-4-73` has no relationship to the entrant in position 73, or to an entrant at all. The shared word is a vocabulary collision between two subjects. Competition deals covers board identity. Competition ties covers result comparison. Neither calculation is present in the current pairing-free source, and neither is needed to explain the opening layout here. ## The small example catches a different mistake With Ada, Bo, Cora and Dev as the complete entry list, the opening matches are Ada with Dev, followed by Bo with Cora. This is not obtained by taking the first two matches of the eight-person example. It is a bracket constructed from the smaller entry list. That observation is useful when reviewing code that represents possible opponents by index. A table of entry positions can be applied to the corresponding list length. A table of names copied from another event cannot. The distinction becomes particularly clear when the same people participate in more than one demonstration but join in a different order. It is also easy for a visual mockup to hide a mismatch between the text and the underlying order. A designer may draw a balanced-looking left and right side while the data is assembled in another traversal. The named example gives reviewers a shared reference independent of whether the visual bracket runs left to right, top to bottom or in a compact list. ## A pairing review on paper A useful review exercise is to write the entry list once, assign its seed values, and trace each participant into the opening layout. In the eight-person example, every name appears once in the opening matches. Each opponent relationship can be checked in both directions: locating Ada also locates Hal; locating Hal leads back to Ada. This exercise reveals three different classes of error. A duplicated participant is a membership problem. Correct opponents in the wrong middle positions are an ordering problem. Correct seed positions attached to the wrong names are an entry-mapping problem. They can produce similar screenshots, but they point to different mistakes in construction. The exercise does not determine who advances. It simply makes the initial structure concrete enough to inspect. Event stages are discussed in competition rounds, and the relationship between an individual finish and local saved results is discussed in competition scores. For an engineer considering test coverage, the two named examples offer direct expectations rather than a second copy of the same pairing algorithm. A test that calculates its expected list with the same loop as the implementation is weak evidence: both can make the same ordering mistake. A literal list of expected opponent names exposes that mistake immediately. ## Unresolved pairing decisions The pairing definition describes the two bracket shapes above. It does not describe a general event for every possible number of entrants. The project has no rule for a vacant place, a late arrival, a withdrawal, replacing a participant or rearranging an event after results exist. These are unresolved product questions rather than branches that can be inferred from a nearest power of two. These boundaries are deliberate. The opening arrangement is small and explicit. General scheduling systems solve much larger problems, but importing their assumptions would add behavior beyond the current game and competition scope. # Competition rounds This page explains the stages of a shared-device bracket and the round text associated with play. A round provides context that the card board cannot provide on its own. A participant may recognize the game immediately and still be unsure where the group has reached. This page concerns that event context; the arrangement of opponents is in competition pairing, and the dimensions of the playing board are in competition boards. ## Names during play The round name describes a stage of the event rather than the current card selection or the number of turns taken. Name each round Quarterfinal, Semifinal or Final, and show it as "Round: NAME" while that round is played. A bracket of four has no Quarterfinal. The resulting vocabulary is small enough for a waiting participant to recognize without interpreting a bracket diagram. For an eight-person event the names progress through Quarterfinal, Semifinal and Final. For a four-person event the names begin with Semifinal and lead to Final. These follow the naming rule. The capital letters in the quoted pattern indicate where the round's name appears. Substituting Semifinal gives `Round: Semifinal`; substituting Final gives `Round: Final`. The pattern does not imply that the screen literally presents the placeholder. It also does not define the name of the participant who is currently using the device. ## Round, match and board are different contexts A round can contain several matches. A match concerns a particular pair of people. The board currently rendered is the puzzle someone is working on. These relationships matter when a screen is refreshed after a handoff: a new game state does not, by itself, establish that the event has moved to another stage. Consider the early part of an eight-person example. The group can still be in its first round while several people have already finished individual attempts. A mockup that advances a round label whenever the completion banner appears would conflate an individual game result with event progress. The existing completion banner reports a board finish; it contains no event interpretation. This is a useful distinction even in static designs. A review can ask what the round text is describing at the exact moment represented by a screenshot. If the answer depends on which person happened to finish last, the design may be mixing stage context with attempt history. The labels above identify the event stage, while the remaining competition pages explain the other subjects. ## What the current status component knows `src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` accepts a `game`, a `best` value and a `celebration` flag. It renders moves, matched pairs, elapsed time, the current best and a completion paragraph when `isWon(game)` is true. It has no round prop and does not query an outer event. The labels in `src/game/status/status-labels.ts` are the four ordinary game statistics. Searching there for the competition round text will not reveal an unconnected implementation waiting to be enabled. The present application simply lacks that event concept. Similarly, `src/game/Game.tsx` is the composition of a solo session. It passes `session.game` to `GameStatus` and uses `session.generation` as the board's React key. Neither operation establishes which stage a group has reached. Status bar explains the existing statistics, and React boundaries explains the surrounding composition. This source boundary is valuable in review. Someone can demonstrate the round text in a prototype without having changed the underlying game mechanics. Conversely, reusing the existing status component does not supply a round label automatically. The product concept and its rendered location are separate matters. ## A generation is not a round counter The `generation` member of `Session` begins at zero in `initialSession`. `replaceGame` increments it when a new game replaces the previous one. The increment lets timer work associated with an earlier game be recognized as stale. It also causes `Game.tsx` to mount a fresh board instance through the keyed component. That counter changes during Restart and successful board or snapshot replacement. A person can perform those actions without any group event existing. Reading generation 2 as the second round would therefore make an event interpretation out of an implementation lifetime counter. The example becomes more concrete during a miss. An ordinary restart clears the previous game and its pending selection. The replacement game has a later generation even though it can have exactly the same board code. The generation's meaning is about callback validity and component lifetime. The board code's meaning is about the deal. Neither is a name for an event stage. `tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` checks the generation before advancing logical time. This check is covered in `src/game/session/session.test.ts`. The test is evidence for game replacement behavior, not evidence for bracket progression. Mismatch interval and new game and restart cover the underlying behavior. ## How a sequence can be reviewed A paper review can show several moments from an event instead of only its opening and final screens. One moment might show a board in progress, another an individual finish, and another a later match within the same round. The round names provide a stable point of reference across those images. The interesting question in that exercise is what changed between images. Card progress can change while the round name remains the same. A different participant can be present while the stage remains the same. Eventually the event context changes as well. Separating those changes makes the review more informative than a single screenshot with every field different. For the four-person example, a screen sequence containing a Quarterfinal would contradict the naming decision above. For the eight-person example, a sequence that jumps straight from the first stage to the Final would be missing context. These are straightforward consequences of the defined stages, and they can be assessed without a complete game implementation. Animations, transition screens, navigation controls and focus destinations are separate interface questions. Focus policy and dialog policy describe the existing interactions.
