# Control bar

This page explains how `Controls.tsx` presents the deal actions and how those actions connect to the session.

The solo bar has a labeled size selector, New Game, Tournament and Restart. It sits above the statistics and board in `SoloGame`, so deal actions and screen entry are available before entering the board. Tournament setup has its own screen and controls; reproduction tools occupy their disclosure below the board.

## Component boundary

`src/game/controls/Controls.tsx` accepts three props: `size`, `newGame(size?: number)` and `restart()`. It does not own a second copy of the selected size, choose a seed, reset a timer or update preferences. Its select is controlled by the `size` prop. That prop comes from `session.game.size`, which makes the displayed choice agree with the board after a size change, board-code load or snapshot import.

The optional argument on `newGame` explains the two call sites. The select converts `event.currentTarget.value` with `Number(...)` and calls `newGame` with that value. New Game calls `newGame()` without an argument. The default in `use-game.ts` takes the current game's size. Restart calls its separate callback. There is no DOM inspection to decide which size to use when either button is pressed.

The select and buttons are native elements. Deal buttons explicitly use `type="button"`; they do not submit the reproduction form farther down the page. The wrapper is a `div` with class `controls`, not a toolbar widget with a separate keyboard model. Tab follows ordinary document order through the select, New Game, Tournament and Restart. Board navigation begins after those controls, as described in Board keyboard navigation.

## Labels and options

`src/game/controls/control-labels.ts` exports `DealControl`. The visible strings are `Grid size`, `New Game` and `Restart`. The label is associated with `id="grid-size"` through `htmlFor="grid-size"`. A user or browser test can therefore find the select by its visible name instead of a CSS class or its position in the bar.

The options come directly from `GRID_SIZES` in `deck.ts`. Their values are the numeric side lengths rendered as native option values, and their text is the side repeated with a lowercase `x`:

| Display | Value | Cards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4x4 | 4 | 16 |
| 6x6 | 6 | 36 |
| 8x8 | 8 | 64 |
| 10x10 | 10 | 100 |
| 12x12 | 12 | 144 |
| 14x14 | 14 | 196 |
| 16x16 | 16 | 256 |

Those are deal sizes, rather than zoom settings. Choosing 16 changes the game to a 16-row, 16-column deck; it does not squeeze the existing sixteen cards into a different arrangement. The larger boards can exceed the available width inside their scroll container. Pointer and touch explains the consequences for reaching cards.

The component itself receives `size: number`, but the session's `newGame` function checks `isValidSize(size)` before making a replacement. That guard is outside the control and also protects callers that do not originate in the native select. The option list is not the only validation boundary.

## Desktop arrangement

`controls.css` uses flex layout with `align-items: end`, `flex-wrap: wrap`, a `12px` gap and a `16px` bottom margin. The size group is another flex row with `align-items: center` and a `12px` gap. The label sits beside its select rather than above it. The outer alignment brings the actions to the same bottom line if control heights differ.

No explicit column count or button width is needed in this layout. Labels and the browser's select affordance contribute to their natural widths. Wrapping is enabled before the phone media query applies, so the bar can also adapt to a constrained content area on a wider window. The maximum content width and page padding come from `game.css`, not the controls stylesheet.

The shared `.control` class comes from `control.css`: `min-height: 44px`, `padding: 8px 12px`, a `1px` neutral border, an `8px` radius, panel background, text color and inherited font. The select and buttons get a pointer cursor. The stylesheet does not replace the select's browser interaction with a drawn menu. Its popup remains the native control's responsibility.

## Phone arrangement

At `max-width: 599px`, `.controls` changes to `align-items: stretch`. The size group occupies the full line with `width: 100%` and `justify-content: space-between`; its label and select move to opposite ends of that row. The direct child buttons each get `flex: 1`, sharing the following row when there is room.

The media query acts on the current DOM hierarchy. Moving a button into an extra wrapper would change the effect of `.controls > button`. A review of such a refactor can compare computed widths and wrapping before deciding that it preserves the arrangement. The apparent simplicity of a wrapper change can hide a layout change on phones.

The breakpoint is not a board-size breakpoint. A 4x4 and a 16x16 game use the same control bar at the same viewport width. The board handles its own width independently. This separation keeps the controls available even when a player has scrolled to the far end of a large board.

## What the actions replace

In `use-game.ts`, `newGame` creates a code using `freshBoardCode(size, current.current.game.seed)`, constructs the new game, resets the clock adapter and commits `replaceGame(...)`. Restart constructs a game from `current.current.game.boardCode` instead. Both begin with a closed selection, no matched positions, zero moves, zero elapsed time and `started: false` because that is what `createGame` returns.

`replaceGame` increments `session.generation`. The Board in `Game.tsx` is keyed by this generation, so it mounts with a fresh remembered tab stop. The BoardCodeForm input is also keyed by generation and receives the current board code as its default value. A reset is therefore observable in several places without each component inventing its own reset event.

The size is saved through the session preferences path. The current size's best record is read independently for the statistics. Choosing a size with no stored record shows `Best: none`; returning to a size with a record displays that size's value. For the exact display boundary, see Status bar and Best score records.

A pending mismatch cannot later alter the replacement deal. Clock reset and generation checks in the session make stale updates harmless. This is why replacing a deal during its short mismatch display is a meaningful controls test, rather than merely checking that the card count changes.

## Focus and continuity

Clicking New Game or Restart leaves focus on the action button. The components do not call `.focus()` on the board after a reset. A user can press the same action again or Tab forward to the new first card. A size change likewise uses the native select interaction rather than an application focus transfer.

Initial page load also does not select a card on the user's behalf. The board's first card is ready as its tab stop, but readiness is separate from current focus. Focus policy describes this distinction and the different treatment needed when Resume removes its own button.

There is no confirmation step in either callback today. Pressing an action replaces the current deal immediately. Do not infer a pending dialog from the text of an action or from the fact that the old game had moves. The separate Dialog policy records the policy for future actions that leave unfinished work.

## A useful review path

The controls checks in `tests/controls.e2e.test.ts` inspect the native option values as well as their displayed text. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks the literal labels. `tests/keyboard.e2e.test.ts` checks the relationship between Restart and the remembered board entry point. Layout coverage includes a narrow `320x640` viewport in `tests/layout.e2e.test.ts` and the equivalent zoom layout in `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`.

These checks cover different failures. A label refactor could preserve a screenshot while breaking name-based selection. A wrapper refactor could preserve all labels while changing the mobile row. A session refactor could keep the bar visually identical while allowing an earlier timer to touch a new deal. Reading the component, CSS and callback together makes those differences visible.

For a manual check, choose a nondefault size, reveal a mismatching pair, then use Restart before it closes. The deck repeats and the counters reset. Use New Game at that same size and confirm that its code changes. Tab into the board after each action to observe the reset entry point. Finally load a valid code of another size from the reproduction panel and look back at Grid size: the controlled select follows the loaded game without another local state update.

# Error message style

This page describes the error wording Neon Pairs currently exposes and the different jobs of browser notices, replay diagnostics and internal exceptions.

The browser has two deliberately short invalid-load notices. The replay CLI gives more specific diagnostics because it works with a file and a structured action list. Neither surface needs to guess who caused the problem. This guide records those existing choices; validation details remain in Import safety policy and the individual format pages.

## The browser notices are exact strings

`SessionNotice` in `src/game/session/session.ts` contains the browser load messages. The invalid notices are “Invalid board code.” and “Invalid snapshot.” `use-game.ts` chooses the appropriate one when parsing fails. It returns before resetting the clock or replacing the game.

| Attempt | Visible error | What was rejected |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load board with an unacceptable code | `Invalid board code.` | The board-code draft. |
| Load snapshot with unacceptable progress | `Invalid snapshot.` | The snapshot draft. |

The noun is useful. A player can distinguish the board field from the larger JSON field without interpreting a generic “Something went wrong”. The wording also avoids an unsupported diagnosis: “invalid” does not assert that the text is corrupted, that the device failed, or that a particular character is responsible.

Both notices end in a period and stand as complete status text. They do not name a function, a parser exception or a schema utility. The code has more knowledge than the short UI exposes, but it does not currently present field-by-field snapshot diagnostics. An example that shows such a diagnostic would describe a different interface.

The related success notices help explain the same design. Unfinished progress says “Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.” Completed progress says “Loaded completed snapshot.” One includes an action because the resulting state needs it. The other reports the state without that instruction. A writing change that makes every load outcome use the same generic sentence would remove useful information.

## Failure preserves the correction context

The browser keeps the entered draft and the current game when a board or snapshot load is invalid. A useful help paragraph can therefore say to correct the text in its field and use the same load action again. There is no need to describe starting over from an empty form, since the current components do not clear failed input.

The board-code path trims surrounding whitespace before calling `parseBoardCode`. The snapshot path validates the whole textarea content. These facts matter when diagnosing a report, but they are not separate error messages. For example, a board code with an unsupported side length still produces the same board-code notice as a code with an invalid prefix.

The board input is an uncontrolled field keyed to session generation. A successful game replacement refreshes it from the active board code. A failed load does not replace the generation, so the draft remains. `Reproduction.tsx` stores snapshot text in local component state. Those are two implementation routes to preserving useful correction context; neither turns the draft into accepted game state.

The notices appear beside the reproduction controls and are also passed through session feedback. A repeated invalid submission is a separate event even if its sentence is identical. Copy review can inspect the text here, while Announcements policy and Error display guide describe its presentation and delivery.

## The replay command has a diagnostic audience

Replay is a developer command rather than a browser control. Run it as `npm run --silent replay -- PATH`. On success it prints the final snapshot JSON to stdout and exits with status 0. On failure it leaves stdout empty, writes a diagnostic to stderr and exits with status 1. This separation allows another program to consume successful output as JSON.

`scripts/replay-cli.ts` builds most failure messages through `fail(file, reason)`. The shape is `Could not replay FILE: reason.` followed by a newline. `FILE` is the argument supplied by the caller. It is not replaced in the message with the internally resolved absolute path. Relative file lookup uses the caller folder, accounting for npm's `INIT_CWD`.

For a file named `broken.json` containing `{`, the diagnostic is:

```text
Could not replay broken.json: the file is not valid JSON.
```

For an absent file named `missing.json`, the message is:

```text
Could not replay missing.json: the file does not exist.
```

A different read failure uses “the file can't be read”. That wording reflects the actual distinction in `isMissing`: `ENOENT` gets the missing-file reason, and other caught read failures get the broader reason. It does not speculate about permissions, locking or a device problem when the adapter has not established that cause.

## Diagnostic specificity follows the parser result

`readReplay` returns either a state or a `problem`, with an optional action position. `ReplayProblem` gives those cases names such as `malformedJson`, `boardCode`, `order` and `index`. The CLI's `PROBLEMS` mapping turns them into explanations. That mapping keeps the core independent of presentation wording.

| Problem kind | Current reason text |
| --- | --- |
| `tooLarge` | `the file is larger than 1048576 bytes` |
| `malformedJson` | `the file is not valid JSON` |
| `format` | `it isn't a version 1 replay with exactly version, boardCode, actions and endMs` |
| `boardCode` | `its board code is invalid` |
| `actions` | `actions must be a list of at most 10000` |
| `endTime` | `endMs must be a nonnegative safe integer` |
| `action` | `needs exactly atMs and index as nonnegative safe integers` |
| `order` | `comes before the previous action or after endMs` |
| `index` | `names a card outside the board` |

For an action-specific problem the CLI inserts a human action ordinal before the reason. The parser's position is zero-based, but the diagnostic adds one. An invalid card index in the second action of `rule.json` therefore reads:

```text
Could not replay rule.json: action 2 names a card outside the board.
```

That number identifies the action's list position. It is not the offending card index. The distinction helps someone find the problem in a longer replay. It also explains why the diagnostic can be useful without quoting the entire action object.

When arguments are absent or there is more than one argument, the command prints its usage line instead of the file-and-reason form:

```text
Usage: npm run --silent replay -- PATH
```

There is no file-specific cause to report in that situation because the invocation itself is unacceptable. The message names the accepted command shape, making the next attempt concrete. Replay format covers the file contents after that invocation succeeds in reading a file.

## Internal exceptions belong to another layer

Not every string containing “Invalid” is an interface notice. `boardCode` and `generateBoard` throw `Error('Invalid board code.')` when called with an unacceptable code. `faceDesign` throws `Error('Invalid face.')` for an invalid face ID. `generateBoard` also guards against unavailable deck entries with “Deck index out of range.”

Those exceptions describe invalid internal calls or an invariant failure. They are not additional browser validation states. The normal browser load path parses the code before creating a game, and snapshot decoding returns `null` for rejected external state. Copying an internal exception into a player help page as though it were a visible notice would confuse these boundaries.

Likewise, storage failures are caught by the storage adapter and leave play available. The current browser does not turn a blocked preference write into an error dialog or an inline save warning. The fallback keeps the game available when storage fails. Storage failure policy covers the underlying behavior.

# React boundaries

This page explains where React participates in Neon Pairs and where ordinary data functions remain independent of rendering.

React mounts the application, holds the session for presentation, owns local UI state and manages browser-effect lifetimes. The game rules are callable outside React. That separation lets the browser UI and replay CLI share behavior without teaching the core about components, effects or DOM events.

## The mounted tree

`src/main.tsx` calls `createRoot` after checking the `root` element and renders `Game` inside `StrictMode`. `Game.tsx` composes deal controls, status, feedback, board and reproduction controls. It calls `useGame` once to obtain the current session and actions.

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store and no router coordinating separate screens. `Controls` receives size and two actions. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

This is the meaningful interpretation of the React boundary: importing a rule in a CLI does not start an effect or require a mounted component. It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Ref for the board's focus interface |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
| `BoardCodeForm.tsx` | Ref for the successful-load focus target |
| `Reproduction.tsx` | Local snapshot draft state |
| `use-game.ts` | Session state and current-value ref |
| `use-session-clock.ts` | Clock/visibility refs and timer effect |
| `use-saved-preferences.ts` | Persistence effect |

`Controls`, `GameStatus` and `Face` contain JSX without importing a React runtime object. The compiler uses `jsx: react-jsx`, so those files do not need the older `import React` pattern. JSX participation and explicit hook imports are related but different observations.

The diagnostic entries also use React DOM. The face sheet renders real cards, while the session harness mounts and unmounts the real game. Their entrypoints are outside `src` and built separately, so they do not become extra runtime controls in the distributed game.

# Session module

This page explains how `src/game/session` connects the pure game model to React, browser lifecycle and saved preferences.

The directory contains both pure transformations and browser adapters. `session.ts` can be called without React; `use-game.ts` provides a controller for components; the clock and storage hooks perform effects. Keeping those roles distinct makes it possible to explain a click as a sequence of ordinary data decisions followed by rendering and persistence.

## The Session value

`Session` contains eight fields. `game` is the complete `GameState`. `paused` gates an imported unfinished game. `generation` identifies replacement lifetimes. `feedback` is the current published result or notice. `loadNotice` retains load-related text for the reproduction controls. `announcement` distinguishes feedback events. `celebration` records whether this session just completed through play. `preferences` contains selected size and best moves.

These fields are not redundant copies of the core. `isWon(game)` derives victory from matched positions; there is no second `won` boolean in the session. `celebration` answers a different question from victory: a completed import is won but has no new-completion treatment. `paused` likewise describes how the browser entered the game, not whether the snapshot describes a legal state.

The game formats serialize game progress, not the whole session. A generation, browser pause, draft form text or feedback event does not appear in an exported snapshot. This lets the same snapshot be reconstructed in another session without carrying browser bookkeeping into the core model.

## Initialization

`initialSession(code, preferences)` creates a game with `createGame`. It initializes `paused` and `celebration` to false, `generation` and `announcement` to zero and both message fields to empty strings. It retains the supplied preferences.

The React controller obtains its browser store once through a lazy `useState(browserStore)`. A second lazy state initializer reads preferences, requests a fresh board for the valid saved size and calls `initialSession`. The first board therefore depends on the saved size but not on an automatically restored progress record. Active progress remains in memory until explicitly exchanged through a snapshot.

`browserStore` catches failure while obtaining `window.localStorage` and returns `null` if access is blocked. `readPreferences` can use that null store and return the default. Initialization is consequently resilient to the storage access failure that browsers can raise before `getItem` is even called.

## The current ref and React state

`useGame` maintains both React's `session` value and a `current` ref. Its `commit(next)` first compares object identity. If nothing changed it returns. Otherwise it updates the ref and then calls `setSession(next)`.

This order gives event handlers and timer callbacks immediate access to the latest committed session even before React has rendered it. Several operations can happen in a single browser task. Reading only the session captured by the last render could make an export or subsequent activation use an older game.

The ref is not an independent state machine. Every change still passes through the same commit operation, and React renders the corresponding state. The clock hook receives the ref and commit function so it can apply deltas to current data rather than a stale closure. React boundaries follows the component consequences.

## Card activation

The exposed `activate(index)` synchronizes the clock, then commits `activateSession(current.current, index)`. Synchronization can close an overdue mismatch before the core decides whether the new activation is allowed. It also accounts for the interval before a final winning match.

`activateSession` rejects input while paused. It calls `activateCard` and returns the same session if the game is unchanged. For a first reveal, whose resulting selection is `one`, it returns a session with only the new game. There is no completed-turn message yet.

For a completed attempt, it derives victory and chooses feedback. A mismatch reports that the cards will close after a short pause. A match reports the matched pair count with singular/plural wording. A final match combines the pair result with the total moves and formatted elapsed time. The function increments `announcement` once for that turn.

A winning activation calls `rememberBest`, and `celebration` becomes true. The source implements direct game-derived transitions rather than a separate event bus.

## Why feedback has an event counter

Two consecutive mismatch attempts can produce identical text. A string comparison alone would make them look like the same event. The session counter gives `Game.tsx` a changing key for the span containing the text, so repeated outcomes remain distinct render events.

A first reveal does not increment the counter. A timer closing a mismatch does not increment it either: `tickSession` changes the game, while the turn result remains the same feedback. A new deal clears the text silently without incrementing the counter. Imports increment it to publish the load notice.

`loadNotice` serves the reproduction area separately from turn feedback. It is populated by imports and invalid load attempts and cleared on replacement without import or on Resume. A later turn result can change `feedback` without treating ordinary play as a new load message.

## Replacing a game

`replaceGame(session, game, imported)` preserves the surrounding session, installs the supplied game and increments generation. It sets the saved size to the new game's size, clears celebration and computes import pause and notices.

If `imported` is false, the replacement is unpaused, its load notice is empty and the last turn feedback is cleared. If true and unfinished, the session is paused with the loaded-snapshot notice. If true and already won, it is unpaused with the completed-snapshot notice. The latter is a static completed state rather than a completion event through activation.

A replacement does not itself call `rememberBest`. This matters for completed imports, whose supplied moves are not treated as a newly played local result. Finishing an unfinished imported game through activations does reach the ordinary completion path and can record its resulting best moves.

The generation increment has two consumers. Timer logic can reject work associated with an earlier game, and `Game.tsx` uses it to remount the board. `BoardCodeForm` also keys the input by generation so a replacement supplies a fresh current-code value. A restart of the same code still gets a new lifetime.

## Controller actions

| Controller action | Validation or preparation | Session effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `newGame(size?)` | Validate size, choose a fresh code excluding the current seed, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game |
| `restart()` | Recreate the current code, reset clock | Replace with a new initial game of that deal |
| `loadBoard(code)` | Trim and parse code; reset clock only on success | Replace, or publish invalid-code notice |
| `loadSnapshot(text)` | Decode complete state; reset clock only on success | Import replacement, or publish invalid-snapshot notice |
| `exportSnapshot()` | Synchronize active clock | Encode latest game and return text |
| `activate(index)` | Synchronize active clock | Apply session activation |
| `resume()` | Reset observation baseline | Clear pause and load feedback |

The exposed load methods return a boolean. `BoardCodeForm` uses that result to move focus only after successful loading. Snapshot loading is a button action on the current textarea string, so it does not replace the draft with a normalized serialization automatically.

The private `notice(feedback)` helper changes both message fields and increments `announcement` while preserving the game. It does not bump generation or reset the clock. An invalid submission therefore leaves progress and board focus lifetime intact.

## Logical ticks

`tickSession(session, generation, milliseconds)` returns unchanged data when the captured generation differs from the current one or when the session is paused. It then delegates to `advanceGame`. If that function returns the existing game, the existing session is returned too.

A logical tick can update elapsed time and close a mismatch. It does not publish a new turn result, save a score or create a fresh board. Those decisions remain with activation and replacement. This small contract makes it possible to test stale-callback rejection without starting a browser timer.

The hook applies an additional generation check before obtaining an observation. Its effect has an active flag and clears scheduled work at cleanup. Session rejection is the final data-level protection, not the only lifecycle defense. Clock design details scheduling, visibility and fractional steps.

## Preferences and effects

`Preferences` contains `size` and `bestMoves`. The key is `neon-pairs.preferences.v1`, and the stored object includes `schemaVersion: 1`. A valid size comes from `GRID_SIZES`; each best score uses a canonical size key and a finite safe integer count between that board's pair count and `MOVES_MAX`.

`rememberBest` returns the original preferences when an existing score is less than or equal to the new count. Otherwise it returns a new preferences object and best map. This reference stability means an ordinary clock tick or an equal result need not trigger another preference effect.

`useSavedPreferences` runs `writePreferences` after preference or store changes. Writing is intentionally outside the transition functions. A session activation can decide the new best without synchronously depending on browser storage. The writer catches failures, so the in-memory game remains playable even when persistence fails.

The reader returns a complete fallback on invalid saved content, including an invalid entry within the best map. It does not salvage a subset of scores from a partly invalid preference object. The writer touches only its own key, and the store interface has no removal or enumeration method.

## Focus is a neighboring concern

The board hook owns its remembered index; `Game` coordinates Resume through the board's limited focus ref before calling the controller. Replacement remounts the board through generation, while Resume retains it. Form drafts likewise remain local to controls. React boundaries explains those lifetimes without adding presentation state to the session.

## Evidence and investigation

`session.test.ts` covers stale generations, paused activations and ticks, completion through play, completed imports and repeated feedback events. It checks that a final imported unfinished game can record a best, and it checks capped move counts. Its feedback snapshot test uses a JSON fixture.

# Status bar

This page explains the statistics and completion output rendered by `GameStatus.tsx`.

The status bar is a view of the current game and the current size's stored best move count. It does not run the clock, decide matches or write preferences. Keeping these jobs outside the component lets the same output describe ordinary play, a paused import and a completed import without separate counter logic.

## Inputs and placement

`src/game/status/GameStatus.tsx` receives `game: GameState`, `best: number | undefined` and `celebration: boolean`. In `Game.tsx`, the best value is selected with `session.preferences.bestMoves[String(game.size)]`. The component follows the deal controls and precedes board instructions. Its statistics remain in normal document flow above the board's internal scroll area.

The four labels come from `src/game/status/status-labels.ts`: `Moves:`, `Pairs:`, `Time:` and `Best:`. The punctuation belongs to each label. Values are separate definition descriptions, so the markup does not build a single visually positioned text string for the whole bar.

`GameStatus` returns a fragment containing a `dl` and, on completion, a paragraph. Each statistic is a `div` containing a `dt` and `dd`. This is a name/value summary of one game. It is not an editable form and does not add tab stops between the deal buttons and the board.

## Reading each value

| Label | Expression | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moves: | `game.moves` | Number of completed two-card attempts |
| Pairs: | `game.matched.length / 2` over `game.deck.length / 2` | Matched pairs and total pairs |
| Time: | `formatElapsed(game.elapsedMs)` | Active elapsed time, formatted for display |
| Best: | `best ?? 'none'` | Stored lowest move count for the current size, or no record |

A first reveal changes the card but does not increment Moves. The next eligible distinct reveal resolves the attempt and adds one move. A repeated first-card activation, matched-card activation or blocked mismatch activation does not add a move. This matters when reviewing a screenshot showing one open card and zero moves: it is a normal intermediate state, not a counter delay.

Matched positions are stored as card indices, with two positions per complete pair. Dividing by two produces the count a player cares about. The denominator is derived from the deck length, so the component does not maintain a second mapping from grid size to pair total. A four-column board begins at `Pairs: 0/8`; a sixteen-column board begins at `Pairs: 0/128`.

The Best value uses nullish fallback. An absent record displays `none`, keeping the label itself stable. A record is chosen by size in the parent, so loading another size can change Best even when the new game's Moves is zero. There is no total across all sizes and no face-specific score in this bar. Scoring and moves gives the gameplay interpretation.

## Clock presentation

`formatElapsed` lives in `elapsed-time.ts`. It floors milliseconds to seconds, floors seconds divided by sixty to get minutes, and pads the seconds remainder to two digits. For example, 999ms displays `0:00`, 1000ms displays `0:01`, and 3600000ms displays `60:00`. Minutes continue to grow; the formatter does not switch to an hours field.

The function only formats a number. It does not advance the game or ask the browser what time it is. A clock render can therefore update the Time value without changing Moves, Pairs or the current turn output. The distinction is useful when debugging a report that the interface announces too often: the statistic and the turn feedback are different render paths.

Elapsed time starts with the first valid reveal, pauses while the document is hidden or an unfinished imported game awaits Resume, and stops at completion. The game caps it at 359999999ms, whose visible value is `5999:59`. Play can continue at that cap. The status bar has no special disabled state for a maximum clock value.

A freshly loaded unfinished snapshot may already have a nonzero elapsed value even though it is paused. That number describes the imported position. It remains still until Resume continues active time. Zero at the start and stillness while paused are both expected; neither is a signal to replace the display with a placeholder.

## Completion output

The component calls `isWon(game)`, which compares matched position count with deck length. When complete, it adds a paragraph with class `victory`. Its text is:

`Every pair found in {moves} moves and {formatted time}. Well played.`

The same values remain in the statistics. The paragraph gives a readable completed-game sentence without requiring a user to assemble the last Moves and Time values mentally. The sentence uses the game's actual counters, including the move cap if it was reached.

A true `celebration` prop adds the `celebrate` class. In `status.css`, that class applies `victory-pulse 600ms ease-out 1`. At the midpoint the background becomes the panel color and opacity is 0.75. After the single animation the banner remains. The reduced-motion media query sets animation to none.

Completion and celebration are separate inputs for a reason. A completed snapshot satisfies `isWon`, so its banner is visible, but importing it sets celebration false. The interface shows the completed result without presenting an imported position as a newly achieved win. Motion policy and Win conditions provide the wider context.

## Statistics and event feedback

The class name `stats` and the component name GameStatus can make it tempting to use this component for every status message. Today, turn feedback is rendered separately in `Game.tsx`, while load text is also visible beside the reproduction panel. Neither the `dl` nor the completion paragraph has an explicit live attribute in this component.

This separation lets a player inspect the persistent values while turn events follow their own publication path. The final matching action produces event feedback containing the match and win, and the persistent completion paragraph appears as part of the completed game. A load error does not replace Moves with an error or turn Best into a status string.

The component also does not attach an alternate accessible label to a `dd`. Its visible value remains the value available in the document. `tests/control-contract.e2e.test.ts` specifically checks that statistics descriptions have no `aria-label` attributes. Screen reader notes explains the reading journey and Announcements policy owns the publication policy.

## Wrapping and typography

`.stats` is a wrapping flex container. Its gap is `12px 24px`, and its bottom margin is `16px`. Each name/value group has a minimum width of `8ch`. A narrow viewport can wrap whole groups onto additional lines instead of compressing four columns into illegibility.

`dt` and `dd` are inline. The term uses secondary color and `14px` text. The description resets its margin and uses `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`. With a supporting system font, equal-width digits reduce visual jitter as Time or Moves changes. The group is still content sized; it is not a fixed-width four-cell scoreboard.

The banner has `12px 16px` padding, a `12px` bottom margin, text color, a neutral `1px` border and an `8px` radius. It is a normal paragraph and can wrap. Its appearance does not reserve a permanent blank banner before completion. Review of completion at narrow widths therefore includes the extra space it adds above the board.

The layout at `640x400` with device scale 2 is covered by `tests/zoom.e2e.test.ts`. That test checks readable controls, statistics and completion text without overlap and keeps the outer page within its viewport. The board may scroll inside its own region, but that is independent of wrapping the statistics.

## Common interpretation mistakes

A best count smaller than the current Moves is expected during a less efficient game. Best records completed play; it is not a target that stops the current attempt. The current move count can also stay still at 999999 while pairs continue to increase. That limit is enforced in `game.ts`, not by formatting the text.

Pairs is not a points label with a hidden multiplier. A match contributes one pair. There is no bonus for speed, no mismatch penalty beyond the move and no display of an accumulated score from previous deals. The page's visual language remains consistent when one size has many more pairs than another.

# Architecture
Architecture is the code structure for Neon Pairs that keeps game rules separate from browser effects.

Status: spec version 2.3.

A card activation changes game data first. React renders that data, then the session adapter handles time and saved preferences. The same rules run in browser tests and replay without a browser.

## Game core

- A01 - Keep deck generation, card transitions, logical time, snapshot validation and replay as pure functions under `src/game`. They receive their inputs directly. They don't read the DOM, storage, external random sources or browser clocks.

- A02 - Keep the board description and deck immutable. Keep matched positions, current selection, moves, active elapsed milliseconds and whether play started in game state. Derive pair count and victory. Serialize progress using the reproducibility formats.

- A03 - Use direct calls and exhaustive branches for the closed, one-card and mismatch states. Keep named states, format versions, timing values and size limits beside the behavior they control.

Proposed game functions:

| Call | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `createGame(boardCode)` | Initial state for a valid board code |
| `activateCard(state, index)` | State after one card activation |
| `advanceGame(state, milliseconds)` | State after logical time advances |
| `isWon(state)` | Whether every position is matched |
| `encodeSnapshot(state)` | Version 1 snapshot JSON |
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |

# Feedback without audio

This page explains how Neon Pairs makes actions, turn results and completion understandable while the game stays silent.

The current contract is Sound, specification version 2.2. Silence covers revealing a card, finding a pair, missing a pair, resetting a deal and finishing the board. The application has no audio files, playback calls or sound control. This is a complete mode of play rather than a muted version waiting for someone to enable its feedback.

## Follow the change from state to display

`src/game/game.ts` owns selection and matching. `src/game/session/session.ts` derives turn feedback after an accepted activation. `src/game/Game.tsx` brings the board, status and feedback together. There is no audio step between a successful state change and its presentation.

| Player action or event | Card and status response | Result feedback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reveal the first eligible card | Its face replaces the back; the clock starts if this is the first reveal | The existing result text is unchanged |
| Activate that same first card again | Selection and moves are unchanged | No new turn result |
| Reveal a matching second card | Both faces remain visible with match marks; moves and pairs update | A pair-found sentence |
| Reveal a nonmatching second card | Both faces remain visible for the mismatch interval; moves update | A no-match sentence |
| Mismatch time expires | Both selected faces return to their common backs | The previous result remains; closing adds no result |
| Activate an already matched card | The matched card stays as it is | No new turn result |
| Find the last pair | All cards are matched; the final status and win banner are visible | A combined pair-found and completion sentence |
| New Game or Restart | The replacement board is closed, with cleared moves and elapsed time | The previous turn text is cleared |

The table describes normal play. An imported unfinished snapshot has an additional paused state, discussed below. The full selection rules belong in Turn resolution and Selection state.

## A closed card and a revealed card carry different information

`Board.tsx` computes the visible positions through `faceUpCards` and passes a face number to `Card.tsx` only for those positions. Every other card receives `face={null}`. In that case the card contains a `.card-back` span, a small neutral diamond, rather than face artwork. The hidden face is also absent from the card's accessible name. Silence does not create a separate information path that reveals identities early.

`describeCard` in `src/game/board/card-state.ts` produces the class state and label from the card's position, visible face and matched flag. The first hidden card on any board is named:

> Row 1, column 1, closed

For face 0, a revealed card at that position is named:

> Row 1, column 1, revealed, cyan solid circle, marker top

After its pair is found, the same position is named:

> Row 1, column 1, matched, cyan solid circle, marker top

The inline SVG is `aria-hidden="true"` and `focusable="false"`. The button name carries the semantic description instead of making the player traverse individual paths and circles. The check SVG is hidden from the accessibility tree in the same way; the button's matched state supplies its meaning. See Screen reader notes and Card artwork.

## Identity survives loss of color

A revealed face uses shape, marker position and fill. Color reinforces the marker distinction. `faceDesign` in `src/game/board/face-design.ts` maps a face ID to those parts and to the phrase used in the button name. Faces 0 and 64 both have a cyan circle with a top marker, but one is solid and the other outlined. The drawing and name preserve that difference. See Pair identity for the full model.

There is also a deliberate difference between a face's marker and a matched card's check. The marker belongs to identity and can appear in different directions. The check belongs to outcome and stays in the card's top-right corner. In `card.css` the check occupies 16% of the card's width and height. The nearby comment explains that a wider mark would reach the top-right identity marker. That is a concrete example of feedback being added around the memory task rather than covering the information the player is trying to retain.

## A match stays readable

A match takes effect on the second eligible reveal. The pair goes into `game.matched`, selection returns to `closed`, and both cards remain face up. The player does not wait for a sound or for an animation to finish before the result exists.

Matched cards use the Green border, `#8BEA7D`, and a check mark in the same color. They retain full opacity. The border helps with scanning; the check makes the matched condition visible without relying on the border's hue. Their faces remain available for orientation as the rest of the board changes.

`Card.tsx` sets `aria-disabled={matched}` rather than using the native `disabled` attribute. A matched card remains reachable by board navigation and still has its position and face name. Its activation has no game effect. This matters when the player crosses a completed part of the board: focus movement remains spatially predictable, and an announced matched state explains why that card cannot start another pair.

Hover does not erase the outcome. The generic hover rule changes a card border to the Text color, but the later `.card.matched` rule retains the Green border on matched cards. A pointer passing over a secured pair therefore does not temporarily make it resemble an ordinary revealed card. The current CSS and `tests/product-contract.e2e.test.ts` both show this behavior.

For the first match, the visible result is:

> Pair found. 1 pair matched.

A later ordinary match substitutes the actual count and plural, for example:

> Pair found. 2 pairs matched.

## A miss has a beginning and an end

A miss first reveals the second face and increments moves. Both faces stay visible for `MISMATCH_MS`, currently 800 active milliseconds. The player can inspect them before they close together. The feedback says:

> No match. Cards close after a short pause.

There is no error tone, red failure panel or loss of previously matched cards. The message explains both the outcome and the upcoming closure. The visible faces provide the useful memory information during the interval.

During this interval, card activation is ignored, while keyboard focus can still move. Focus and selection are distinct: moving the white outline onto a third card does not reveal it. This distinction is particularly useful in silence, because the visible pair can remain stable while the player prepares the next selection. It also explains a common apparent nonresponse: pressing Enter during the mismatch pause does not queue a reveal for later.

`advanceGame` subtracts active milliseconds from `selection.remainingMs`. When the remainder reaches zero, selection becomes `closed`; `faceUpCards` then omits those two positions. Closure changes the board without generating another result sentence. `tickSession` updates the game but leaves the previous feedback and announcement value alone. The no-match sentence can therefore remain visible after the faces have closed. It describes the latest turn, rather than acting as a label for the instantaneous selection state.

Hiding the document suspends active timing. Returning continues the remaining interval. A player who switches away shortly after a miss does not lose the rest of that face-viewing interval while the game is hidden. The implementation is in `use-session-clock.ts`; timing details and boundary cases belong in Mismatch interval and Elapsed time rules.

## Status gives a persistent account

`GameStatus.tsx` renders a definition list with moves, matched pairs, elapsed time and the saved best for the current size. These values are available before any turn result and continue to be available after it. A short result message need not carry all the context the player might want to inspect.

## The result text is also accessible feedback

`Game.tsx` renders `session.feedback` inside a paragraph with `role="status"`, `aria-live="polite"` and `aria-atomic="true"`. The sentence is ordinary visible text as well as accessible status content. It is not a transcript of audio generated by the application.

The child span uses `key={session.announcement}`. A new resolved turn increments that value in `activateSession`. Two consecutive misses have identical feedback strings, but distinct event values cause the span to be replaced for the second miss. A text-only equality check would miss that distinction and could leave an assistive technology user without evidence that another turn had resolved.

This event mechanism deliberately does not follow the clock. `tickSession` can create a new game object many times while leaving the event value unchanged. Focus changes and the first reveal likewise do not publish a fresh turn result. That is why a time update, an arrow-key press or mismatch closure does not repeatedly present the last result as if it had just happened.

“Silent” here describes what the game itself plays. A screen reader may speak the accessible names and status supplied by the page according to the user's own setup. Neon Pairs does not call `speechSynthesis.speak` to read its messages. A user choosing speech output is using their assistive technology; that does not require a game-level sound switch. See Announcements policy for the announcement contract and Audio research notes for the design rationale.

## Completion remains after the moment passes

The last match produces a combined result. With eight moves and a displayed elapsed time of 0:03, the feedback is:

> Pair found. All pairs found in 8 moves and 0:03.

The visible banner is separate:

> Every pair found in 8 moves and 0:03. Well played.

Both derive their moves and formatted time from the completed game. The board also remains fully matched, and the status stays present. A player who looks away at the final activation can recover the result from the page afterwards. There is no need to have heard a brief victory cue.

A completion reached through play sets `session.celebration` to true. `GameStatus` adds the `celebrate` class to the `.victory` paragraph. `status.css` gives it a single 600ms `victory-pulse`, with a panel background and reduced opacity at its midpoint. The banner then stays visible. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, the animation is disabled. Card border transitions are also disabled under that preference; normally they last 120ms.

## Replacement, import and pause

New Game and Restart replace the current session game through `replaceGame`. That clears the previous feedback and load notice, removes the celebration flag and increments the generation. The board is keyed by that generation in `Game.tsx`, which resets its remembered focus position with the replacement. The player sees a closed board and cleared counters rather than a reset sound.

An unfinished snapshot is different from a new deal. Its visible cards, matched positions and counters describe saved progress, but the imported session is paused. Its status says:

> Loaded snapshot. Select Resume to continue.

A Resume button appears beside the load notice. Activation and active time stay blocked until Resume. The cards themselves are not all given matched styling to indicate this pause; a paused unmatched card is still unmatched. The explicit notice explains why a revealed face might remain on screen longer than the ordinary mismatch interval.

The Resume handler in `Game.tsx` focuses the board's remembered card and then calls the controller's resume action. That action clears feedback and load notice while leaving the imported game intact. If the imported selection was a mismatch, its remaining active interval can now continue. Resume does not manufacture a new pair result for the saved selection.

A completed snapshot reports `Loaded completed snapshot.` and shows its completed board and banner without the celebration class. Invalid data reports `Invalid board code.` or `Invalid snapshot.` while retaining the current game. Load notices appear beside the reproduction controls and in session feedback. See Reproduction panel and Snapshot selection notes.

## Finding the evidence

The following tests cover the feedback behavior:

- `tests/browser-environment.e2e.test.ts` instruments audio constructors, media playback and synthesized speech, counts media requests, finishes a board and restarts. It also checks that no audio or video element is present.
- `tests/announcements.e2e.test.ts` observes result DOM changes. It covers repeated misses, focus movement, clock advancement, closure and repeated load notices.
- `src/game/session/session.test.ts` checks event increments, unchanged events during closure, paused imports and the distinction between played completion and imported completion.
- `tests/matched-mark.e2e.test.ts` checks the check mark against every face on a 16x16 board at a small viewport. It looks for overlap with either the main shape or its marker.
- `tests/motion.e2e.test.ts` checks border transition duration, the completion pulse and reduced motion.
- `tests/accessibility.e2e.test.ts` follows a complete keyboard game and captures names, states and result text in Chromium accessibility trees.
| `decodeSnapshot(text)` | Valid restored state or `null` |
| `replayGame(text)` | Final replay state or `null` |

## Browser session

- A04 - Keep React state, timer lifecycle and browser visibility handling in `src/game/session`. Use a monotonic browser clock. Clear pending work on unmount and invalidate callbacks when the deal changes. A callback from an earlier deal can't change the current one.

- A05 - Keep preference and best-score reads in the session storage module. Treat saved JSON as unknown input. Validate grid sizes and finite integer scores. Catch read, parse and write failures. Keep unrelated storage keys untouched. A failure leaves the game playable.

- A06 - Keep active game progress in memory until you export or import a snapshot. Importing a completed snapshot doesn't update best scores or play a celebration. Completing an unfinished imported game records a local best under R10.

# Accessibility audit
This page records accessibility evidence and findings from the Neon Pairs source and tests.

The README identifies Chromium 156.0.8078.4 and Playwright 1.64.1 for the recorded accessibility-tree journey. It says a screen reader was not run and leaves spoken confirmation to user acceptance.

## Audit scope and disposition

The review covers native controls, keyboard movement, information available in card names, result events, focus visibility, scrolling, reduced motion, face distinctions and the equivalent-zoom layout. It follows Input, Controls, Visuals and the journeys in Acceptance.

The disposition is supported implementation with outstanding manual confirmation. It is not a declaration of conformance to an accessibility standard. The visual specification itself cautions that choosing a minimum card target size does not establish complete conformance.

| Area | Evidence present in source | Qualification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complete keyboard play | Keyboard journey and full Chromium tree test | Spoken output remains unverified |
| Card information | Pure name tests and exact hidden-DOM assertions | Stored name expectations and tree assertions |
| Result events | Session event tests and DOM mutation observations | Speech was not tested |
| Large-board focus | Bounds, remembered-entry and clipped-edge cases | Automated geometry in Chromium |
| Touch movement | Tap completion and CDP scroll journeys | Real-device long press remains acceptance work |
| Equivalent zoom | 640x400 viewport at scale 2 | Does not exercise every browser zoom implementation |
| Face identity | 128-face geometry and screenshot comparisons | Human distinguishability still needs review |
| Reduced motion | Computed-style assertions | Automated style checks |

The qualifiers identify where evidence stops. They are not findings that the game necessarily fails those behaviors. Known issues covers test-input dependencies and unverified compatibility.

## Native controls and discoverability

`Card.tsx` renders a native button for each position. The main size choice is a native select, action controls are buttons, and reproduction uses a details/summary disclosure with labeled fields. This gives the browser established focus and activation behavior instead of reproducing it with generic clickable containers.

The browser tests locate Grid size, New Game and the reproduction actions by role or label. The accessibility journey captures control nodes before entering the board. Literal contract tests complement the shared label constants, so renaming a constant cannot silently change both the UI and every test lookup.

## Result feedback and repeated events

`session.ts` distinguishes first reveals from completed turns. A second eligible reveal produces match or miss feedback; a winning turn produces feedback containing the match and final result. Clock updates and closing a miss do not create a new turn event. The rendered status is polite and atomic, so its complete text is exposed as the result.

The session tracks an announcement number, and `Game.tsx` keys the feedback span with that event value. Identical wording can therefore represent successive events. The announcement tests install a MutationObserver and compare observed result changes with the expected sequence, including repeated invalid loads and repeated misses.

This is a useful approximation of what assistive software can receive. It does not prove what a particular screen reader speaks, whether its queue interrupts a prior message, or how quickly it announces the final turn. The source comment about observer callbacks is an explanation of the test model, not a speech recording.

Finding: event progression and DOM exposure have targeted tests. Spoken output remains outstanding acceptance evidence, especially for consecutive equal results and the final match. Screen-reader notes and Announcements policy provide the related user-facing contract.

## Focus after actions and scrolling

New Game, Restart, load and export actions preserve focus on their initiating control. Resume is different because it removes itself: `Game.tsx` calls the board's remembered-focus method before clearing pause. The control-contract and snapshot browser cases inspect that ordering.

For keyboard focus, `use-board-focus.ts` suppresses the browser's centering scroll and uses the nearest-scroll behavior. Card CSS provides a 6px scroll margin. The visible focus outline is white, 3px wide and offset by 2px. The bounds helper includes both dimensions when checking visibility.

Pointer focus has a separate timing concern. Scrolling a partially visible card during the press can move the release target. The implementation allows the click to complete and scrolls afterward. Coordinate-based mouse and touch cases exercise slivers at clipped edges, while the focus-entry suite checks outlines when keyboard navigation follows a pointer click.

Finding: the most difficult cases are explicitly represented, including remembered entry after scrolling away and an interior 16x16 card. Automated bounds checks tolerate only small geometry rounding. They do not substitute for reviewing focus visibility on an actual display or in an untested browser engine.

## Layout, targets and equivalent zoom

The large-board checks render all 256 positions and preserve card size while allowing the board to scroll. At 360x800 and 1280x800, tests reach both ends by keyboard and touch. A further 1280x1400 case exercises the viewport height cap. A 320x640 check covers the default board and main controls.

# CSS organization

This page maps the Neon Pairs stylesheets to their components and explains the global cascade, layout formulas and visual-test seams.

Styles sit beside the behavior they present and are imported by components. They remain ordinary global CSS. File adjacency makes ownership discoverable, while selector choice and the cascade determine actual reach. There is no CSS module transformation, CSS-in-JS runtime or component-library theme layer in this source.

## Stylesheet ownership

| Stylesheet | Importing component or entry | Main responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `src/game/game.css` | `Game.tsx`; face-sheet entry also imports it | Root theme, page geometry, typography, focus outline and result space |
| `board/board.css` | `Board.tsx` | Viewport scrolling and grid dimensions |
| `board/card.css` | `Card.tsx` | Card states, back, face sizing and matched mark |
| `controls/control.css` | Deal and reproduction components | Shared native-control surface |
| `controls/controls.css` | `Controls.tsx` | Size selector and deal-button arrangement |
| `controls/reproduction.css` | Reproduction components | Disclosure, forms, textarea and load notice |
| `status/status.css` | `GameStatus.tsx` | Statistics and completion presentation |
| `art/face-sheet.css` | Face-sheet entry | Diagnostic placement of real cards |

A component import brings its styles into the application graph, and the build embeds the resulting CSS in the finished HTML. The source HTML has no separate stylesheet link to distribute. Build pipeline describes that assembly.

## Global foundation

`game.css` sets `system-ui, sans-serif`, a 16px root font size, 24px line height, light text on a dark background and `color-scheme: dark`. It defines the shared variables `--text`, `--secondary`, `--panel`, `--back`, `--face`, `--border` and `--green`.

The current values are `#f4f6ff` for text, `#b8bdd2` for secondary text, `#141827` for panels, `#1b2034` for card backs, `#111625` for face surfaces, `#757c9a` for borders and `#8bea7d` for matched green. The page background is `#090b14`.

The root also defines `--content-max: 1120px` and `--page-padding: 16px`. A global border-box reset applies to every element, body margin is zero and main uses full width up to that maximum with centered margins and page padding. These foundational rules affect diagnostics that deliberately import `game.css` as well as the main game.

Headings, paragraphs and help text have a small set of explicit margins and font sizes. Secondary text is generally 14px. The global `:focus-visible` outline is 3px white with a 2px offset. Because it is global, its interaction with scroll-container padding matters for cards as well as ordinary controls.

## Artwork and non-color distinctions

Faces derive from eight shapes, eight marker positions and two fills, for 128 identities. Color repeats the marker distinction. The art build renders each face at 44px, and tests save color, grayscale and neutral sheets. Neutralized rendered silhouettes are checked for uniqueness.

This catches a legibility problem that inspecting the matched border alone would miss.

The game does not depend on sound to reveal a card, report a miss or show a win. Browser tests instrument audio-related APIs, check media elements and watch media requests during play and reset. ## The mounted tree

The component tree is intentionally direct. There is no React context carrying a global game store or router. `Controls` receives size, solo actions and the Tournament entry callback. `GameStatus` receives a game, an optional best and a celebration flag. `Board` receives the game and activation action. `Reproduction` receives current code context, exchange actions and pause-related presentation. Tournament components receive event data and callbacks from `useTournament`.

These props describe the existing contracts. A component can render data it does not own without gaining responsibility for deciding a turn. The core still computes matches, move counts, elapsed advancement and victory.

## The data-only side

`deck.ts`, `game.ts`, `selection.ts`, `elapsed-time.ts`, `saved-format.ts`, `snapshot.ts`, `snapshot-selection.ts` and `replay.ts` do not import React. They accept values and return values. `session/session.ts` is also a data transformation module, although it lives beside hooks that import React.

The board has data-only helpers too. `keyboard.ts` computes a target from keys and coordinates. `card-state.ts` computes a state description. `face-design.ts` maps an integer identity to design values. These helpers can be tested without rendering `Board` or building a synthetic browser tree.

It is not a claim that every file ending in `.ts` is independent of React. `use-board-focus.ts`, `nearest-scroll.ts` and the session hooks are TypeScript modules with hooks and browser behavior.

## React imports in application code

| Module | React mechanisms used |
| --- | --- |
| `main.tsx` | `StrictMode`; root rendering through React DOM |
| `Game.tsx` | Screen state, shared tournament announcement callback, ref for returning focus |
| `SoloGame.tsx` | Solo `useGame` session, board ref and Resume handoff |
| `TournamentScreen.tsx` | Tournament history and controller composition, heading focus |
| `Board.tsx` | Memoized derivations, refs, stable callback, layout effect and imperative handle |
| `Card.tsx` | `memo` and a keyboard event type |
| `use-board-focus.ts` | Local state, refs and callbacks |
| `nearest-scroll.ts` | Ref, effect and callback |
