# Test strategy
This page explains how Neon Pairs divides evidence between game tests, browser journeys, source checks and user acceptance.

The product contract is specification version 2.2. The README records a successful named compatibility run. Known issues tracks verification limits, and Fixtures explains why replacing reviewed JSON expectations with current output would weaken the evidence.

## Start with the question

A deck test asks whether a code produces the published cards. A browser test asks whether a player can reach and activate those cards through rendered controls. An accessibility-tree capture asks what Chromium exposes to assistive software. None can substitute for the others.

The useful division follows the architecture's existing boundaries:

| Question | Existing evidence | What it cannot establish |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does a turn change the right data? | Vitest tests beside `game.ts` | Native focus, scrolling or pointer dispatch |
| Does the seeded deal match the format? | Literal vectors and `tests/deal-oracle.ts` | Whether hidden identities leak into markup |
| Does the browser adapter count active time? | Pure clock tests plus controlled browser clocks | Real device scheduling latency |
| Can a player finish through the interface? | Built-page keyboard and touch journeys | Spoken screen-reader output |
| Does local storage survive reload? | HTTP-origin persistence journeys | Cross-browser behavior of disk-origin storage |
| Does the distribution stand alone? | Offline disk navigation and built-output inspection | Every browser engine or operating system |
| Does the layout survive difficult geometry? | Large-board, scrollbar, zoom and focus tests | Every possible window size |

This is a map of current checks, not a demand to create one test of each kind for every change. A correction to snapshot validation usually needs parser evidence first. A clipped focus ring needs browser geometry. A change to explanatory copy may need only the relevant reviewed expectation and a visual check. Unit tests and Browser tests show the local conventions.

## Pure behavior carries the broad matrix

`vitest.config.ts` includes `src/**/*.test.ts` and `scripts/**/*.test.ts`. The package's `test` script is `vitest run`. Most of these tests import `test` from Vitest and assertions from `node:assert/strict`. They do not mount React to prove a card transition.

The core state includes the immutable board description, its deck, matched positions, selection, moves, elapsed milliseconds and the started flag. Selection has closed, one-card and mismatch branches. Tests exercise transitions directly, allowing exact questions such as whether advancing a pending miss by 799ms leaves it open and whether the next millisecond closes both cards.

The suite checks complete pairs at all seven supported sizes. `completion.test.ts` finishes each size through `activateCard`; it does not infer that a 4x4 success proves a 16x16 finish. `deck.test.ts` checks the published seed-one vector, generator states, the inclusive maximum seed, frozen data and independent generation at each size. `deck-rejection.test.ts` targets uncommon rejection-sampling boundaries using separately stored expected decks.

The game tests also make negative cases visible. A fractional or out-of-range card index returns the old state. Repeating the first selected card adds no move. During a miss, every activation is ignored. Invalid elapsed steps leave the game unchanged. Keeping the original object in those cases is observable behavior in these tests; asserting identity can distinguish an ignored action from an unnecessary reconstruction.

Snapshot and replay tests carry a different matrix: exact object fields, integer ranges, byte limits, valid selections and action ordering. A round trip is useful, but two matching mistakes can round trip successfully. Independent expected fields and malformed inputs provide the stronger evidence. A valid started game with one revealed card and zero moves is the baseline for several invalid-counter cases, so rejection can be attributed to the changed counter rather than an unrelated invalid state.

## Session tests connect results to browser-independent policy

`src/game/session/session.ts` is a data adapter. Its tests create sessions and call `activateSession`, `replaceGame` and `tickSession` directly. This makes several integration rules cheap to check without pretending to test browser effects.

A replacement increments `generation`. A tick carrying an earlier generation has no effect. An unfinished imported game is paused and cannot accept card input or active time until resumed. A locally completed game can improve the appropriate saved move record. A completed import follows the import path instead of the live completion path. These are separate causes even when both render a completed board.

Session feedback tests inspect event progression as well as text. Two misses with the same wording still represent two turns. Focus movement and time advancement do not represent new turn results. Browser announcement tests then verify that these data changes become the intended DOM updates. Checking both layers helps distinguish a missing session event from a rendering problem.

Storage tests use the narrow `PreferenceStore` interface. A Map-backed implementation covers round trips and per-size minima; a throwing implementation covers failures without a browser. Browser tests separately exercise a denied `window.localStorage` getter. The distinction matters because failure while obtaining the store occurs before either `getItem` or `setItem` can run.

## Browser journeys use the shipped shape

The package's `test:e2e` command runs the main build, builds diagnostic entries, and then invokes Node's test runner over `tests/*.e2e.test.ts` with concurrency set to one. Playwright drives Chromium, while `node:test` owns the tests. There is no Playwright Test project configuration controlling this suite's retry or worker behavior.

Most journey files import the wrapper in `tests/browser-test.ts`. It launches a browser, creates a fresh context per case, collects page errors and closes resources. `tests/artifact-server.ts` serves the freshly built HTML on a private loopback port. `GAME_URL` points at the same build on disk. Persistence journeys use the served URL; offline-delivery checks use the disk URL.

Fresh contexts isolate browser storage, permissions and page-installed instrumentation. They do not make every global resource independent: the artifact server and browser belong to file-level hooks, and the runtime record has a shared output location. The serial command is part of the implementation being documented. Flaky-test notes discuss the timing consequences.

The browser tests use public controls to load `np1-4-1`. They know its deck from the documented format and test fixture, rather than asking the application for hidden state. The board's hidden buttons expose positions and closed state. The tests inspect that absence directly in `input-contract.e2e.test.ts`, including the neutral back and lack of face artwork. A solver that depended on hidden SVGs would invalidate this evidence.

## Contract checks complement shared labels

Ordinary journey helpers import the control-label constants so they can focus on behavior. Contract tests also contain literal labels and limits. This prevents changing a production constant and every test lookup together from silently changing the public contract.

`control-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers native reproduction controls, their input limits, invalid statuses and action focus. `product-contract.e2e.test.ts` covers status presentation, continuing minutes and successful load size selection. `persistence-contract.e2e.test.ts` checks record comparisons, saved sizes and fresh progress after reload. These overlap broader journeys at specific seams, where a shared helper could otherwise conceal a mistake.

Overlap is useful when the assertions answer different questions. Loading a snapshot appears in parser tests, session tests and browser tests because validation, paused data and Resume focus are different behaviors. Repeating the same serializer implementation as an expected-value helper would add little protection. The suite's independent literal expectations are intended to break that circularity.

## Visual and accessibility evidence are concrete

The art entry renders every face at the minimum card size. Tests capture color, grayscale and neutral versions. Neutral silhouettes are compared for uniqueness, and separate assertions inspect marker geometry and palette application. This establishes machine-distinguishable geometry; a person still reviews whether the distinctions are usable. Accessibility audit explains that limit.

Layout tests inspect page width, card bounds, board scrolling and complete focus outlines. The large-board checks cover 360x800 and 1280x800 CSS-pixel viewports. A separate equivalent-zoom journey uses 640x400 with device scale 2. Visible-scrollbar cases remove Chromium's default scrollbar-hiding launch argument and test widths where scrollbar space changes the available board area.

The accessibility journey uses the Chromium DevTools Protocol to capture the accessibility tree during a complete keyboard game. It checks controls, revealed and matched names, disabled state exposure, results, completion, Tab exit and a fresh game. The artifact records browser and Playwright versions and explicitly records that a screen reader was not run. User acceptance owns the spoken journey. Tree assertions support that review; they do not prove speech delivery.

## Source and delivery checks

`source-audit.test.ts` inspects package pins, lockfile agreement, compiler settings and source conventions required by the architecture and technology specifications. It reads authored files rather than the compiled bundle. `source-conventions.test.ts` checks current export ownership, question-shaped predicate names, behavior-oriented test names and the small set of environment reads the runners use.

These are text checks with intentionally limited reach. The core effect scan names particular source files. It is not an analysis of every transitive call. The TypeScript source scan can reject spelling patterns, but cannot prove full semantic purity. Review remains necessary when moving behavior to a new module. Code review and Source audit notes provide related architectural context.

The built-output test searches the emitted HTML for `fetch(` and the preload helper's `relList` marker. The offline journey blocks network access and checks that only the document request occurs while a card remains playable. Together they cover bundle content and observed loading. Neither measures first-render duration; Performance budget documents that evidence gap.

## Following through

Choose the smallest test that exposes the changed behavior, then follow it into the browser where native interaction or effects matter. Regression catalogue shows paired investigations, and Release checklist assembles the complete verification sequence. The remaining evidence gaps are tracked in Known issues.
# Browser support
This page explains which Neon Pairs browser and tool combinations have recorded evidence and which conditions are represented by the current test suite.

The README records Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0, Playwright 1.64.1 and Chromium 156.0.8078.4 as the named tested combination. It says the locked install, type check, Vitest tests, current-source build and Chromium journeys passed with named-combination enforcement enabled.

## Tested, supported and unrecorded

The technology specification supports Node 24.19 or later. Its named compatibility combination supplies a concrete verification point within that range. A version meeting the supported floor is not automatically a version for which this repository has a recorded successful run.

| Environment | Evidence in the project | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Named Node/npm/Playwright/Chromium set | Explicit README pass record and exact runner comparison | Recorded tested combination |
| Other Node versions at or above 24.19 | Allowed by technology specification | Need their own run result |
| Other Chromium executables | Runner accepts an executable override | Actual version is recorded; success is not assumed |
| Firefox | No launch path or project in this suite | No recorded result here |
| WebKit or Safari | No launch path or project in this suite | No recorded result here |
| Mobile Chromium emulation | Touch and viewport contexts in browser tests | Emulated interaction coverage |
| Physical phones or tablets | No device run recorded | Physical-device compatibility unverified |
| Screen reader with a browser | README records no screen-reader run | Spoken journey remains user acceptance |

The package version `1.0.0` and specification version 2.2 are not browser support versions. The build targets ES2023 through Vite. That target describes emitted syntax; it does not replace tests of native focus, scrolling, storage or accessibility behavior in a browser engine.

## How the runner establishes identity

`tests/browser-test.ts` reads the running Node version, obtains npm's version from its script environment or a fallback command, reads the installed Playwright package version and asks the launched browser for its version. It writes the result to `test-results/browser-runtime.json`.

With `NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION=1`, the setup compares those values with the named set. A mismatch fails the run. Without the flag, versions are still recorded but are not required to equal the named set. A successful unflagged run can supply evidence for its actual combination; it cannot be relabeled as a named-combination pass if the values differ.

`PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` changes the executable path passed to `chromium.launch`. It is useful for investigating another Chromium build. The runner still records that browser's reported version and, when the named flag is set, compares it normally. Setting the override does not suppress the compatibility check.

The README's install example uses PowerShell and records project-local browser and temporary directories. That is a reproducible setup example, not evidence that every test ran on every operating system with PowerShell available. The runtime JSON does not include an operating-system field, so the four version values alone cannot establish a broader OS matrix.

## Browsers are driven by Node tests

The suite uses Node's test runner with Playwright as an automation library. It does not define Firefox and WebKit projects in a Playwright Test configuration. The package command runs matching browser files serially after building both the distribution and diagnostic entries.

The wrapper creates a fresh browser context for each ordinary case. This isolates storage and page instrumentation between cases. A shared browser instance still supplies the engine being tested. Starting a new context does not create a different browser version or simulate a separate operating system.

Some cases use the Chromium DevTools Protocol directly. The accessibility helper requests the full accessibility tree, and touch-scroll cases dispatch touch events through a CDP session. These tests cannot be assumed to run unchanged against another engine. A future compatibility result for another engine would need to distinguish portable journeys from Chromium-specific evidence.

## Viewport and input coverage

The suite represents several concrete layouts rather than a continuous device catalogue:

| Configuration | Main coverage |
| --- | --- |
| 360x800 CSS pixels | Phone layout, large-board navigation, taps and touch scrolling |
| 1280x800 CSS pixels | Desktop large-board layout and touch-scroll counterpart |
| 640x400, device scale 2 | Equivalent layout for the specified zoom scenario |
| 320x640 | Default-board fit and main control/card dimensions |
| 1280x1400 | Large-board viewport-height cap |
| 900x600, 1000x600 and 360x640 | Intermediate boards beside visible scrollbars |

The art sheet uses a separate 1200x900 viewport for captures. That page is diagnostic artwork evidence, not an additional phone or desktop support tier. Pointer-focus cases reuse the phone, desktop and equivalent-zoom dimensions while arranging clipped targets near a board edge.

Touch contexts set `hasTouch` and `isMobile`; they exercise taps and scrolling with Chromium's emulation. Keyboard cases use native Tab, arrows, Enter and Space. Coordinate-based cases test hit targets after scrolling, where automatic locator scrolling would otherwise make the test easier than the real interaction.

These checks establish particular browser conditions. A 360-pixel viewport is not a named phone model, and a touch-enabled desktop-size context is not proof of a physical tablet run. Device-scale configuration affects pixels per CSS pixel; it does not by itself change the CSS layout width.

## Zoom and visible scrollbars

The equivalent-zoom journey combines a smaller CSS viewport with scale 2. It checks readable controls, status and completion, small-board play, paused imports, Resume focus and large-board reachability. Text rectangles are inspected for clipping and overlap.

This is the specification's equivalent layout setup. It does not automate the browser zoom menu, prove pinch behavior on every device or cover arbitrary zoom factors. The game leaves zoom available and relies on responsive layout plus internal board scrolling for the specified cases. Zoom behaviour carries the full layout contract.

The normal browser hides scrollbars by default. For visible-scrollbar tests, the wrapper launches a second browser without the `--hide-scrollbars` default argument. Each case verifies that the page scrollbar actually takes space before checking width. The result is evidence for that scrollbar mode in Chromium, not a universal claim about every platform's overlay-scrollbar settings.

## Origins and offline play

The distribution is tested directly as a disk file with the context offline. The request list is observed, the default board appears and a card can be revealed. This checks the intended self-contained delivery path in the tested Chromium combination.

Persistence cases use an HTTP server bound to loopback and an available private port. That origin is stable across reloads inside a context. It serves the same emitted HTML rather than the development server's module graph. This lets the tests inspect saved size and score behavior without relying on file-origin storage semantics.

The technology specification explicitly notes that disk-origin storage varies among browsers. The adapter catches unavailable-store and JSON failures so the session stays playable. There is no compatibility promise that a moved HTML file will preserve its previous browser storage association. Private browsing notes and Storage testing discuss the related limits.

## Accessibility evidence is engine-specific

The full journey captures Chromium's accessibility tree, including names, states, feedback and completion. Its record identifies the browser and Playwright and records no screen-reader run. Tree structure can differ between engines, and speech remains user acceptance. Accessibility audit describes the findings and qualifications.

A new compatibility report is most useful when its artifact, actual runtime, origin and input path are clear. A CDP helper failing before play is different from a game interaction failing. The current support claim remains the recorded combination, specified runtime floor and conditions listed above. Release checklist explains how a run becomes a release record.
# Documentation style

This guide explains how to write and maintain Neon Pairs documentation so that a reader can connect an explanation to the implemented behavior.

The documentation serves engineers and coding agents working on a small browser game. Its useful detail comes from actual transitions, source boundaries and examples, rather than a formal tone. A reader should be able to find the relevant behavior, understand its limits and decide what evidence would support a change.

## Start with the page's job

The existing specification pages open with a title and a sentence identifying the document. The rules page says it is a game contract; architecture explains the separation between rules and browser effects; acceptance identifies itself as journeys that check requirements. Those opening sentences help a reader decide whether to continue or follow a related page.

A useful explanation then starts with the behavior a person can observe. For a mismatch, that is two different faces staying visible before they close. The next paragraph can explain active time and the session adapter. Starting with the adapter's hook names would make the reader reconstruct the product behavior from implementation details.

Different page types need different shapes. A glossary works as entries, a format page benefits from tables and literal examples, and an incident needs a sequence of cause and consequence. A short decision can be shorter than a reference page. Uniform headings across all of them would not make their contents more useful.

Rules, Controls, Input and the other subject specifications define the product. A sentence in an explanatory guide can clarify an existing constraint without quietly expanding it.

## Give each claim the right status

There are three common kinds of statement: what the current game does, what the specification defines, and what someone proposes. They can appear together, but their wording should let a reader distinguish them. “The component renders” identifies an implementation observation. “R04 defines” identifies a requirement. “A possible follow-up” identifies a proposal.

For example, `src/game/snapshot.ts` exports `SNAPSHOT_VERSION = 1`, while the specification identifies itself as version 2.2. An accurate sentence names both subjects. “The current version is 2.2” is ambiguous on a page about JSON because a reader might change an exported format field on that basis.

History can explain a decision, but it should not replace a current behavior description. A release discussion about clock drift is useful context for the measured-delta design. A reader still needs the present boundary: pure game functions receive durations, while the browser session supplies them. Clock design is a better destination for that explanation than an unrelated release note.

## Trace a behavior through its layers

Source references are most useful when they explain responsibility. `src/game/game.ts` owns card transitions and logical time. `src/game/session/session.ts` wraps them with feedback and preferences. `src/game/session/use-game.ts` connects loading, exporting and React state. `src/game/Game.tsx` composes the screen. A page about a turn can begin in the core and follow only the layers relevant to its question.

The same discipline helps avoid false shortcuts. Saying “React counts a move on click” combines rendering, input and rules into one inaccurate sentence. A second eligible activation increments the counter in `activateCard`; browser controls route input to the shared action. That description also explains why keyboard and pointer input have the same move behavior.

## Examples answer a particular question

The code `np1-4-1` is a good common example because the specification publishes its deck. Positions 0 and 11 form one pair, while positions 0 and 1 differ. Those facts let a writer explain a match or a miss without depending on an unknown fresh deal. A precise example identifies whether its numbers are positions, face IDs or human rows and columns.

A snapshot example answers a state question: what progress will load? A replay example answers a sequence question: which activations and timing lead to a result? Substituting one for the other can omit the very detail a report needs. Sharing FAQ explains the choice, while the format pages define acceptable data.

Complete format examples can be copied and checked. Fragments can be clearer when discussing just one branch, provided the prose identifies them as fragments. An object showing only `kind` and `index` is a selection example, not an entire snapshot. Calling it a snapshot would imply that the decoder accepts missing top-level fields.

Placeholders also need context. In a sentence explaining a completion message, `N` can stand for a move count. Inside a JSON block intended as valid input, an unquoted `N` is not a valid number. The difference is about the example's purpose, rather than a preference for more or less code on the page.

## Explain the boundary that changes the answer

“The cards close after a delay” is enough in a quick introduction. An engineering explanation needs the active-time distinction because a hidden page or paused import changes when the interval finishes. “The game saves locally” needs a similar boundary: preferences and best moves persist, while ongoing progress is restored through explicit snapshot tools.

There is no need to repeat the complete timing or persistence model every time those subjects appear. A sentence can name the relevant condition and link to Mismatch interval or Persistence overview. Repetition is particularly risky for numeric limits and exact strings, which can become inconsistent when copied into many pages.

The best edge case is one that clarifies the rule being explained. Repeating the first revealed card demonstrates why activation is not the same as a move. A stale timer after Restart demonstrates why session generation exists. An unsupported side length demonstrates board-code validation. Adding an unrelated browser limitation to each of those examples would distract from the point.

## Evidence has a scope

Reading `formatElapsed` establishes how the formatter computes text. A browser test establishes how the status component exposes that value in a built page. A screen-reader journey involves another layer of evidence. These observations support different claims and do not automatically stand in for one another.

The repository README records a named runtime combination and says that spoken screen-reader output was not run. That is a useful model of a bounded evidence statement: it reports what was checked and leaves the unperformed part visible. A documentation edit alone does not supply a new test run or expand the tested browser matrix.

For command instructions, `package.json` is the source for the available scripts. `npm run test:e2e` builds before executing the browser journeys; `npm run build` type checks before Vite emits the HTML. Describing the command's defined behavior is different from claiming it passed in the writer's environment. Test strategy covers the larger evidence plan.
# Release checklist
This checklist assembles the existing build, test and acceptance steps for a Neon Pairs release.

It follows specification version 2.2 and the commands in the package. Known issues records verification limits.

## Establish the candidate

- Identify the source being released and use a complete writable checkout for commands that install, build or write test artifacts.
- Read the current specification and Acceptance, especially the journey affected by the change.
- Check that reviewed test inputs are present. The suite reads nine reviewed JSON files; the inventory is in Fixtures guide.
- Inspect the package and lockfile together. The project uses exact dependency versions and separate TypeScript compiler projects.

The package's version is currently `1.0.0`, while the README says it implements product specification 2.2. Those numbers describe different things. Board codes, snapshots and replays remain at format version 1. Do not infer a format migration from the product specification number alone; Format versioning explains that distinction.

The release candidate is the emitted game HTML built from the selected source. A diagnostic sheet or a previously built file is not evidence for that candidate. The normal browser command performs a fresh build specifically to keep source and tested artifact connected.

## Install and identify the tools

Use the locked install:

```sh
npm ci
```

The technology specification supports Node 24.19 or later. The named compatibility combination is Node 26.12.1, npm 11.20.0, Playwright 1.64.1 and Chromium 156.0.8078.4. The README contains a prior successful record for that exact combination; other versions need their own results.

The README's PowerShell setup puts the npm cache, downloaded browser and browser temporary work inside the checkout. It installs Chromium through Playwright. The environment variables and browser installation are runner setup, not runtime requirements for opening the delivered game.

`PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_EXECUTABLE` can select another executable. That override does not make its version equal to the named Chromium build. Read the generated runtime record to establish what launched. Browser support describes the compatibility claim that each result can support.

## Run the source checks

```sh
npm run typecheck
npm test
npm run format:check
```

The typecheck command invokes the app, Node and e2e compiler projects in sequence. A successful Vite build alone would not establish TypeScript correctness. Vitest selects the tests under `src` and `scripts`, including pure rules, parsers, session behavior, command-line replay and source audits.

Read failures by category. A missing reviewed fixture is not an assertion about game behavior. A source-pattern assertion is not a browser layout failure. A command-line test can fail because stdout contains extra text even if the final state calculation is correct. Unit test guide explains these seams.

Formatting has a check mode and a write mode. The release check uses `format:check`; `format` rewrites files. If a correction changes the candidate, the affected verification applies to that corrected source, rather than to the earlier version whose checks ran first.

## Build and run the browser journeys

For named-combination evidence in a POSIX shell:

```sh
NEON_PAIRS_NAMED_COMBINATION=1 npm run test:e2e
```

The README gives the equivalent PowerShell assignment before `npm run test:e2e`. Without the flag, the runner still writes its versions, but does not require equality with the named set.

The command typechecks and builds the game, builds the art and session entries, then runs browser files serially through Node. The `&&` chain prevents a failed build from falling through to older output. The tests use fresh browser contexts and close browsers and the local server through their hooks.

Review the result in context:

- `test-results/browser-runtime.json` identifies Node, npm, Playwright and Chromium and records whether named enforcement was requested.
- Per-test directories contain only the artifacts their tests explicitly write. The face-sheet cases write PNGs; the accessibility journey writes a normalized JSON capture.
- The wrapper checks uncaught page errors after successful test bodies. A passing visible assertion should not conceal a page exception reported later by that check.
- The diagnostic `.art` and `.session` outputs are test inputs. The distributable remains `dist/index.html`.

There is no configured automatic browser retry policy or trace-on-every-failure mechanism in the local wrapper. A rerun can assist diagnosis, but an unexplained intermittent failure remains unexplained. Flaky-test notes describes the existing deterministic controls.

## Review the delivery path

The offline browser case opens the built file while network access is blocked, checks the card count and reveals a card. Its observed request list contains only the document. A separate emitted-HTML check looks for the unwanted fetch and module-preload markers.

Review those results together with the distribution specification. Inline script, styles and SVG artwork are part of the delivered file. External fonts, services or sibling asset files are not needed for play. The developer CLI and diagnostic builds are separate from that distribution.

Saved-preference evidence uses the local HTTP origin. Reload tests check the remembered size and per-size move records, while progress starts afresh. Browser-specific storage on a disk URL is not used as the persistence compatibility result. Denied storage and corrupt saved data have their own cases, preserving play when persistence is unavailable.

## Follow the acceptance journeys

Acceptance defines the journeys. The most relevant evidence groups are:

| Journey | Existing test and review evidence |
| --- | --- |
| Finish and reset | Pure completion at every size, browser keyboard/tap completion, restart during a pending miss |
| Active time | Hidden-page, idle-pause, fractional-clock and between-tick export cases |
| Reproduction | Literal board, snapshot validation and round trips, replay ordering and CLI output |
| Focus and navigation | Edge stops, remembered entry, Resume handoff, Tab exit and clipped-pointer cases |
| Difficult layouts | Largest board, visible scrollbars, equivalent zoom and readable text checks |
| Appearance | Face sheets, computed styles, matched-mark clearance and reduced motion |
| Local records | Better/equal/worse completion, saved size, reload and denied-store cases |

A complete 4x4 keyboard game also has an accessibility-tree journey. Its record names Chromium and Playwright and states whether a screen reader was used. The README currently records no screen-reader run. Spoken output and real-device long-press behavior remain user acceptance tasks under the specification.

Visual review of the 44px grayscale sheet complements automated silhouette uniqueness. The audit records what those images can establish and what still needs human judgment. See Accessibility audit before turning automated geometry into a broader accessibility claim.

## Read the limits before writing the result

The suite has no quantitative startup or input benchmark. A passing browser journey establishes behavior under its conditions, not a measured latency budget. The supported runtime floor is also different from the one exact compatibility combination recorded as tested.

The README records a successful run for its named combination. A release note should identify the candidate, executed checks and remaining acceptance evidence for the release.

Finish by stopping any development servers or watchers started for the work. The browser harness owns its own server cleanup; a separately launched Vite server is outside those hooks. Preserve the concrete test result and runtime information used for the release record. Changelog style and Browser support help describe the resulting evidence without overstating it.
# ADR 052: Use release tags as historical checkpoints

This record explains the release-tag rationale and separates product, package and data-format versions.

## Context of the decision

A game can have several meaningful versions at once. The specification identifies itself as version 2.2, the package manifest currently says 1.0.0, and board generation, snapshot and replay retain their first format versions. Treating any one of those numbers as a substitute for the others would make a report ambiguous.

The release discussion favored tags as named source checkpoints: a way to associate a delivered game and its evidence with the source that produced them.

## What a checkpoint answers

A release checkpoint helps answer “which implementation was built?” It does not answer “which board did the player receive?” A board code supplies the latter. A snapshot adds progress on that deal, and a replay adds actions. These identifiers work together because they refer to different layers.

A source tag also differs from a package version. The package is private and its scripts build the game locally. Nothing in the current manifest establishes a public registry publishing process. Describing a tag as a checkpoint avoids implying that changing the package number is itself a deployment or that every game copy is fetched from a registry.

## Why format versions remain separate

Generation version `np1` fixes the deck algorithm. Snapshot and replay objects carry `version: 1`. A release that corrects focus scrolling or copy can preserve those data meanings. Incrementing a data format simply to match a release label would make old reproducible examples harder to use without any changed representation to justify it.

Conversely, a changed generation algorithm cannot hide behind a release tag while continuing to give the same board-code prefix a different meaning. The format contract is what lets independent tools reconstruct a deal. Format versioning guide and ADR 009 explain that stability.

## Alternatives considered

Relying only on the latest branch would make older bug reports hard to associate with the source used at the time. Naming a downloaded HTML file manually could help a person but would not identify a repository checkpoint. Embedding a release service in the browser would be a much larger feature and would conflict with the independent offline artifact.

The tag rationale was therefore modest: make history pointable without turning version checking into runtime behavior. There is no update polling or in-game release selector in the current implementation. A local copy remains a local copy until someone replaces it.

## Evidence at the checkpoint

The existing commands provide locked installation, type checking, focused tests, a production build and browser journeys. The browser wrapper records actual runtime versions. These are the relevant materials for assessing a built revision; a tag by itself cannot prove that any of them ran.

The README records successful checks on the named combination. Release checklist, ADR 029 and ADR 055 explain the neighboring review concerns.

A useful release history preserves which source was intended, which behavior was specified and which evidence actually exists. Tags help with the first of those. Keeping that role narrow makes them useful even when the game is delivered as a file rather than through a continuously deployed service.

## The package identity is a separate datum

The private package version identifies the source package declaration. It is not the board-generation prefix or a claim about repository tags.

# ADR 009: Identify a deal with a board code

This record explains why a compact versioned code identifies the initial deck separately from progress.

## Context

A report such as “the second card looked wrong” is hard to investigate when a fresh shuffle changes every position. Restart also needs to mean something more precise than making another random board at the same size. The project needed a stable description of a deal that a person could copy without carrying a full list of face IDs.

The chosen code is `np1-N-seed`, with a supported side length and a decimal seed from 1 through 2147483646. `np1-4-1` is a concrete example. The prefix fixes the generation algorithm, not the product release number. Spec version 2.2 still uses this generation version.

## Decision

A board code names the starting arrangement. It contains no moves, elapsed time, matches or selected cards. `createGame` generates that arrangement and adds empty progress. Restart calls `createGame` with the current code. New Game obtains a different seed before creating its state. These two actions can therefore share construction without sharing meaning.

The parser accepts canonical decimal syntax: no leading zeros, no signs and no alternate separators. The browser control trims surrounding whitespace before parsing, while the core parser itself expects the exact code. This separation allows forgiving copy and paste at the input boundary without broadening the format accepted inside snapshots or replay files.

The seed and size regenerate a frozen board description and deck. No face list needs to be serialized into the code. That keeps the identifier short and lets independent tools reconstruct the deal using the documented algorithm. ADR 021 explains the shuffle; Board code format gives the parser details.

## Why not a URL or deck dump

A shareable URL would tie the identifier to an origin and route scheme. The playable distribution can open from disk and has no router, so a plain text code fits its delivery model better. An application can be served from many locations without changing the meaning of the deal.

A complete deck dump would be explicit but cumbersome to enter or quote. It would also create another source of disagreement if supplied alongside a seed. The current formats derive the deck from the code and validate progress against it. A photograph might show artwork, but it would not establish a canonical arrangement or allow replay to apply actions deterministically.

## Versioning cost

The compact representation is only useful if its generation contract stays stable. A seemingly harmless change to draw order, rejection sampling or the shuffle loop can change all downstream positions. That is why tests include independent literal vectors rather than merely checking that two calls to the same implementation agree.

An algorithm change would need a different generation version. A visual correction that preserves face identity is a separate question: the code specifies face IDs and order, while the design table specifies how those identities look and are named. Format versioning guide discusses this distinction.

## Limits

A code is a reproducibility tool, not a claim about how somebody played. It is easy to inspect or generate its deal outside the game. The shipped UI still keeps closed face identity out of the DOM, and tests use documented formats rather than a solver endpoint. A snapshot answers the different question of progress on a deal; see ADR 010. A replay records actions instead; see ADR 015.

## Canonical parsing and construction

The core returns null for an invalid code and the constructor checks its own output through the same parser.

```ts
export function parseBoardCode(code: string): { size: number; seed: number } | null {
  const parts = new RegExp(`^${BOARD_VERSION}-([1-9]\\d*)-([1-9]\\d*)$`).exec(code);
  if (!parts) return null;
  const size = Number(parts[1]);
  const seed = Number(parts[2]);
  return isValidSize(size) && Number.isSafeInteger(seed) && seed <= SEED_MAX
    ? { size, seed }
    : null;
}

export function boardCode(size: number, seed: number): string {
  const code = `${BOARD_VERSION}-${size}-${seed}`;
  if (!parseBoardCode(code)) throw new Error('Invalid board code.');
  return code;
}

```

item.text:
Implemented Tournament mode with 4 or 8 players, shared deals for each match, bracket results, turn and match controls, early leave, and a champion screen. Completed events are saved locally and can be exported or loaded as tournament JSON. Tournament play preserves solo preferences and best scores.

Updated the project docs, including the new [Tournament mode guide](/work/docs/tournament-mode.md). Main implementation is in [TournamentScreen.tsx](/work/src/game/tournament/TournamentScreen.tsx), with match handling in [use-tournament.ts](/work/src/game/tournament/use-tournament.ts) and history storage in [storage.ts](/work/src/game/tournament/storage.ts).

Verification passed: typecheck, 149 unit tests, all 80 browser tests, and Prettier checks for changed files.
